days.guide: Draft the remaining sections with one short quotation and its source.

questions.q: How do you include a quotation?
questions.a: Put exact words in quotation marks and name the source: According to the National Park Service, "..."

days.guide: Practice commas in series and after introductory phrases; apply to the draft.

questions.q: Add commas: 'In 1864 President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant protecting the valley and the giant sequoias.'
questions.a: 'In 1864, President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, protecting the valley and the giant sequoias.' (The comma after 1864 is the key correction.)

days.guide: Write the conclusion and a source list in a consistent format.

questions.q: Show one source entry.
questions.a: 'Yosemite National Park. National Park Service. nps.gov/yose.'

weeks.assessment_key: Draft check (4-point): 4 = hook intro, 3-4 headed sections paraphrased from notes, one cited quotation, conclusion, consistent source list of 3+ sources; 3 = all parts, minor gaps; 2 = missing sections or sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Computer, printer, images (with source credits), a blank map of California.
misconceptions: Captions that just name the picture ('Half Dome'). A good caption explains what it shows and why it matters.
Lowercasing proper nouns (sierra nevada). Names of specific places, mountains and deserts are capitalized.

days.guide: The child rereads aloud, marks confusing sentences and revises so each section begins with its main idea.

questions.q: What should the first sentence of a section do?
questions.a: State the main idea of that section.

days.guide: Edit for proper nouns, commas and spelling with a checklist and dictionary.

questions.q: Correct: 'the mojave desert is in southern california.'
questions.a: 'The Mojave Desert is in Southern California.' (southern may be lowercase as a direction; both accepted)

days.guide: Add a labeled map and two captioned images.

questions.q: Write a caption for a photo of Half Dome.
questions.a: Example: 'Half Dome rises about 4,700 feet above Yosemite Valley; glaciers helped shape its sheer face.'

days.guide: Type and print the final report with headings, visuals and source list.

questions.q: What final checks before printing?
questions.a: Headings in place, images credited, page numbers/title, source list complete, spelling checked.

days.guide: Self-assess with the rubric; write two sentences on strongest and weakest parts.

questions.q: What is a useful self-assessment sentence?
questions.a: One that names a specific part and evidence: 'My strongest part is the Glaciers section because...'

weeks.assessment_key: Research report rubric: 4 = clear focus; intro hook; 3-4 headed sections with accurate paraphrased facts; at least one cited quote; labeled map and 2 captioned images; conclusion; correct proper nouns and commas; consistent source list of 3+ credible sources. 3 = all parts, minor errors. 2 = missing visuals or sources, several errors. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Slides software or poster board, a timer, a recording device. Prepare the Unit 8 test with two short texts about the same event (one firsthand, one secondhand) — key below.
misconceptions: Reading slides word for word. Slides show key facts and pictures; the speaker explains.
Answering audience questions with guesses. Say 'I'm not sure, but my notes say...' or look it up.

days.guide: The child turns the report into 5 slides or a poster: one key fact and visual per section.

questions.q: How much text belongs on a slide?
questions.a: A title and a few key words or one fact — not paragraphs.

days.guide: Rehearse a 3-minute talk with a timer, practicing eye contact, volume and pace.

questions.q: What should you do if you finish early?
questions.a: Add an example or a fact from your notes; aim for about 3 minutes.

days.guide: Record a 30-second narrated intro or add a fitting nature sound clip.

questions.q: Why add audio?
questions.a: To engage listeners and help them imagine the place.

days.guide: Present to family and answer at least three questions with facts from notes.

questions.q: How do you answer a question well?
questions.a: Listen fully, repeat the question, answer with a specific fact, check if it answered them.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What does it mean to integrate information from two texts?
questions.a: Combine facts from both to explain a topic more completely than either text alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = organized 3-minute talk, slides/poster with key facts and visuals, eye contact, clear volume and pace, accurate answers to 3 questions; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads notes or very short; 1 = incomplete. Unit 8 test key: 1) Identify each text as firsthand or secondhand 2) Focus of the firsthand text: personal experience and feelings 3) Focus of the secondhand: facts, dates, overview 4) One piece of information only in text A, one only in text B 5) Write a paragraph integrating both (proficient: uses information from each with transition words). Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: A grade 4 passage of similar difficulty to week 1, graph paper for WCPM, reading log; end-of-year assessment with one literary and one informational passage (e.g., from ReadWorks or CommonLit, using their answer keys); library visit.
misconceptions: Thinking reading faster is always better. Fluency includes accuracy and expression.
Summary instead of reflection. A reflection explains why the book mattered to you, with scenes as evidence.

days.guide: The child reads 1 minute; compute WCPM, graph it against week 1, and celebrate growth.

questions.q: If you read 132 words with 4 errors in 1 minute, what is your WCPM?

days.guide: The child writes a one-page reflection citing two memorable scenes.

questions.q: What makes a reflection strong?
questions.a: Clear statement of why the book mattered, two specific scenes described, and the reader's feelings or lessons.

days.guide: The child gives a 2-minute book talk with a short read-aloud excerpt.

questions.q: What should a book talk avoid?
questions.a: Giving away the ending.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year reading assessment.

questions.q: What strategies help on a reading test?
questions.a: Read questions first, reread to find evidence, cross out wrong answers, check that answers are supported by the text.

days.guide: Build a summer reading list of 10 books across genres, with reasons.

questions.q: Name four genres to include.
questions.a: Examples: realistic fiction, fantasy, mystery, biography, informational, poetry, graphic novel, historical fiction.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year reading assessment: use the passage source's answer key; score literary questions (theme, character, inference, vocabulary in context, summary) and informational questions (main idea, text structure, text features, evidence). Proficient: 80%. Fluency: compare WCPM to week 1 and to grade 4 end-of-year norms (roughly 120-140 WCPM).

weeks.prep: Writing folder with all pieces from the year; a cumulative grammar test (key below); three on-demand opinion prompts (e.g., Should kids have homework? Is it better to live in a city or the country? Should every student learn an instrument?).
misconceptions: Choosing portfolio pieces only by length. Pick pieces that show your best skills and growth.
Rushing on-demand writing without planning. Spend 5 minutes planning reasons before drafting.

days.guide: The child selects the best narrative, report, opinion essay and poem and labels why each was chosen.

questions.q: What is a good reason to choose a piece?
questions.a: It shows a specific skill well (e.g., strong dialogue, well-supported reasons) or shows growth.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection letter comparing week 4's narrative with a recent piece, naming two improvements.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific improvement.
questions.a: 'In September I had no dialogue; now I punctuate dialogue correctly and use it to show feelings.'

days.guide: Give the cumulative grammar assessment.

questions.q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: 'The girl ___ bike is red lives next door.'
questions.a: whose.

questions.q: Write 'I read' in the future progressive.
questions.a: I will be reading.

days.guide: The child chooses one prompt and writes an opinion piece in 45 minutes.

questions.q: What should the first 5 minutes be used for?
questions.a: Planning: opinion, three reasons and quick evidence notes.

days.guide: Author celebration: share the portfolio and write three grade 5 goals.

questions.q: Write one specific goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will read 25 books next year, including 5 biographies.'

weeks.assessment_key: Grammar test key (sample): 1) who/whose/which/that items — The boy who...; the dog whose...; the book that/which... 2) Progressive: was walking / is walking / will be walking 3) Modals: must (necessity), may (permission), can (ability), should (advice) 4) Commas: 'I packed apples, cheese, and bread.' 'After lunch, we hiked.' 'It rained, but we played.' 5) Quotation marks: "Where are you going?" asked Dad. Proficient: 80%. On-demand writing rubric: 4 = clear opinion, 3 reasons with supporting details, linking words, conclusion, few errors; 3 = 2 reasons or some errors; 2 = weak organization; 1 = off-topic. Portfolio: complete with 4 pieces, labels and reflection letter.

HEALTH.overview: Fourth-grade health runs in short daily lessons that pair a fact with a skill: reading a label, planning and cooking a meal, tracking activity, practicing refusals. Model the skill, have the child practice with you (role-plays work best when you play the other person), then have them explain or teach it back. Units on medicines, tobacco/vaping and alcohol (weeks 21–33) should be previewed by the parent; keep the tone factual and calm, share your family's rules, and remind the child they can always come to you with questions.

weeks.prep: Set up a health journal (composition notebook) and markers. Print or write a 15-item habit checklist (e.g., slept 9+ hours, drank water, ate fruit, ate vegetables, 60 minutes of activity, brushed teeth twice, washed hands before eating, ate breakfast, limited screens, talked with a friend, helped someone, felt calm/managed stress, wore a helmet/seatbelt, read for fun, went to bed on time). Prepare the 5 quick-check questions in the key.
misconceptions: Thinking health only means not being sick or being physically fit. Health has physical, mental/emotional and social sides, and all three affect each other.
Thinking one healthy choice makes you healthy. Health comes from habits repeated over time.

days.guide: Draw a triangle and label the sides physical, mental/emotional and social. Explain each (body; thoughts and feelings; relationships). The child lists 3 habits per side.

questions.q: Name the 3 sides of the health triangle.
questions.a: Physical, mental/emotional, and social health.

questions.q: Give a habit for social health.
questions.a: E.g., spending time with friends, being kind, solving conflicts calmly, talking with family.

days.guide: The child completes the 15-item habit checklist honestly for a typical day and circles strengths. Point out one area to work on without judgment.

questions.q: Which side of the triangle does 'getting 9–12 hours of sleep' help?
questions.a: Physical health (and also mental/emotional health, because rest helps mood and focus).

days.guide: Set up the journal with a title page and date. The child writes 4–5 sentences about a healthy habit the family already has and why it helps.

questions.q: Why is a health journal useful?
questions.a: It helps you track habits and goals and notice patterns over time.

days.guide: Plan an ideal healthy day on a schedule: wake and bed times (9–12 hours of sleep), 3 meals and snacks, 60 minutes of activity, limited recreational screen time, homework and family time.

questions.q: If you go to bed at 8:30 p.m. and wake at 6:30 a.m., how much sleep do you get? Is it enough?
questions.a: 10 hours — yes, within the 9–12 hours recommended for children ages 6–12.

questions.q: How many minutes of physical activity should kids get each day?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes.

days.guide: The child explains the health triangle to family, then answers the 5 quick-check questions in the key orally or on paper.

questions.q: Feeling stressed before a test affects which side of the triangle?
questions.a: Mental/emotional health (and it can also affect physical health, like a stomachache).

weeks.assessment_key: Health triangle rubric: 4 = triangle labeled physical, mental/emotional, social with 3 accurate habits each. Quick check key: 1) Name the 3 dimensions of health — physical, mental/emotional, social. 2) Sleeping and eating vegetables belong to — physical health. 3) Talking about your feelings belongs to — mental/emotional health. 4) Playing a game fairly with friends belongs to — social health. 5) How much sleep do 9-year-olds need? — 9–12 hours. Proficient = triangle complete and 4 of 5 correct.

weeks.prep: Make a decision-making worksheet with the 5 steps: Stop, Think of options, Consider consequences (healthy? safe? legal? respectful? family rules?), Choose, Check (how did it go?). Prepare 3 scenario cards and a 2-week tracking chart template.
misconceptions: Thinking a goal like 'eat better' is enough. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound so you can tell if you met them.
Skipping the 'Check' step. Reflecting after a decision helps you make better choices next time.

days.guide: Teach the 5 steps with hand motions. Apply them together to choosing a snack (chips, apple with peanut butter, cookies, yogurt): list options, consider consequences, choose and explain.

questions.q: What are the 5 decision-making steps?
questions.a: Stop, Think of options, Consider consequences, Choose, Check.

questions.q: What questions help you consider consequences?
questions.a: Is it healthy? Safe? Legal? Respectful? Does it follow family rules? How will I feel later?

days.guide: Work through 3 scenarios with the model: skipping breakfast because you're late, choosing between two after-school activities, and someone at a party offers you a drink you don't recognize.

questions.q: At a party someone offers you an unknown drink. What is a healthy decision?
questions.a: Say no thanks, choose a drink you know is safe (like water or one from a trusted adult), and tell a trusted adult if it seems unsafe.

questions.q: What's a better option than skipping breakfast when you're late?
questions.a: Grab a quick healthy breakfast like a banana and a cheese stick, or yogurt, or whole-grain toast to eat on the way.

days.guide: Teach SMART. The child rewrites 4 vague goals: 'eat better,' 'be more active,' 'drink more water,' 'sleep more.'

questions.q: Rewrite 'drink more water' as a SMART goal.
questions.a: E.g., 'I will drink 5 cups of water every day for the next 2 weeks and track it on my chart.'

questions.q: What does the T in SMART stand for?
questions.a: Time-bound — the goal has a deadline or time frame.

days.guide: The child writes a personal 2-week SMART goal for eating or activity and makes a 14-day tracking chart.

questions.q: How will you know if you met your goal?
questions.a: The chart shows checkmarks or numbers each day that can be compared to the goal.

days.guide: The child explains the decision steps to a parent using a real choice they made today.

questions.q: Walk me through a real choice you made using the steps.
questions.a: The child names the situation, at least 2 options, consequences, the choice and how it turned out.

weeks.assessment_key: SMART goal and tracking chart rubric: 4 = goal is Specific (what), Measurable (number), Achievable, Relevant to eating/activity, Time-bound (2 weeks), e.g., 'I will eat 1 vegetable at lunch and dinner every day for 2 weeks'; chart has 14 days and a way to record; 3 = missing one SMART part; 2 = vague goal or no chart; 1 = no goal.

weeks.prep: Paper for a hand tracing, phone numbers for trusted adults. Find a health product ad (e.g., a supplement or 'miracle' snack ad) and a KidsHealth (kidshealth.org/kids) article on a related topic. Write the Poison Control number 1-800-222-1222 on a card.
misconceptions: Thinking anything online that looks professional is reliable. Check who wrote it, why (to inform or to sell), when it was updated, and whether it uses evidence.
Thinking you should handle health worries alone. Trusted adults and health helpers are there to help.

days.guide: Trace the child's hand. On each finger write a trusted adult (parent, grandparent, teacher, doctor, coach, neighbor) and how to reach them.

questions.q: What makes an adult 'trusted'?
questions.a: They are caring and responsible, keep you safe, listen, and help you get what you need.

questions.q: Who could you ask if a parent isn't available?
questions.a: Another trusted adult from your hand, e.g., a grandparent, teacher, school nurse or doctor.

days.guide: Compare the ad and the KidsHealth article. List clues: author/organization, purpose (inform vs. sell), date, evidence, exaggerated claims ('cures everything').

questions.q: Name 3 clues that a health source is reliable.
questions.a: Written by experts or a trusted health organization (.gov, .edu, hospitals), up to date, shows evidence, aims to inform rather than sell, no 'miracle' claims.

questions.q: Why is an ad less reliable than a health article?
questions.a: The ad's goal is to sell, so it may exaggerate or leave out facts.

days.guide: Role-play asking a trusted adult a health question: get their attention, say what's going on, ask clearly, and keep asking someone else if the first adult can't help.

questions.q: What should you do if the first adult you ask doesn't help?
questions.a: Keep telling other trusted adults until someone helps.

days.guide: Identify community health helpers and their roles: school nurse, pharmacist (explains medicines), doctor, dentist, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222), 911 for emergencies.

questions.q: What is the Poison Control phone number?
When do you call 911 instead?
questions.a: In a life-threatening emergency, like someone not breathing, unconscious, a fire, or serious injury.

days.guide: Quiz (see key) and a quick check of the SMART goal tracker.

questions.q: A website selling vitamins says they 'cure all illnesses.' Reliable?
questions.a: No — it is trying to sell and makes an exaggerated claim without evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Trusted adult tracing: 5 trusted adults with contact info. Quiz key: 1) Name a reliable source of health information — e.g., a doctor, school nurse, KidsHealth, CDC, MyPlate.gov. 2) What is the main purpose of an ad? — to sell a product. 3) Poison Control number — 1-800-222-1222. 4) Who explains how to take medicine safely at the pharmacy? — the pharmacist. 5) What do you do if a trusted adult can't help? — tell another trusted adult. Proficient = tracing complete and 4 of 5 correct.

weeks.prep: Collect food packages (bread, cereal, peanut butter, cheese, crackers, oil) and pictures of foods; chart paper. Have a white bread and a 100% whole-wheat bread label.
misconceptions: Thinking all fat is bad. The body needs some fat; unsaturated fats (avocados, nuts, olive oil, fish) are healthier choices than lots of saturated fat and fried foods.
Thinking carbohydrates are only sugar. Carbs include sugars, starches and fiber; whole grains, fruits and vegetables are healthy carb sources.

days.guide: Teach the jobs: carbohydrates = main energy source; proteins = build and repair muscles, skin and other tissues; fats = stored energy, help absorb some vitamins, protect organs and keep you warm. Make a 3-column chart with jobs and example foods.

questions.q: What is the main job of carbohydrates?
questions.a: To give the body (and brain) energy.

questions.q: What is the job of protein?
questions.a: To build and repair muscles, skin and other body tissues.

days.guide: Sort 20 foods by main macronutrient: carbs (bread, rice, pasta, fruit, potatoes, oatmeal), protein (chicken, fish, eggs, beans, tofu), fats (butter, oil, avocado, nuts — note nuts also have protein).

questions.q: Which macronutrient is rice mainly?
questions.a: Carbohydrate.

questions.q: Which macronutrient are eggs mainly?
questions.a: Protein (they also have some fat).

days.guide: Compare the two bread labels: whole wheat lists 'whole wheat flour' first and has more fiber. Explain fiber slows digestion, so energy lasts longer and you feel full.

questions.q: Why do whole grains give longer-lasting energy?
questions.a: They keep the bran and germ, which have fiber; fiber slows digestion so energy is released slowly and you stay full longer.

questions.q: How can you tell bread is whole grain on the label?
questions.a: The first ingredient says 'whole' (e.g., whole wheat flour).

days.guide: Compare healthy fats (avocado, nuts, olive oil, fish — mostly unsaturated) with fats in fried foods and many baked snacks (more saturated and sometimes trans fats).

questions.q: Which is a healthier fat source: avocado or french fries?
questions.a: Avocado — it has unsaturated fat and nutrients; fries are fried and high in less healthy fat and salt.

days.guide: Quiz: match carbs/proteins/fats to their jobs and to 10 foods (see key).

questions.q: Which macronutrient protects organs and helps absorb some vitamins?
questions.a: Fat.

weeks.assessment_key: Macronutrient quiz key: Jobs — carbohydrates: main energy source; proteins: build and repair body tissues; fats: stored energy, protect organs, help absorb vitamins A, D, E, K. Foods — 1) bread: carbohydrate 2) chicken: protein 3) olive oil: fat 4) banana: carbohydrate 5) beans: protein (also carbs/fiber) 6) butter: fat 7) pasta: carbohydrate 8) fish: protein 9) avocado: fat 10) oatmeal: carbohydrate. Proficient = 11 of 13.

weeks.prep: Measuring teaspoons, clear cups, sugar, and labels from a 12-oz soda, a juice drink and a 20-oz sports drink. Key fact: 4 grams of sugar = about 1 teaspoon. Use KidsHealth or MyPlate for vitamin/mineral research.
misconceptions: Thinking juice drinks and sports drinks are healthy because they have fruit pictures or are for athletes. Many have as much sugar as soda; water is best for everyday thirst.
Thinking you only need water when you feel thirsty. Drink water throughout the day, especially when active or hot.

days.guide: Research one vitamin and one mineral. Example: vitamin C (citrus, strawberries, peppers; helps heal wounds and fight infection) and calcium (milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy milk, leafy greens; builds strong bones and teeth).

questions.q: What does vitamin C do, and where do you get it?
questions.a: It helps heal cuts, keeps gums healthy and helps fight infections; found in oranges, strawberries, kiwi, bell peppers and broccoli.

questions.q: What does calcium do?
questions.a: It builds strong bones and teeth (and helps muscles and nerves work).

days.guide: Explain water's jobs: cools the body through sweat, carries nutrients, removes waste, cushions joints. Track water cups for one day.

questions.q: How does water help control body temperature?
questions.a: When you get hot you sweat; as sweat evaporates from the skin it cools you down.

days.guide: Read grams of sugar on each label and divide by 4 to get teaspoons. Measure that many teaspoons into clear cups.

questions.q: A 12-oz soda has 39 g of sugar. About how many teaspoons is that?
questions.a: 39 ÷ 4 ≈ 9¾, about 10 teaspoons.

questions.q: A sports drink has 34 g of sugar. About how many teaspoons?
questions.a: 34 ÷ 4 = 8½ teaspoons.

days.guide: Make a chart of 6 drink swaps with teaspoons of sugar saved (e.g., soda 10 tsp → sparkling water with lemon 0 tsp = 10 tsp saved; chocolate milk → plain milk saves the added sugar).

questions.q: If you swap a 39 g soda for water, how many teaspoons of sugar do you save?
questions.a: About 10 teaspoons (39 ÷ 4 ≈ 9.75).

days.guide: The child writes 3 reasons water is the best drink choice.

questions.q: Give 3 reasons water is the best drink.
questions.a: It has no sugar or calories, it is what the body needs to cool down and carry nutrients, it doesn't harm teeth, and it's usually free.

weeks.assessment_key: Sugar-in-drinks chart: proficient chart lists each drink, grams of sugar from the label, and teaspoons calculated by dividing by 4 (e.g., 39 g soda ≈ 10 tsp; 34 g sports drink ≈ 8½ tsp; juice drink: label g ÷ 4), with sugar measured into cups. Paragraph rubric: 4 = 3 accurate reasons water is best plus evidence from the chart; 3 = 2 reasons; 2 = 1 reason; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Paper plate, markers, the MyPlate Kids poster (myplate.gov), magazines, scissors, glue, measuring cups, a cereal bowl, cereal, milk and fruit.
misconceptions: Thinking each group gets an equal quarter. Fruits and vegetables fill half the plate (vegetables a bit more than fruits); grains a bit more than protein; dairy on the side.
Thinking a portion is whatever fits in the bowl. Measure servings sometimes to learn what a cup or ounce looks like.

days.guide: Label a paper plate: vegetables (largest section), fruits, grains, protein, with dairy as a cup on the side.

questions.q: Which two groups fill half the plate?
questions.a: Fruits and vegetables.

questions.q: Which section is the largest?
questions.a: Vegetables.

days.guide: Cut magazine pictures and glue them into the correct food group sections.

questions.q: Which group does yogurt belong to?
questions.a: Dairy.

questions.q: Which group do beans belong to?
questions.a: Protein (they can also count as vegetables).

days.guide: Pour cereal into a bowl as usual, then measure it; compare to the serving on the box (often about 1 cup). Do the same with milk (1 cup) and fruit.

questions.q: You poured 2 cups of cereal and the serving size is 1 cup. How many servings did you pour?
questions.a: 2 servings.

days.guide: Identify food groups in tamales (masa = grains, meat or beans = protein, cheese = dairy, chile sauce = vegetables), stir-fry (vegetables, protein like chicken or tofu, rice = grains), pasta (grains, tomato sauce = vegetables, cheese = dairy, meatballs = protein).

questions.q: Which food group is the masa in a tamale?
questions.a: Grains (corn).

questions.q: What food groups are in vegetable stir-fry with tofu over rice?
questions.a: Vegetables, protein (tofu) and grains (rice).

days.guide: Quiz (see key).

questions.q: At least how much of your grains should be whole grains?
questions.a: At least half.

weeks.assessment_key: MyPlate quiz key: 1) Name the 5 food groups — fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 2) Which groups make up half the plate? — fruits and vegetables (more vegetables). 3) Give 2 examples of grains — e.g., brown rice, oatmeal, whole-wheat bread, tortillas, pasta. 4) Give 2 examples of protein — e.g., chicken, fish, eggs, beans, nuts, tofu. 5) Give 2 dairy foods — milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy milk. 6) Where does dairy go on MyPlate? — the cup on the side. 7) How much of your grains should be whole? — at least half. Proficient = 6 of 7.

weeks.prep: Breakfast ingredients (e.g., whole-grain toast, eggs, fruit, yogurt, oatmeal), a 3-day rainbow tracker (red, orange, yellow, green, blue/purple, white/tan), and 3 new fruits or vegetables to taste (e.g., kiwi, jicama, purple cabbage).
misconceptions: Thinking breakfast doesn't matter if you're not hungry. Breakfast refuels the brain and body after a night without food and helps focus and energy.
Thinking all fruits and vegetables have the same nutrients. Different colors have different vitamins, minerals and plant nutrients, so eat a variety.

days.guide: Read about breakfast and the brain (KidsHealth). The child lists 5 quick healthy breakfasts with at least 2–3 food groups each.

questions.q: Why is breakfast called 'brain fuel'?
questions.a: After sleeping all night, the brain and body need energy (glucose) from food to focus, think and have energy.

questions.q: Give one quick healthy breakfast and its food groups.
questions.a: E.g., oatmeal with berries and milk = grains, fruit, dairy.

days.guide: The child prepares a breakfast with 3 food groups (with adult help for the stove).

questions.q: Name the food groups in your breakfast.
questions.a: Answers vary; must name 3 correct groups, e.g., egg (protein), toast (grains), orange slices (fruit).

days.guide: Start a 3-day rainbow tracker: color in a box for each color of fruit or vegetable eaten.

questions.q: Why 'eat the rainbow'?
questions.a: Different colored fruits and vegetables give different vitamins, minerals and nutrients.

days.guide: Taste 3 new fruits or vegetables. Rate each 1–5 and describe taste and texture.

questions.q: Why try a new food more than once?
questions.a: Taste can change; it often takes several tries to like a new food.

days.guide: Write a paragraph about the benefits of breakfast and fruits and vegetables, using the tracker as evidence.

questions.q: Name 2 benefits of eating fruits and vegetables.
questions.a: They give vitamins, minerals and fiber; they help digestion, help fight illness, and lower the risk of diseases later.

weeks.assessment_key: Rainbow tracker and paragraph rubric: 4 = tracker completed 3 days with colors recorded; paragraph has a topic sentence, 2+ breakfast benefits (energy, focus) and 2+ fruit/vegetable benefits (vitamins, fiber, health), and evidence from the tracker; 3 = tracker mostly complete, paragraph with 3 benefits; 2 = 1–2 benefits; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print a 3-day food log (columns: time, food/drink, amount, food group) with an activity-minutes row. MyPlate daily amounts for ages 9–13 (moderately active): about 2 cups vegetables (girls) to 2½ cups (boys), 1½ cups fruit, 5–6 oz grains, 5 oz protein, 3 cups dairy — check myplate.gov/myplate-plan for your child.
misconceptions: Forgetting drinks, snacks and sauces in the log. Everything eaten and drunk counts.
Counting mixed foods as only one group. A burrito can count for grains, protein, vegetables and dairy.

days.guide: Model logging breakfast. The child records everything eaten and drunk today with amounts and food groups.

questions.q: Why include amounts in a food log?
questions.a: To compare how much you ate from each group with the recommended amounts.

days.guide: Continue logging and add minutes of activity.

questions.q: A turkey and cheese sandwich on whole-wheat bread with lettuce counts for which groups?
questions.a: Grains, protein, dairy and vegetables.

days.guide: Log a third day including a weekend meal. Total servings (cups/ounces) per group for each day.

questions.q: Why include a weekend day?
questions.a: Eating patterns are often different on weekends, so it gives a truer picture.

days.guide: Compare totals to MyPlate recommendations. Identify one group to increase and plan how.

questions.q: Your log shows 1 cup of vegetables a day and the goal is about 2 cups. What could you change?
questions.a: Add about 1 more cup a day, e.g., carrot sticks at lunch and a salad or broccoli at dinner.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test (see key).

questions.q: What is 1 teaspoon of sugar in grams?
questions.a: About 4 grams.

weeks.assessment_key: Food log analysis: proficient = 3 complete days with amounts and groups, totals for each group, comparison to MyPlate, and one group to increase with specific foods. Unit 2 test key: 1) Main job of carbohydrates — energy. 2) Main job of protein — build and repair tissues. 3) A healthy fat source — avocado, nuts, olive oil or fish. 4) Why whole grains — fiber, longer-lasting energy. 5) A food high in calcium — milk, yogurt, cheese. 6) A food high in vitamin C — orange, strawberry, bell pepper. 7) Best everyday drink — water. 8) 40 g of sugar ≈ how many teaspoons — 10. 9) The 5 food groups — fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 10) What fills half the plate — fruits and vegetables. Proficient = 8 of 10.

weeks.prep: Collect 5 food packages with Nutrition Facts labels (cereal, crackers, granola bar, chips, yogurt) and a highlighter. Print a blank Nutrition Facts panel (FDA website). Prepare a new package for Friday's quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking the calories listed are for the whole package. Label numbers are per serving; check servings per container.
Thinking a high % Daily Value is always bad. High (20%+) is good for fiber, vitamins, calcium and iron; low (5% or less) is better for sodium, saturated fat and added sugars.

days.guide: Label a printed panel: serving size, servings per container, calories, total fat, saturated fat, sodium, total carbohydrate, dietary fiber, added sugars, protein, % Daily Value.

questions.q: Where do you look first on a Nutrition Facts label?
questions.a: The serving size and servings per container.

questions.q: What does % Daily Value tell you?
questions.a: How much of a day's recommended amount of a nutrient one serving gives (based on a 2,000-calorie diet).

days.guide: For 3 snacks, compare serving size to the whole package. Calculate servings and total calories.

questions.q: A bag of chips has 2.5 servings and 150 calories per serving. How many calories in the whole bag?
questions.a: 2.5 × 150 = 375 calories.

questions.q: A box has 12 servings of 1 cup. How many cups in the box?
questions.a: 12 cups.

days.guide: Teach the 5/20 rule. On 3 labels, mark nutrients as low (5% DV or less) or high (20% DV or more).

questions.q: Sodium is 25% DV. Is that high or low?
questions.a: High (20% or more).

questions.q: Fiber is 3% DV. Is that high or low?
questions.a: Low (5% or less) — you'd want more fiber.

days.guide: Find the cereal or snack in the pantry with the most fiber and the least added sugar; record the grams.

questions.q: Which is the better choice: cereal A (5 g fiber, 4 g added sugar) or cereal B (1 g fiber, 12 g added sugar)?
questions.a: Cereal A — more fiber and less added sugar.

days.guide: Quiz using a new package (see key, adapt numbers to the package).

questions.q: If you eat 2 servings, how does that change the numbers?
questions.a: Everything doubles (calories, sugar, sodium, etc.).

weeks.assessment_key: Label-reading quiz (use any package; adapt answers to its label): 1) What is the serving size? — read from label. 2) How many servings in the package? — read from label. 3) Calories per serving and for the whole package — calories × servings. 4) Is sodium high or low by the 5/20 rule? — ≤5% low, ≥20% high. 5) How many grams of added sugars, and about how many teaspoons? — grams ÷ 4. 6) Name one nutrient you want a high %DV for — fiber, calcium, iron, vitamin D or potassium. Proficient = 5 of 6 correct.

weeks.prep: An apple, a cup of applesauce (preferably unsweetened plus a sweetened label if available) and an apple-flavored fruit snack package; 4 snack options for the decision; labels for chips, pretzels, popcorn and nuts; ingredients for a snack (veggies and hummus or yogurt, fruit and granola).
misconceptions: Thinking 'made with real fruit' means the snack is as healthy as fruit. Fruit snacks are mostly sugar and lack the fiber and vitamins of whole fruit.
Thinking only salty-tasting foods are high in sodium. Pretzels, bread, cheese and many processed foods are high in sodium.

days.guide: Compare the apple, applesauce and fruit snack. Rank by nutrients (fiber, vitamins, added sugar). Explain 'whole' vs. 'processed.'

questions.q: Which is most nutrient-dense: an apple, applesauce or apple fruit snacks? Why?
questions.a: The whole apple — it has the most fiber and vitamins and no added sugar; fruit snacks are mostly added sugar.

questions.q: What does 'processed' mean?
questions.a: Changed from its natural form by cooking, adding ingredients, or packaging; heavily processed foods often have added sugar, salt or fat.

days.guide: Use the decision model to choose from 4 after-school snacks (e.g., cookies, cheese and crackers, chips, apple with peanut butter). The child explains the choice.

questions.q: Which snack gives lasting energy: apple with peanut butter or cookies? Why?
questions.a: Apple with peanut butter — fiber from the apple and protein/healthy fat from peanut butter keep you full longer; cookies are mostly sugar.

days.guide: Record sodium per serving for chips, pretzels, popcorn and nuts and make a bar graph. Note daily limit for kids is roughly 1,800–2,300 mg.

questions.q: Pretzels have 450 mg sodium per serving and unsalted nuts have 0 mg. How much more sodium do the pretzels have?
questions.a: 450 mg more.

questions.q: Why limit sodium?
questions.a: Too much sodium over time can raise blood pressure and harm the heart.

days.guide: Prepare a nutrient-dense snack and list its food groups.

questions.q: What does 'nutrient-dense' mean?
questions.a: A food with lots of nutrients (vitamins, minerals, fiber, protein) for its calories.

days.guide: The child writes a 'Snack Smart' guide with 5 tips and 5 snack ideas.

questions.q: Give a Snack Smart tip.
questions.a: E.g., combine two food groups; choose whole foods; check the label for added sugar and sodium; drink water; portion out snacks instead of eating from the bag.

weeks.assessment_key: Snack Smart guide rubric: 4 = 5 accurate tips (e.g., pair 2 food groups, choose whole over processed, use the 5/20 rule for sodium and added sugar, portion snacks, drink water) and 5 nutrient-dense snack ideas with food groups named; neat and clear; 3 = 4 tips/ideas; 2 = 2–3; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Cereal boxes (one sugary, kid-marketed) and 3 food ads you have previewed (YouTube or recorded TV). Poster paper or an empty cereal box for the ad design.
misconceptions: Thinking ads just give information. Food ads are designed to make you want the product, often using fun, prizes or characters rather than nutrition facts.
Thinking 'part of a complete breakfast' means the cereal is complete. The phrase usually means it's eaten alongside other foods like milk and fruit.

days.guide: Watch 3 food ads. Record techniques: cartoons/characters, prizes or toys, celebrities, catchy songs, 'everyone has it' (bandwagon), fun/excitement, health claims.

questions.q: Name 3 advertising techniques aimed at kids.
questions.a: Any 3: cartoon characters, prizes/toys, celebrities, catchy jingles, bandwagon, bright colors, health claims, 'limited time.'

days.guide: Compare the front of the sugary cereal box (claims like 'good source of vitamin D,' characters, games) with its Nutrition Facts (added sugars per serving).

questions.q: What might the front of a cereal box leave out?
questions.a: How much added sugar it has, the small serving size, or low fiber.

days.guide: Make a web with 'My food choices' in the center and branches: family, culture, friends, media/ads, cost, taste, convenience. Give an example for each.

questions.q: Give an example of how culture influences food choices.
questions.a: E.g., a family eats tamales at holidays or rice with most meals because of their cultural traditions.

days.guide: Design a cereal box or poster for a healthy food using ad techniques honestly (true claims, an appealing character).

questions.q: How can you use an ad technique honestly?
questions.a: Use attractive design and true facts (e.g., 'high in fiber' only if it's 20% DV or more) without exaggerating.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on how ads influence kids and 3 critical-thinking questions to ask.

questions.q: What questions should you ask about an ad?
questions.a: Who made it and why? What are they trying to sell? What techniques are used? What's left out? What does the label say?

weeks.assessment_key: Healthy ad and paragraph rubric: 4 = ad promotes a healthy food using at least 2 techniques with only true claims; paragraph names at least 3 techniques, explains that ads aim to sell, and gives critical questions to ask; 3 = 2 techniques, basic paragraph; 2 = ad makes false claims or paragraph vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Health journal, a family recipe and the family cook's time for an interview. Prepare 3 role-play situations (restaurant, friend's house, grocery store). Prepare the Unit 3 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking asking for healthy food means complaining about family food. Use respectful I-messages and offer to help.
Thinking traditional dishes can't be healthy. Most traditional foods contain several food groups and can be adjusted with small changes.

days.guide: Teach the I-message formula: 'I feel ___ when ___. Could we ___?' Practice 3 I-messages asking for healthy foods.

questions.q: What are the parts of an I-message?
questions.a: I feel (feeling) when (situation); could we (request)?

questions.q: Turn 'We never have good snacks!' into an I-message.
questions.a: E.g., 'I feel hungry after school when there's only chips; could we buy apples or yogurt?'

days.guide: Role-play asking for a healthy option at a restaurant (water instead of soda, fruit instead of fries), at a friend's house (politely asking for water), and at the grocery store (asking to buy a new vegetable).

questions.q: How could you politely ask for a healthier side at a restaurant?
questions.a: E.g., 'May I please have the fruit cup instead of fries?'

days.guide: Interview a family member about a traditional family dish: its history, ingredients, and when it's eaten. Identify the food groups.

questions.q: Name a good interview question about a family dish.
questions.a: E.g., 'Who taught you to make it?' or 'When does our family eat it?'

days.guide: Suggest one healthy twist (more vegetables, whole grains, baking instead of frying, less salt) and discuss respectfully with the cook.

questions.q: Give an example of a healthy twist.
questions.a: E.g., use brown rice instead of white, add spinach, or bake instead of fry.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test (see key).

questions.q: What does the 5/20 rule say?
questions.a: 5% DV or less of a nutrient is low; 20% DV or more is high.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) What should you check first on a label? — serving size and servings per container. 2) 2 servings at 120 calories each = 240 calories. 3) 5/20 rule: 5% DV or less is low; 20% or more is high. 4) Is 30% DV sodium high or low? — high. 5) Name 2 ad techniques — e.g., cartoon characters, prizes, celebrities, jingles. 6) Name 3 influences on food choices — family, culture, friends, media, cost, taste. 7) Write an I-message asking for a healthy food — must include feeling, situation and request. 8) Why is a whole apple better than fruit snacks? — more fiber and vitamins, no added sugar. Proficient = 6 of 8. Family interview: complete with dish, ingredients, food groups and one healthy twist.

weeks.prep: MyPlate template, 3 sample dinner menus (e.g., spaghetti with garlic bread; chicken nuggets and fries; tacos with beans, lettuce, cheese and salsa), a local grocery flyer or online store prices, calculator.
misconceptions: Thinking a meal must be expensive to be healthy. Beans, eggs, rice, oats, frozen vegetables and seasonal produce are healthy and affordable.
Forgetting fruit, vegetables or dairy in a meal plan. Check the plan against all 5 groups.

days.guide: Analyze 3 sample dinners: list the food groups present and missing in each.

questions.q: Chicken nuggets and fries: which groups are missing?
questions.a: Fruits, vegetables (fries are mostly starch and fried) and dairy; it's also low in whole grains.

questions.q: Spaghetti with meat sauce and garlic bread: what is missing?
questions.a: Fruit and dairy (and more vegetables would help).

days.guide: Plan a family dinner with all 5 food groups (e.g., bean and chicken tacos on corn tortillas, lettuce and tomato, cheese, a side of mango, milk).

questions.q: Check your dinner: name a food for each of the 5 groups.
questions.a: The child names one food for each of fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy.

days.guide: Price each ingredient from the flyer and total the cost. Stay within $20.

questions.q: Chicken $6.50, tortillas $2.25, beans $1.20, lettuce $1.80, cheese $3.50, mangoes $2.00. Total? Under $20?

days.guide: Plan two healthy snacks for the week, each combining two food groups.

questions.q: Why combine two food groups in a snack?
questions.a: It adds more nutrients and staying power, e.g., fiber plus protein keeps you full longer.

days.guide: Present the menu and budget to family and explain how it follows MyPlate.

questions.q: How does your plan follow MyPlate?
questions.a: It includes all 5 groups with half the plate fruits and vegetables and whole grains when possible.

weeks.assessment_key: Meal plan with budget rubric: 4 = dinner includes all 5 food groups with half the plate fruits/vegetables, ingredients priced correctly with an accurate total at or under $20, two snacks each with 2 food groups, and a clear MyPlate explanation; 3 = one small error; 2 = missing a food group or total over budget; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: The week 13 meal plan and shopping list, a simple recipe, measuring cups and spoons, cutting board, a child-appropriate knife (adult supervision always), colander. Review hot-surface and knife safety first.
misconceptions: Thinking you need soap to wash produce. Rinse fruits and vegetables under cool running water (rub or scrub firm produce); do not use soap or bleach.
Holding food with flat fingers while cutting. Use the 'claw grip' — fingertips curled under, knuckles guiding the knife.

days.guide: Teach kitchen safety: wash hands 20 seconds, tie back hair, adult supervises knives and stove, turn pot handles inward, use oven mitts, wipe spills right away.

questions.q: Why turn pot handles toward the back of the stove?
questions.a: So no one bumps them and spills hot food.

questions.q: How long should you wash hands with soap before cooking?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds.

days.guide: Shop for the meal (in person or online) and read labels to choose items (e.g., whole-grain tortillas, low-sodium beans).

questions.q: Two cans of beans: 480 mg sodium vs. 140 mg sodium per serving. Which do you choose?
questions.a: The 140 mg (low-sodium) can.

days.guide: Wash produce under running water. With supervision, practice the claw grip on soft foods (cucumber, banana).

questions.q: What is the claw grip?
questions.a: Curling your fingertips under and holding food with your knuckles forward so the knife can't cut your fingertips.

days.guide: Cook the dinner with an adult, measuring ingredients carefully.

questions.q: How do you measure 1 cup of flour accurately?
questions.a: Spoon it into the cup and level it off with a straight edge.

days.guide: Write a reflection on the meal's food groups and taste.

questions.q: What food groups were in your meal?
questions.a: Answers must correctly list the groups in the cooked meal.

weeks.assessment_key: Cooked meal and reflection rubric: 4 = follows all safety rules (handwashing, claw grip, adult supervision), helps shop using labels, measures correctly, cooks the planned meal, and reflection lists the correct food groups and an honest taste review with one change for next time; 3 = minor reminders needed; 2 = several reminders or reflection incomplete; 1 = minimal participation.

weeks.prep: Glitter (or lotion with cinnamon) to model germs, soap, an instant-read food thermometer, a refrigerator thermometer. Safe cooking temperatures (USDA): poultry 165°F; ground beef and pork 160°F; whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb 145°F with a 3-minute rest; fish 145°F; leftovers reheat to 165°F. Refrigerator 40°F or below; freezer 0°F.
misconceptions: Thinking you can tell if meat is done by color. Use a food thermometer; color isn't reliable.
Leaving leftovers out to cool before refrigerating. Refrigerate within 2 hours (1 hour if it's above 90°F).

days.guide: Put glitter on the child's hands, have them touch objects, and see how 'germs' spread. Practice 20-second handwashing: wet, lather (backs, between fingers, under nails), scrub 20 seconds, rinse, dry.

questions.q: When should you wash your hands in the kitchen?
questions.a: Before cooking and eating, after touching raw meat, eggs or poultry, after using the bathroom, and after touching trash or pets.

days.guide: Explain cross-contamination. Use separate cutting boards for raw meat and produce; store raw meat on the bottom shelf in a sealed container. Sort grocery items for safe storage.

questions.q: Why store raw meat on the bottom shelf?
questions.a: So its juices can't drip onto ready-to-eat foods and spread bacteria.

questions.q: What is cross-contamination?
questions.a: When germs spread from one food or surface (like raw chicken) to another food that won't be cooked.

days.guide: Learn safe internal temperatures. With an adult, insert a thermometer into the thickest part of cooked food and read it.

questions.q: What is the safe temperature for chicken?
Where do you put the thermometer?
questions.a: In the thickest part of the food, not touching bone.

days.guide: Check the refrigerator temperature (40°F or below). Learn leftovers rules: refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3–4 days; reheat to 165°F.

questions.q: What temperature should a refrigerator be?
questions.a: 40°F or below.

questions.q: How long can leftovers stay at room temperature?
questions.a: No more than 2 hours (1 hour if above 90°F).

days.guide: Make a Clean–Separate–Cook–Chill poster with one rule and picture for each.

questions.q: Name the 4 food safety steps.
questions.a: Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill.

weeks.assessment_key: Food safety poster rubric: 4 = all 4 steps with an accurate rule each — Clean (wash hands 20 seconds and surfaces), Separate (raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods, separate boards), Cook (use a thermometer; chicken 165°F, ground beef 160°F), Chill (refrigerate within 2 hours; fridge 40°F or below) — clear pictures; 3 = all 4 steps, one rule vague; 2 = 2–3 steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A restaurant kids' menu and a fast-food restaurant's online nutrition information. Conversation question cards for a family meal. Prepare the Unit 4 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking restaurant portions are single servings. Many restaurant portions are 2–3 MyPlate servings; share, box half, or order smaller sizes.
Thinking every fast-food choice is equally unhealthy. Grilled options, fruit sides, water or milk, and smaller sizes are better choices.

days.guide: Read the kids' menu and choose a balanced meal and drink that covers at least 3–4 food groups.

questions.q: Which drink is the best choice on a kids' menu?
questions.a: Water or low-fat/plain milk.

days.guide: Compare restaurant portions with MyPlate amounts (e.g., a large plate of pasta may be 3–4 cups, many servings of grains).

questions.q: A restaurant pasta dish is 3 cups and the grain serving is about ½ cup cooked pasta (1 oz). How many ounce-equivalents is that?
questions.a: 3 cups = 6 half-cups, so 6 ounce-equivalents of grains — more than a whole day for many kids.

questions.q: What can you do with a large restaurant portion?
questions.a: Share it, eat half and take the rest home, or order a smaller size.

days.guide: Use online nutrition info to find 3 swaps (grilled instead of fried chicken, apple slices instead of fries, water instead of soda) and note the differences.

questions.q: Why is grilled chicken a healthier swap than fried?
questions.a: It has less fat and fewer calories because it isn't breaded and cooked in oil.

days.guide: Plan a screen-free family meal with 5 conversation questions.

questions.q: Name 2 benefits of family meals.
questions.a: Family connection and conversation, healthier eating, better manners and communication skills.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test (see key).

questions.q: What are the 4 food safety steps?
questions.a: Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) Name the 4 food safety steps — Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill. 2) How long to wash hands — 20 seconds. 3) Safe temperature for chicken — 165°F. 4) Refrigerator temperature — 40°F or below. 5) Leftovers must be refrigerated within — 2 hours. 6) Plan a dinner with all 5 food groups — any meal with one food from each group. 7) Name a healthy restaurant swap — e.g., water for soda, fruit for fries, grilled for fried. 8) Knife safety grip — claw grip. 9) Why use separate cutting boards — prevent cross-contamination from raw meat. 10) One way to handle a large restaurant portion — share it or take half home. Proficient = 8 of 10.

weeks.prep: Stopwatch, health journal, a safe area for jumping and walking. CDC guideline: kids 6–17 need 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous aerobic, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days a week each.
misconceptions: Thinking activity only helps the body. It also improves mood, sleep, focus and friendships.
Thinking only sports count. Walking, dancing, biking, playing tag and chores like raking all count.

days.guide: Make a 3-column list: physical benefits (strong heart, muscles, bones, healthy weight, better sleep), mental benefits (better mood, less stress, better focus), social benefits (friends, teamwork).

questions.q: Name one physical, one mental and one social benefit of activity.
questions.a: Physical: stronger heart/muscles/bones. Mental: better mood, less stress. Social: making friends, teamwork.

days.guide: Sort activities: aerobic (running, biking, swimming), muscle-strengthening (climbing, push-ups, tug-of-war), bone-strengthening (jumping rope, hopscotch, running). Note some fit more than one.

questions.q: Is jumping rope aerobic, bone-strengthening or both?
questions.a: Both — it gets your heart pumping and the impact strengthens bones.

questions.q: Give a muscle-strengthening activity.
questions.a: E.g., climbing on playground equipment, push-ups, tug-of-war, gymnastics.

days.guide: Measure heart rate (15 seconds × 4) before and after 3 minutes of jumping. Record and compare.

questions.q: Before: 20 beats in 15 seconds; after: 35 beats. What are the heart rates per minute?
questions.a: Before 80 bpm; after 140 bpm.

days.guide: Rate mood 1–5 before and after a 15-minute walk, and write what changed.

questions.q: Why might your mood improve after a walk?
questions.a: Activity releases brain chemicals (endorphins) that improve mood and lower stress; fresh air and a break help too.

days.guide: Quiz (see key).

questions.q: How many minutes of activity should kids get daily?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes.

weeks.assessment_key: Activity benefits quiz key: 1) Recommended daily activity for kids — 60 minutes or more. 2) Three types of activity — aerobic, muscle-strengthening, bone-strengthening. 3) How many days a week for muscle- and bone-strengthening — at least 3 each. 4) Give an aerobic activity — running, biking, swimming, dancing. 5) Name 3 benefits — any physical, mental and social benefits (stronger heart, better mood, better sleep, friendships). 6) Why does heart rate rise during exercise — muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps more blood. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Print a 3-day activity log (activity, start/end time, minutes, light/moderate/vigorous) and screen-time log. Discuss the family's screen-time limits ahead. Timer.
misconceptions: Thinking any movement counts as moderate or vigorous. Moderate makes you breathe harder (can talk but not sing); vigorous makes it hard to say more than a few words.
Counting homework on a computer as recreational screen time. Log recreational screens (TV, games, videos) separately.

days.guide: Teach intensity levels: light (slow walk, stretching), moderate (brisk walk, bike ride — can talk, not sing), vigorous (running, soccer, jump rope — hard to talk). Log activity for 3 days.

questions.q: How can you tell if an activity is vigorous?
questions.a: You breathe hard and fast and can only say a few words without stopping for breath.

questions.q: Is a brisk walk light, moderate or vigorous?
questions.a: Moderate.

days.guide: Log recreational screen time with start and end times for the same 3 days.

questions.q: You watched TV from 3:45 to 5:15. How many minutes?
questions.a: 90 minutes (1 hour 30 minutes).

days.guide: Total each day's activity and compare to 60 minutes; total screen time and compare to family limits.

questions.q: Day 1: 25 + 20 + 10 minutes of activity. Did you meet 60?
questions.a: No — 55 minutes, 5 minutes short.

days.guide: List 5 active alternatives to screen time (indoor and outdoor) and try one today.

questions.q: Give 2 indoor active alternatives to screens.
questions.a: E.g., a dance party, an indoor obstacle course, a kids' yoga video, balloon volleyball or a jumping-jacks challenge.

days.guide: Write a paragraph about patterns (e.g., more screens on weekends) and one specific change for next week.

questions.q: What makes a good change statement?
questions.a: It is specific and measurable, e.g., 'I will play outside for 30 minutes before any screen time on school days.'

weeks.assessment_key: Activity and screen time analysis rubric: 4 = 3 complete days of both logs with correct minute totals and intensity labels; compares to the 60-minute goal and family limits; paragraph describes a pattern with evidence and one specific, measurable change; 3 = minor math errors or general change; 2 = logs incomplete; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Goal tracker and calendar, stickers, health journal. The week 18 logs for reference.
misconceptions: Thinking barriers mean you can't be active. Most barriers have solutions (rainy day = indoor activity menu).
Giving up after missing a day. Adjust the plan and keep going; progress, not perfection.

days.guide: List barriers to activity (weather, time, screens, no one to play with, darkness) and a solution for each.

questions.q: Barrier: it's raining. Solution?
questions.a: Do an indoor activity: dance, yoga video, jumping jacks circuit, active games inside.

questions.q: Barrier: no time after homework. Solution?
questions.a: Be active in short bursts (three 10-minute sessions), walk or bike to errands, or play before homework.

days.guide: Write a 3-week SMART activity goal.

questions.q: Make this SMART: 'I'll play outside more.'
questions.a: E.g., 'I will play outside for 30 minutes after school 5 days a week for the next 3 weeks and mark it on my calendar.'

days.guide: Make an activity menu with indoor and outdoor choices for rainy and sunny days.

questions.q: Why have a menu of choices?
questions.a: So you always have an option no matter the weather or time, which helps you stick to the goal.

days.guide: Begin tracking with stickers and a one-word feeling each day.

questions.q: Why note how you feel each day?
questions.a: To see the connection between activity and mood/energy, which motivates you.

days.guide: After 5 days, check progress and adjust the plan if needed.

questions.q: You met your goal 3 of 5 days. What could you adjust?
questions.a: Identify what blocked the other days and plan a solution (e.g., an indoor option or earlier time), or adjust the goal to be achievable.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal tracker check-in rubric: 4 = SMART goal written with all 5 parts, barriers listed with realistic solutions, activity menu with indoor/outdoor options, 5 days tracked with feelings, and a thoughtful adjustment based on data; 3 = one part missing; 2 = tracking incomplete; 1 = no goal or tracking.

weeks.prep: Poster paper and markers, outdoor equipment (balls, jump rope, chalk), the 3-week goal tracker. Prepare the Unit 5 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking adults don't need activity. Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus muscle-strengthening; family activity helps everyone.
Thinking an advocacy poster only needs a picture. It needs a clear message, accurate facts and a call to action.

days.guide: Design a one-week family activity challenge with a daily task and a way to track (checklist on the fridge).

questions.q: Give 2 family challenge ideas.
questions.a: E.g., a walk after dinner, a 10-minute dance party, a bike ride, a backyard relay.

days.guide: The child leads the family in a 15-minute active game, explaining rules and safety.

questions.q: What makes a good activity leader?
questions.a: Clear rules, a safety reminder, encouraging everyone, and including all ages and abilities.

days.guide: Make a poster encouraging 60 minutes of play a day with a slogan, 2 facts and a call to action.

questions.q: What is a call to action?
questions.a: A clear statement telling the audience what to do, e.g., 'Play 60 minutes every day!'

days.guide: Review the 3-week tracker and reflect: Did you meet the goal? What helped? What got in the way?

questions.q: How do you know if you met your goal?
questions.a: Compare the tracker data to the measurable target in the goal.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test (see key).

questions.q: Name the three types of physical activity kids need.
questions.a: Aerobic, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: 1) Daily activity for kids — 60 minutes or more. 2) Three types — aerobic, muscle-strengthening, bone-strengthening. 3) Example of vigorous activity — running, soccer, jump rope, swimming laps. 4) Example of moderate activity — brisk walking, easy biking. 5) Two benefits for mental health — better mood, less stress, better sleep/focus. 6) One barrier and a solution — e.g., rain → indoor dance. 7) What does SMART stand for — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. 8) Rewrite 'be more active' as SMART — any goal with activity, amount, frequency and time frame. Proficient = 6 of 8; plus family challenge completed and tracked.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: this unit begins medicine safety. Have an EMPTY over-the-counter medicine box (or one you hold and keep control of) and a sample prescription label (photo of an old label with personal info covered). Keep all real medicines locked and out of reach. Prepare the medicine quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking medicine is always safe because it helps people. Any medicine can harm you if taken the wrong way, in the wrong amount, or if it isn't meant for you.
Thinking kids can take medicine on their own if they know what it is. Only a parent, guardian or trusted adult (or school nurse with permission) should give a child medicine.

days.guide: List reasons people take medicine: treat illness (antibiotics for some bacterial infections), prevent disease (vaccines), relieve symptoms or pain (pain relievers, allergy medicine), manage long-term conditions (inhaler for asthma). Then list risks of misuse (overdose, side effects, allergic reaction, addiction).

questions.q: Name 3 reasons people take medicine.
questions.a: To treat illness, prevent disease, relieve pain or symptoms, or manage a long-term condition.

questions.q: What is medicine misuse?
questions.a: Taking medicine in a way it wasn't meant — wrong amount, wrong person, wrong time, or for the wrong reason.

days.guide: Compare a prescription label and an OTC Drug Facts label in a Venn diagram.

questions.q: What is the difference between prescription and OTC medicine?
questions.a: Prescription medicine needs a doctor's order and is for one specific person; over-the-counter (OTC) medicine can be bought without a prescription.

questions.q: What do both kinds of labels include?
questions.a: The medicine name, directions/dose, warnings and an expiration date.

days.guide: Explain doctors diagnose and prescribe; pharmacists prepare medicines and explain how to take them safely. The child writes 3 questions for a pharmacist.

questions.q: Give a good question to ask a pharmacist.
questions.a: E.g., 'How much and how often should I take this?' 'Should it be taken with food?' 'What side effects might happen?' 'Can it be taken with my other medicines?'

days.guide: Discuss why some medicines (chewables, gummy vitamins) look or taste like candy, and why that is dangerous for young children. Medicine is never candy; only adults give it.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to call medicine 'candy'?
questions.a: Children might take it on their own and swallow too much, which can cause poisoning or overdose.

questions.q: What should you do if you find a pill?
questions.a: Don't touch or taste it; tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key).

questions.q: Who should give you medicine?
questions.a: A parent, guardian or trusted adult (or the school nurse with permission).

weeks.assessment_key: Medicine quiz key: 1) Prescription medicine needs — a doctor's order and is for one person only. 2) OTC means — over-the-counter, bought without a prescription. 3) Who prepares prescriptions and explains them — a pharmacist. 4) Who should give a child medicine — a parent/guardian or trusted adult. 5) Name a reason to take medicine — treat, prevent, relieve symptoms, manage a condition. 6) Is it OK to share a prescription? — No. 7) Why is medicine not candy? — too much can poison you. Proficient = 6 of 7.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: an EMPTY OTC box or the parent holds the bottle while the child reads the Drug Facts label. Highlighter. Never let the child handle real medicines unsupervised.
misconceptions: Thinking more medicine works faster or better. Taking more than the label or doctor says can cause an overdose.
Thinking expired medicine is fine. It may not work or may be unsafe; an adult should dispose of it properly (drug take-back).

days.guide: With an adult, find and highlight on the Drug Facts label: active ingredient, uses, warnings, directions (dose by age/weight), and expiration date.

questions.q: Which part of the Drug Facts label tells how much to take?
questions.a: The Directions section.

questions.q: What does the active ingredient do?
questions.a: It is the part of the medicine that makes it work.

days.guide: Explain side effects (unwanted effects like drowsiness, upset stomach, rash). Tell an adult right away if you feel unwell after medicine; trouble breathing or swelling is an emergency (call 911).

questions.q: What is a side effect?
questions.a: An unwanted effect of a medicine, like sleepiness or an upset stomach.

questions.q: What should you do if you get a rash after taking medicine?
questions.a: Tell a parent or trusted adult right away; if you have trouble breathing or swelling, call 911.

days.guide: Write 5 safe medicine rules: only take medicine from a trusted adult; follow the label or doctor's directions exactly; never share or take someone else's prescription; never take medicine that's not labeled or that you find; store medicine out of reach in its original container.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you take a friend's prescription?
questions.a: It was prescribed for their body and illness; it could be the wrong medicine or dose for you and could harm you.

days.guide: Act out: a friend offers a pill 'that helps you focus'; you find a pill on the floor. Practice saying no and telling an adult.

questions.q: A friend offers you a pill at school. What do you do?
questions.a: Say 'No thanks,' don't take it, walk away and tell a trusted adult (teacher or school nurse).

days.guide: Create a safe medicine checklist and teach it to a younger sibling or parent.

questions.q: Name 3 items on your safe medicine checklist.
questions.a: Any 3 rules: from a trusted adult only; follow directions; check expiration date; never share; tell an adult about side effects; store out of reach.

weeks.assessment_key: Safe medicine checklist rubric: 4 = at least 5 accurate rules (only from trusted adult, follow directions/dose, never share prescriptions, check expiration, report side effects, store safely), clearly explained to another person; 3 = 4 rules; 2 = 2–3 rules or an unsafe rule; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: with an adult, look at household product labels (cleaners, bleach, bug spray, aerosol cans) WITHOUT opening them. Lock up chemicals. Write the Poison Control number 1-800-222-1222 near the phone. Prepare the Unit 6 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking 'natural' or common products are harmless. Cleaners, bleach, button batteries, essential oils and even vitamins can poison children.
Thinking sniffing markers, glue or sprays is harmless fun. Inhaling fumes can damage the brain, heart and lungs and can cause death even the first time.

days.guide: With an adult, find 10 products with warning labels. Record the signal word. Explain: CAUTION = least harmful, WARNING = more harmful, DANGER = most harmful (POISON with skull and crossbones = highly toxic).

questions.q: Which signal word means the most dangerous?
questions.a: DANGER (especially DANGER–POISON).

questions.q: Put in order from least to most harmful: Danger, Caution, Warning.
questions.a: Caution, Warning, Danger.

days.guide: Explain inhalants: chemicals in some products (glue, aerosols, permanent markers, gasoline) make fumes that are poisonous to breathe on purpose. Sniffing can cause brain damage, heart problems and sudden death ('sudden sniffing death').

questions.q: Why is sniffing fumes from products dangerous?
questions.a: The chemicals go straight to the brain and can damage it, make the heart beat irregularly, and can cause death even the first time.

questions.q: Why use markers and glue only in a well-ventilated room?
questions.a: Fresh air keeps fumes from building up.

days.guide: With an adult, help organize cleaning products in a high or locked cabinet, away from food, in original containers.

questions.q: Why keep products in their original containers?
questions.a: So the label and warnings stay with them and no one mistakes them for food or drink.

days.guide: Learn the Poison Control number. Role-play a call: say what was swallowed/touched, how much, the person's age and weight, and follow directions. Call 911 if the person is unconscious, having seizures or trouble breathing.

questions.q: What number do you call for a possible poisoning?
questions.a: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222 (or 911 if the person can't breathe, is unconscious or has a seizure).

questions.q: What information should you have ready?
questions.a: The product container, what and how much was swallowed or touched, when it happened, and the person's age and weight.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test (see key).

questions.q: What should you do if you find a cleaning product open on the floor?
questions.a: Don't touch or smell it; keep younger kids away and tell an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) Prescription vs. OTC — prescription needs a doctor's order for one person; OTC can be bought without one. 2) Where to find dose — Directions section of the label. 3) What is a side effect — an unwanted effect of a medicine. 4) Should you share prescriptions — no. 5) Signal words from least to most harmful — Caution, Warning, Danger. 6) Poison Control number — 1-800-222-1222. 7) Why are inhalants dangerous — fumes damage the brain/heart and can cause death. 8) Where to store cleaners — high or locked, away from food, in original containers. 9) If you find a pill — don't touch it, tell an adult. 10) When to call 911 instead of Poison Control — unconscious, not breathing, seizure. Proficient = 8 of 10.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: tobacco unit. Two kitchen sponges, molasses or dark syrup, a bowl, straws (one per person), a lungs diagram (KidsHealth or the American Lung Association). Stop the straw activity immediately if the child feels dizzy; skip it for children with asthma.
misconceptions: Thinking smoking only harms the lungs. Tobacco damages the heart, blood vessels, mouth, teeth, skin and nearly every organ.
Thinking a person can easily quit whenever they want. Nicotine is very addictive; most people who smoke want to quit but find it hard.

days.guide: Teach 3 harmful substances: nicotine (addictive drug that speeds up heart rate and raises blood pressure), tar (sticky substance that coats the lungs and contains cancer-causing chemicals), carbon monoxide (poison gas that takes the place of oxygen in the blood).

questions.q: What does tar do to the lungs?
questions.a: It coats the lungs with a sticky residue, damages the cilia and air sacs, and contains chemicals that can cause cancer.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide harmful?
questions.a: It takes the place of oxygen in the blood, so the body gets less oxygen.

days.guide: Soak one sponge in water and one in dark syrup. Squeeze both and compare how easily they take in and release liquid, like healthy lungs vs. tar-coated lungs.

questions.q: What does the syrup sponge represent?
questions.a: A smoker's lungs coated with tar, which can't take in and push out air as well.

days.guide: Jog in place 30 seconds, then breathe only through a straw for up to 30 seconds (stop if dizzy). Discuss how it felt — like lung disease (emphysema) that makes breathing hard.

questions.q: How did breathing through a straw feel, and what does it model?
questions.a: Hard to get enough air; it models how damaged lungs (like emphysema from smoking) make breathing difficult.

days.guide: Read how nicotine causes addiction: the brain gets used to it and craves more; without it a person feels irritable, anxious and restless (withdrawal).

questions.q: What is addiction?
questions.a: When the body and brain depend on a drug and a person feels a strong need to keep using it, even when it causes harm.

questions.q: What are withdrawal symptoms?
questions.a: Uncomfortable feelings when a person stops using a drug, like irritability, anxiety, trouble focusing and cravings.

days.guide: Draw a body outline and label 6 effects of tobacco.

questions.q: Name 2 effects of tobacco besides on the lungs.
questions.a: Any 2: heart disease and stroke, yellow teeth and bad breath, gum disease, mouth/throat cancer, wrinkled skin, less sense of taste and smell, less energy for sports.

weeks.assessment_key: Body effects diagram rubric: 6 accurate labeled effects placed on the right body part, e.g., brain — nicotine addiction; mouth — bad breath, stained teeth, gum disease, mouth cancer; lungs — tar buildup, lung cancer, emphysema, coughing; heart — faster heart rate, heart disease; blood — carbon monoxide reduces oxygen; skin — early wrinkles; also stroke, less stamina. 4 = 6 accurate effects; 3 = 4–5; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: vaping unit. Print the FDA's 'The Real Cost' or CDC fact sheets on e-cigarettes for kids/teens. Prepare 10 myth/fact cards (see Day 2). Have 2–3 sample e-cigarette ad images from health-education sites (e.g., Stanford Tobacco Prevention Toolkit) rather than live marketing.
misconceptions: Thinking vape aerosol is 'just water vapor.' It is an aerosol that can contain nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals, heavy metals like nickel, tin and lead, and cancer-causing chemicals.
Thinking vapes without nicotine are always nicotine-free. Labels are sometimes wrong, and some products labeled nicotine-free have been found to contain nicotine.

days.guide: Read the fact sheet. List what can be in e-cigarette aerosol: nicotine, flavorings (some linked to lung disease), ultrafine particles, heavy metals (nickel, tin, lead), volatile organic compounds, cancer-causing chemicals.

questions.q: What is an e-cigarette?
questions.a: A battery-powered device that heats a liquid (usually containing nicotine and flavorings) into an aerosol that is inhaled.

questions.q: Name 3 things that can be in vape aerosol.
questions.a: Any 3: nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals, heavy metals (nickel, tin, lead), cancer-causing chemicals.

days.guide: Sort 10 statements. Myths: 'It's just water vapor'; 'Vaping isn't addictive'; 'Most kids vape'; 'Flavors are harmless'; 'Vaping can't hurt your lungs.' Facts: 'Most e-cigarettes contain nicotine'; 'Nicotine is addictive'; 'Nicotine can harm the developing brain'; 'Aerosol can contain heavy metals'; 'It is illegal to sell vapes to anyone under 21.'

questions.q: Myth or fact: 'Vaping is just harmless water vapor.'
questions.a: Myth — it is an aerosol with nicotine and other harmful chemicals.

questions.q: Myth or fact: 'Most kids vape.'
questions.a: Myth — most young people do not vape.

days.guide: Look at sample ad images. Note bright colors, candy and fruit flavors, cartoon-like designs and devices shaped like USB drives or highlighters — features that appeal to young people.

questions.q: Why do companies use candy and fruit flavors?
questions.a: Flavors appeal to young people and make vaping seem harmless, which can get them started and addicted.

days.guide: Explain the brain keeps developing until about age 25. Nicotine can harm the parts that control attention, learning, mood and impulse control, and makes young people more easily addicted.

questions.q: How can nicotine affect a young person's brain?
questions.a: It can harm attention, learning, memory, mood and impulse control, and causes addiction more easily.

days.guide: Write a public service message correcting one myth, with a fact and a source.

questions.q: What makes a strong PSA?
questions.a: A clear, short message, an accurate fact from a reliable source (FDA, CDC), and a call to action.

weeks.assessment_key: PSA message rubric: 4 = names a specific vaping myth, corrects it with an accurate fact (e.g., 'Vape aerosol is not water vapor — it can contain nicotine, heavy metals and cancer-causing chemicals'), cites a reliable source (FDA, CDC, NIDA), and ends with a positive call to action; 3 = accurate correction but no source; 2 = vague message; 1 = inaccurate or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find a simple chart of California youth tobacco data (California Department of Public Health 'California Student Tobacco Survey' or the CDC National Youth Tobacco Survey) showing most students do not use tobacco. Poster paper. Prepare the Unit 7 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking secondhand smoke only matters if you're in the same room for a long time. There is no safe level of secondhand smoke; children's lungs are especially sensitive.
Thinking 'everyone' smokes or vapes. Data show most young people do not use tobacco or vape.

days.guide: Explain secondhand smoke (smoke from the tip of a cigarette and smoke breathed out) and secondhand vape aerosol. In children it can trigger asthma attacks, cause ear infections, bronchitis and more colds.

questions.q: What is secondhand smoke?
questions.a: Smoke breathed in by people nearby from someone else's cigarette (from the burning end and what the smoker exhales).

questions.q: How can secondhand smoke affect children?
questions.a: It can cause or worsen asthma, ear infections, coughing, bronchitis and pneumonia.

days.guide: Read about California laws: it's illegal to sell tobacco or vapes to anyone under 21; smoking is banned in workplaces, restaurants and bars and in cars when anyone under 18 is present; many cities ban smoking in parks and beaches, and state parks and beaches are smoke-free.

questions.q: In California, can someone smoke in a car with a child?
questions.a: No — it is illegal to smoke in a vehicle when a minor (under 18) is present.

questions.q: What is the legal age to buy tobacco or vapes in California?

days.guide: Read the survey data and make a bar graph showing that most students have never used tobacco or vapes. Discuss 'social norms' (what most people actually do).

questions.q: What is a social norm?
questions.a: What most people in a group actually do or think is normal behavior.

questions.q: Why is it helpful to know most kids don't vape?
questions.a: It shows that not using is normal, making it easier to say no.

days.guide: Role-play 3 polite ways to avoid secondhand smoke: move away, ask to open a window or for the person to smoke outside, tell a trusted adult.
