Facts: delegates met at Colton Hall, Monterey, in September-October 1849; 48 delegates including 8 Californios such as Mariano Vallejo; the constitution was published in English and Spanish, banned slavery, set the capital at San Jose, and protected married women's separate property; voting was limited to white men. California became the 31st state on September 9, 1850, as part of the Compromise of 1850.
misconceptions: Thinking California was a territory first. It skipped the territory stage and became a state directly.
Thinking 'free state' meant everyone had equal rights. Native Californians, Chinese immigrants, African Americans and women were denied many rights.

days.guide: Discuss why Gold Rush California needed a government.

questions.q: Why did California need a government quickly?
questions.a: Crime, disputes over mining claims and land, and no courts or laws to settle them as the population exploded.

days.guide: Read about the convention at Colton Hall.

questions.q: Where and when was California's first constitution written?
questions.a: Colton Hall in Monterey, in the fall of 1849.

days.guide: Read constitution excerpts; list 4 key decisions.

questions.q: Name four decisions in the 1849 constitution.
questions.a: Banned slavery; printed laws in English and Spanish; set boundaries; married women could own separate property; (also capital in San Jose; voting limited to white men).

days.guide: Read about the Compromise of 1850.

questions.q: Why was California's admission controversial?
questions.a: Adding a free state would upset the balance between free and slave states in the Senate; the Compromise of 1850 settled this with deals for both sides.

days.guide: Build the statehood timeline.

questions.q: When did California become a state and which number?
questions.a: September 9, 1850; the 31st state.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline key: June 1846 Bear Flag Revolt; July 1846 U.S. flag raised at Monterey; Dec 1846 Battle of San Pasqual; Jan 1848 gold discovered; Feb 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; 1849 Gold Rush and constitutional convention at Colton Hall; Sept 9, 1850 statehood (31st state, free state, Compromise of 1850). Proficient: 6 events in correct order with illustrations.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Civic Buildings in California History,' an image of the Great Seal of California. Capitals: San Jose (1849-51), Vallejo (1852-53), Benicia (1853-54), Sacramento (1854-present). Unit 8 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking the new government gave everyone a voice. Only white men could vote; Native people could not testify against whites in court.
Thinking the bear on the seal is the main symbol. The central figure is Minerva, Roman goddess of wisdom.

days.guide: Compare lawmaking and rights under Spanish, Mexican and American rule.

questions.q: Who made laws under Spain?
questions.a: The king and his appointed officials (viceroy, governors); under Mexico, a national congress and appointed governors with local councils; under the U.S. state system, elected legislators.

days.guide: Discuss who was left out of rights.

questions.q: Name one way early state laws limited Native Californians.
questions.a: They could not vote, could not testify against white people in court, and a 1850 law allowed them to be forced into labor.

days.guide: Trace the capital's moves.

questions.q: List California's capitals in order.
questions.a: San Jose, Vallejo, Benicia, Sacramento.

days.guide: Analyze the Great Seal.

questions.q: What do the symbols on the Great Seal mean?
questions.a: Minerva (wisdom; California became a state without being a territory, like Minerva born grown), grizzly bear (strength), wheat and grapes (agriculture), miner (Gold Rush), ships (trade), Sierra Nevada, 'Eureka' ('I have found it'), 31 stars (31st state).

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What does 'Eureka' mean?
questions.a: 'I have found it.'

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test key: 1) Need for government during the Gold Rush 2) Colton Hall, Monterey, 1849 3) Constitution: no slavery, English/Spanish 4) Compromise of 1850; statehood Sept 9, 1850 5) 31st state 6) Comparison of Spanish, Mexican and American government 7) Groups denied rights: Native Californians, Chinese, African Americans, women 8) Capital moves ending in Sacramento 9) Seal symbols. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: U.S. map, Morse code chart, flashlight, stopwatch. Facts: Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoaches (1858-61) carried mail from Missouri to San Francisco in about 25 days; the Pony Express (April 1860-October 1861) carried mail about 1,900 miles from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento in about 10 days, with riders changing horses every 10-15 miles; the transcontinental telegraph was completed October 24, 1861.
misconceptions: Thinking the Pony Express lasted for decades. It lasted only about 18 months.
Thinking one rider rode the whole way. Riders relayed the mail, each covering roughly 75-100 miles.

days.guide: Read about Butterfield Overland Mail.

questions.q: How long did the stagecoach mail take?
questions.a: About 25 days.

days.guide: Read about the Pony Express; calculate travel time.

questions.q: If the Pony Express covered about 1,900 miles in 10 days, about how far per day?
questions.a: About 190 miles per day.

questions.q: Where did the route start and end?
questions.a: St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California.

days.guide: Read about the 1861 telegraph; send a Morse message.

questions.q: How long did a telegraph message take?
questions.a: Minutes (almost instantly).

days.guide: Chart message times by ship, stagecoach, Pony Express and telegraph.

questions.q: Order the methods from slowest to fastest.
questions.a: Ship (weeks to months), stagecoach (about 25 days), Pony Express (about 10 days), telegraph (minutes).

days.guide: Write why the Pony Express ended.

questions.q: Why did the Pony Express end?
questions.a: The transcontinental telegraph (October 1861) sent messages almost instantly, and the Pony Express lost money.

weeks.assessment_key: Speed chart: ship around Cape Horn months / via Panama weeks; stagecoach ~25 days; Pony Express ~10 days; telegraph minutes. Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains the telegraph's speed made it obsolete and that it was costly, with dates (1860-61, ~18 months); 3 = main reason only; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'The Transcontinental Railroad,' map. Facts: the Central Pacific (from Sacramento, begun 1863) was led by the 'Big Four' — Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker; Chinese workers (about 12,000-20,000, most of the workforce) blasted tunnels and built through the Sierra Nevada for lower pay than white workers and without board; the lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869 (Golden Spike) — Chinese workers were not shown in the famous celebration photograph.
misconceptions: Thinking the railroad was built by one company from both coasts. Central Pacific built east from Sacramento; Union Pacific built west from Omaha.
Overlooking Chinese workers' role. They did the most dangerous work in the Sierra.

days.guide: Read about the Big Four.

questions.q: Who were the Big Four?
questions.a: Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker — Sacramento merchants who ran the Central Pacific.

days.guide: Read about Chinese workers.

questions.q: Why was the Sierra Nevada the hardest part?
questions.a: Workers had to blast tunnels through solid granite, build on steep cliffs and work through deep snow and avalanches.

questions.q: How were Chinese workers treated unfairly?
questions.a: They were paid less than white workers, had to buy their own food and lodging, and did the most dangerous jobs.

days.guide: Analyze railroad photographs and write captions.

questions.q: What should a good caption include?
questions.a: Who/what is shown, where and when, and why it matters.

days.guide: Read about the Golden Spike ceremony.

questions.q: When and where were the rails joined?
questions.a: May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah.

questions.q: Who was left out of the famous photo?
questions.a: Chinese workers.

days.guide: Write how the railroad changed California's economy.

questions.q: Name two economic effects.
questions.a: Goods and people traveled coast to coast in about a week instead of months; California farm products could be shipped east; more settlers and businesses came.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = topic sentence plus 3 accurate effects (faster travel ~1 week, shipping crops east, population growth, cheaper goods, rise of railroad monopoly), mention of Chinese labor, conclusion; 3 = two effects; 2 = one; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'Chinese Exclusion Act' and 'Diversity in the Changing State,' world map. Facts: the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) banned Chinese laborers from immigrating — the first U.S. law to bar a specific ethnic group; it was extended and not repealed until 1943. Chinese Americans fought back in court (e.g., Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 1886; Wong Kim Ark, 1898, which confirmed citizenship for people born in the U.S.).
misconceptions: Thinking the act was about all immigrants. It specifically targeted Chinese workers.
Thinking immigrants accepted unfair laws silently. Many organized, sued and won important court cases.

days.guide: Map immigrant origins 1850-1900.

questions.q: Name four countries California immigrants came from 1850-1900.
questions.a: China, Mexico, Ireland, Germany (also Chile, Japan, Italy).

days.guide: Analyze 'Diversity in the Changing State' images; list communities.

questions.q: Name a community that formed in this era.
questions.a: Chinatown in San Francisco (also Japanese, Italian, Portuguese, Mexican communities).

days.guide: Read about the Chinese Exclusion Act; analyze a document.

questions.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act do?
questions.a: It stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating to the U.S. (from 1882) and kept Chinese immigrants from becoming citizens.

questions.q: When was it repealed?

days.guide: Read about people who defended immigrants' rights.

questions.q: What did the Wong Kim Ark case decide?
questions.a: A person born in the U.S. (even to Chinese parents) is a U.S. citizen (1898).

days.guide: Write whether the act was fair, with two pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that it was unfair.
questions.a: It singled out one ethnic group, even though Chinese workers had built the railroad and contributed to California's economy.

weeks.assessment_key: Response rubric: 4 = clear answer (most will argue it was unfair), two specific pieces of evidence (targeted one group; Chinese contributions to railroad/farming; families separated; repealed in 1943), conclusion; 3 = one piece of evidence; 2 = opinion only; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Calisphere set 'Everyday Life and People in Late 19th Century California,' citrus crate label images, population data: San Francisco 1850 ~35,000 (1852 state census), 1870 149,473, 1890 298,997, 1910 416,912, 1920 506,676; Los Angeles 1850 1,610, 1870 5,728, 1890 50,395, 1910 319,198, 1920 576,673. Unit 9 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking Los Angeles was always California's biggest city. San Francisco was larger until Los Angeles passed it by 1920.
Thinking crate labels are just art. They were advertising that sold California as a sunny paradise to attract settlers.

days.guide: Read about the 1880s land boom.

questions.q: What caused the 1880s Los Angeles land boom?
questions.a: Railroads (Southern Pacific, then the Santa Fe) reached LA, and a fare war made tickets very cheap, bringing thousands of newcomers.

days.guide: Read about citrus and oil; analyze crate labels.

questions.q: Who discovered oil in Los Angeles in 1892?
questions.a: Edward Doheny.

questions.q: What image did crate labels give of California?
questions.a: Sunny, healthy, abundant land — advertising to attract buyers and settlers.

days.guide: Analyze everyday life images.

questions.q: Name one change in everyday life by the 1890s.
questions.a: Electric streetcars, telephones, larger cities, new schools.

days.guide: Graph SF and LA populations 1850-1920.

questions.q: When did Los Angeles pass San Francisco in population?

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test.

questions.q: Name the Big Four.
questions.a: Stanford, Huntington, Hopkins, Crocker.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key: 1) Overland Mail ~25 days 2) Pony Express 1860-61, ~10 days 3) Telegraph 1861 ended the Pony Express 4) Big Four and Central Pacific 5) Chinese workers' role and unequal pay 6) Golden Spike May 10, 1869 at Promontory Summit 7) Chinese Exclusion Act 1882 8) Immigrant origins 9) LA boom after railroads 10) LA passed SF by 1920. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: California water project map (California Department of Water Resources), rainfall and population maps, Calisphere set 'Building Bridges, Dams and Power Plants.' Facts: most rain and snow fall in the north and the Sierra, while most people live in the south; William Mulholland's Los Angeles Aqueduct (1913) carried Owens Valley water about 230 miles, leading to conflict ('California Water Wars') as the valley dried; Hetch Hetchy (O'Shaughnessy Dam, 1923) supplies San Francisco despite John Muir's opposition; Shasta Dam (completed 1945) anchors the federal Central Valley Project; the State Water Project (Oroville Dam, California Aqueduct) carries water south.
misconceptions: Thinking water is evenly spread. About two-thirds of precipitation falls in the northern part of the state, but most people live in the south.
Thinking water projects had no downsides. They flooded valleys, harmed fish, and took water from other communities.

days.guide: Compare rainfall and population maps.

questions.q: What problem do the maps show?
questions.a: Most water falls in the north and mountains, but most people and farms are in the south and Central Valley.

days.guide: Read about Mulholland and the LA Aqueduct.

questions.q: Why were Owens Valley residents angry?
questions.a: Los Angeles bought land and water rights and diverted the river, drying up Owens Lake and harming farms; some residents dynamited the aqueduct.

days.guide: Map Hetch Hetchy, Shasta Dam, CVP and SWP.

questions.q: Which city gets water from Hetch Hetchy?
questions.a: San Francisco.

questions.q: Why did John Muir oppose Hetch Hetchy Dam?
questions.a: It flooded a beautiful valley in Yosemite National Park.

days.guide: Analyze photos of dams and power plants.

questions.q: Besides storing water, what do dams provide?
questions.a: Hydroelectric power and flood control.

days.guide: Draw water's path from Sierra snow to your faucet.

questions.q: Describe the path.
questions.a: Snow melts in the Sierra → flows into rivers → stored behind dams in reservoirs → carried by aqueducts/canals → treated at a plant → pipes → your faucet.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram rubric: 4 = labeled steps from snowpack, rivers, reservoir/dam, aqueduct, treatment, pipes to faucet, naming at least one real project; 3 = steps correct without real project; 2 = missing steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Calisphere sets 'The Great Depression: Hard Times,' 'Dust Bowl Migration,' 'Life on the Home Front During World War II' and 'Japanese American Internment'; Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936, Nipomo, California). Facts: Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most U.S. citizens, to camps such as Manzanar and Tule Lake; the U.S. formally apologized and paid reparations in 1988. Preview: discuss unfairness and fear sensitively.
misconceptions: Thinking the Japanese American incarceration was about crimes. No one was charged; it was based on ancestry and prejudice.
Thinking Dust Bowl migrants were welcomed. Many were called 'Okies,' faced prejudice and lived in poor camps.

days.guide: Read about the Depression in California; analyze images.

questions.q: What was the Great Depression?
questions.a: A severe economic crisis in the 1930s when banks failed, businesses closed and many people lost jobs.

days.guide: Analyze 'Migrant Mother' and Dust Bowl photos.

questions.q: What does 'Migrant Mother' show?
questions.a: A worried mother with her children in a pea-pickers' camp in 1936, showing the hardship of migrant farm workers.

questions.q: Why did Dust Bowl families come to California?
questions.a: Drought and dust storms ruined farms in Oklahoma, Texas and nearby states; they hoped for farm work in California.

days.guide: Read about the home front.

questions.q: How did WWII change jobs in California?
questions.a: Shipyards (like Kaiser in Richmond) and aircraft factories hired huge numbers of workers, including women ('Rosie the Riveter') and African Americans who moved west.

days.guide: Read about EO 9066; analyze photos.

questions.q: What did Executive Order 9066 lead to?
questions.a: The forced removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans in camps like Manzanar.

questions.q: Was it justified?
questions.a: No — no one was charged with a crime; in 1988 the U.S. apologized and paid reparations.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on how one event changed California.

questions.q: Name one long-term change from WWII.
questions.a: Population and industry boomed; aerospace and defense industries grew; more diverse population.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = names an event, explains 2-3 specific changes with dates or facts (e.g., Dust Bowl migration to the Central Valley; shipyards in Richmond; EO 9066 and Manzanar), conclusion; 3 = one change; 2 = summary; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: California map, Ansel Adams Yosemite photographs, library books on Steinbeck, Lange, Hollywood and Walt Disney. Facts: the 1960 Master Plan for Higher Education organized the University of California, California State University and community college systems; Disneyland opened in Anaheim in 1955; Steinbeck's 'The Grapes of Wrath' (1939) told of Dust Bowl migrants. Unit 10 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking Silicon Valley is a real valley named for sand. It is the Santa Clara Valley area, nicknamed for silicon computer chips.
Thinking art doesn't change history. Adams' photos helped protect wilderness; Lange's and Steinbeck's work drew attention to migrant workers.

days.guide: Map industries.

questions.q: Where is Silicon Valley and what is made there?
questions.a: The Santa Clara Valley/San Jose area; computer and technology industries.

questions.q: Where is aerospace concentrated?
questions.a: Southern California.

days.guide: Read about California's public education system.

questions.q: Name the three parts of public higher education in the 1960 Master Plan.
questions.a: University of California, California State University, community colleges.

days.guide: Study Adams' photos; read about Steinbeck and Lange.

questions.q: How did Ansel Adams' photographs matter?
questions.a: They showed the beauty of wilderness like Yosemite and helped support conservation of national parks.

days.guide: Read about Hollywood and Walt Disney.

questions.q: How did Hollywood spread California culture?
questions.a: Movies shown worldwide made California's places, styles and dreams famous.

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: What is EO 9066?
questions.a: The 1942 order that led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test key: 1) Rainfall north vs. population south 2) LA Aqueduct 1913, Mulholland, Owens Valley conflict 3) Hetch Hetchy and Muir 4) Great Depression and Dust Bowl migrants 5) 'Migrant Mother' by Dorothea Lange 6) WWII shipyards, aircraft, women workers 7) EO 9066 and Manzanar 8) Industries: aerospace, Silicon Valley, Central Valley agriculture 9) UC, CSU, community colleges 10) Contributions of Adams, Steinbeck, Disney. Proficient: 80%.

weeks.prep: U.S. Constitution (DocsTeach or archives.gov), California Constitution preamble ('We, the People of the State of California, grateful to Almighty God for our freedom, in order to secure and perpetuate its blessings, do establish this Constitution.'). Article I of the California Constitution is the Declaration of Rights.
misconceptions: Thinking the state constitution is the same as the U.S. Constitution. States have their own constitutions; they can't conflict with the U.S. Constitution.
Mixing up branches. Legislative makes laws; executive carries them out; judicial interprets them.

days.guide: Read the Preamble; identify six goals.

questions.q: List the six goals in the Preamble.
questions.a: Form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare, secure the blessings of liberty.

days.guide: Chart the three branches.

questions.q: Name the branches and their jobs.
questions.a: Legislative (Congress) makes laws; executive (President) carries out laws; judicial (Supreme Court and courts) interprets laws.

questions.q: Why have three branches?
questions.a: Separation of powers and checks and balances so no branch gets too much power.

days.guide: Read the California preamble and Declaration of Rights.

questions.q: What is the California Declaration of Rights?
questions.a: Article I of the California Constitution, listing people's rights (like free speech, privacy and equal protection).

days.guide: Venn diagram comparing federal and state governments.

questions.q: How are they alike?
questions.a: Both have constitutions and three branches (legislature, executive, courts).

questions.q: How are they different?
questions.a: Federal: President, Congress, U.S. Supreme Court, national issues (defense, money). State: Governor, Legislature (Assembly and Senate), California Supreme Court, state issues (schools, highways).

days.guide: Give the constitution quiz.

questions.q: What branch is the President in?
questions.a: Executive.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 'We the People' — government's power comes from the people 2) Six Preamble goals 3) Legislative = makes laws (Congress; CA Legislature) 4) Executive = carries out laws (President; Governor) 5) Judicial = interprets laws (U.S. Supreme Court; CA Supreme Court) 6) Checks and balances 7) California Declaration of Rights = Article I 8) State constitution cannot conflict with the U.S. Constitution. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: State government website (gov.ca.gov, legislature.ca.gov 'Find Your Representative' at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov), a district map. Facts: the Legislature has an 80-member Assembly (2-year terms) and a 40-member Senate (4-year terms); the governor serves a 4-year term (maximum two terms); the California Supreme Court has a chief justice and six associate justices. Look up who currently holds your offices, since officials change after elections.
misconceptions: Thinking the governor makes laws alone. The Legislature passes bills; the governor signs or vetoes them.
Confusing state and federal legislators. State: Assembly member and state senator; federal: U.S. Representative and U.S. Senators.

days.guide: Read about the governor and other statewide officials.

questions.q: What does the governor do?
questions.a: Leads the executive branch, signs or vetoes bills, proposes the state budget, and commands the state National Guard.

days.guide: Read about the Assembly and Senate and how a bill becomes law.

questions.q: List the steps of a bill becoming a law in California.
questions.a: A legislator introduces a bill → committee hearings → vote in the first house → same in the other house → governor signs it (or vetoes; the Legislature can override with a two-thirds vote).

days.guide: Look up your Assembly member and state senator.

questions.q: How many members are in the Assembly and Senate?
questions.a: 80 Assembly members; 40 senators.

days.guide: Read about state courts.

questions.q: What is the job of the judicial branch?
questions.a: To interpret laws and decide cases, including whether laws follow the constitution.

days.guide: Write a letter to your state legislator.

questions.q: What parts belong in the letter?
questions.a: Date, greeting, who you are, the issue, your opinion with reasons, a specific request, polite closing and signature.

weeks.assessment_key: Letter rubric: 4 = correctly addressed to the child's own legislator, clearly states an issue and opinion with 2-3 reasons, a specific request, formal tone, correct letter format; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = vague issue or informal; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: County map, local government websites (city, county, school district), information on a nearby California tribal government (rancheria or reservation). End-of-year assessment (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking tribes are 'part of' county government. Federally recognized tribes are sovereign nations with their own governments.
Confusing city and county roles. Cities run local services like police and parks in town; counties run courts, elections, public health and services for unincorporated areas.

days.guide: Identify your city, county, school district and nearest rancheria or reservation.

questions.q: What does a county government do?
questions.a: Runs elections, courts, jails, public health, property records and services for areas outside cities.

days.guide: Watch part of a city council meeting; list topics.

questions.q: Who leads a city?
questions.a: A city council and a mayor (sometimes a city manager).

days.guide: Read about a California tribal government.

questions.q: What services might a tribal government provide?
questions.a: Health clinics, housing, education and language programs, environmental protection, courts and police.

days.guide: Build a California history timeline.

questions.q: Put in order: missions begin, statehood, Gold Rush, Chinese Exclusion Act.
questions.a: Missions begin 1769, Gold Rush 1848, statehood 1850, Chinese Exclusion Act 1882.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year HSS assessment.

questions.q: What year did California become a state?

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year key (sample): 1) California's four regions 2) latitude/longitude definitions 3) two California Indian nations and adaptations 4) Cabrillo 1542 5) first mission San Diego 1769; 21 missions 6) Mexico independent 1821; ranchos 7) Bear Flag Revolt 1846 8) Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848 9) Gold discovered 1848 at Sutter's Mill 10) Statehood Sept 9, 1850 11) Transcontinental railroad 1869 12) Chinese Exclusion Act 1882 13) Three branches of government 14) Assembly 80, Senate 40. Proficient: 80%. Timeline: proficient includes 10+ correctly ordered events.

MATH.overview: Teach each 60-minute lesson as: a 5-10 minute warm-up (facts or a number talk), a modeled example with objects or drawings, guided practice where you watch the first problems, and independent practice you check the same day. Always connect concrete models (base-ten blocks, fraction strips, grids) to written methods before moving to algorithms, and ask the child to explain reasoning aloud. Fractions (weeks 17-25) are the heart of grade 4 — do not rush them; review weak skills from quizzes in the next week's warm-ups.

weeks.prep: Print or write a 20-question diagnostic (10 multiplication/addition facts, 5 place-value items, 5 third-grade fraction items). Draw a place value chart from hundred thousands to ones with a comma between periods. Gather base-ten blocks (or paper flats/rods/units) and 10 index cards numbered 0-9.
misconceptions: Reading 406,215 as 'four hundred six, two hundred fifteen' — teach that the comma is where you say the period name: 'four hundred six THOUSAND, two hundred fifteen.'
Forgetting zeros in standard form (writing 70,000 + 3,000 + 8 as 7,308). Have the child write the number in a place value chart so empty places get a 0.

days.guide: Give the diagnostic without help and mark only what is wrong; note which areas (facts, place value, fractions) need review. Then do the number talk: write 99 + 46, let the child solve mentally and explain, and model 'make 100': 99 is 1 less than 100, so 100 + 46 - 1.

questions.q: Solve 99 + 46 in your head and explain.
questions.a: 145 — 100 + 46 = 146, then subtract the extra 1.

questions.q: What is 7 × 8?

days.guide: Model 2,345 with blocks (2 thousand-cubes or drawn squares, 3 flats, 4 rods, 5 units), then write it in the chart. Have the child build 3-4 more numbers, including a 5-digit one, and record each with a comma separating the thousands period.

questions.q: In 34,215, how many ten-thousands are there and what is their value?
questions.a: 3 ten-thousands, worth 30,000.

questions.q: Where does the comma go in 52307?
questions.a: 52,307 — after the thousands period, three digits from the right.

days.guide: Model one number in all three forms on the board, reading it aloud by periods. The child writes ten numbers in standard, word and expanded form and reads each aloud to you; check that 'and' is not used for whole numbers.

questions.q: Write 406,215 in word form and expanded form.
questions.a: Four hundred six thousand, two hundred fifteen; 400,000 + 6,000 + 200 + 10 + 5.

questions.q: Write 70,000 + 3,000 + 40 + 8 in standard form.
questions.a: 73,048 (zero in the hundreds place).

days.guide: Draw 6 digit cards and arrange them into a 6-digit number; ask 'What is the value of the 7?' The child explains using the chart (digit × place). Repeat with new arrangements, alternating who makes the number.

questions.q: In 573,129, what is the value of the 7? Of the 3?
questions.a: 7 is in the ten-thousands place: 70,000. 3 is in the thousands place: 3,000.

questions.q: Make the largest number with 9, 7, 3, 1, 0, 5. What is the value of the 7?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently (about 20 minutes). Score it together right away and have the child correct each miss, saying out loud where the error was.

questions.q: What is the value of the 8 in 284,615?

weeks.assessment_key: Sample 8-item quiz with answers (each item: standard, word, expanded; 1 point per form). 1) 52,084 = fifty-two thousand, eighty-four = 50,000 + 2,000 + 80 + 4. 2) 310,560 = three hundred ten thousand, five hundred sixty = 300,000 + 10,000 + 500 + 60. 3) 9,407 = nine thousand, four hundred seven = 9,000 + 400 + 7. 4) 765,312 = seven hundred sixty-five thousand, three hundred twelve = 700,000 + 60,000 + 5,000 + 300 + 10 + 2. Digit value: 5) the 6 in 465,201 = 60,000; 6) the 9 in 19,358 = 9,000; 7) the 4 in 804,117 = 4,000; 8) the 2 in 723,980 = 20,000. 80% target = at least 26 of 32 points; reteach any form missed twice.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, the place value chart extended to millions, a calculator. Look up (or use) these 2020 census populations: Los Angeles 3,898,747; San Diego 1,386,932; San Jose 1,013,240; San Francisco 873,965; Fresno 542,107.
misconceptions: Thinking a digit one place to the left is worth '1 more' instead of '10 times as much.' Use blocks: 10 rods make a flat, so each place is ten of the place to its right.
Saying 'add a zero' when multiplying by 10 — that rule fails later with decimals. Say 'each digit moves one place to the left.'

days.guide: Have the child count 10 unit cubes and trade them for a rod, then 10 rods for a flat. Model the sentence frame 'The 4 in 40 is 10 times the 4 in 4,' then have the child write 4 more sentences for hundreds and thousands.

questions.q: How many tens are in one hundred? How many hundreds in one thousand?
questions.a: 10 tens = 100; 10 hundreds = 1,000.

questions.q: Finish: The 6 in 600 is ___ times the 6 in 60.
questions.a: 10 times.

days.guide: Start at 3 on the calculator and press × 10 = repeatedly, recording each result in the chart. Ask the child to describe what happens to the 3 each time (it moves one place left; zeros hold the empty places).

questions.q: List the results from 3 to 3,000,000.
How many times did you multiply by 10 to get from 3 to 3,000,000?
questions.a: 6 times (six zeros/six places moved).

days.guide: Show how the millions period works (millions, thousands, ones). The child writes each of the five city populations in word and expanded form and reads them aloud.

questions.q: Write 3,898,747 (Los Angeles) in word form.
questions.a: Three million, eight hundred ninety-eight thousand, seven hundred forty-seven.

questions.q: Write 873,965 (San Francisco) in expanded form.

days.guide: Model one problem in the chart: place 5,200 and 520 under each other and see the 5 is one place farther left, so it is 10 times as much. The child solves 10 problems and explains one in writing.

questions.q: How many times greater is the 5 in 5,200 than the 5 in 520?
How many times greater is the 3 in 3,000 than the 3 in 30?
questions.a: 100 times — two places left (10 × 10).

days.guide: The child draws 2 thousand-cubes and 2 flats, then explains in writing why the first is ten times the second. Check that the explanation mentions that 1,000 = 10 hundreds.

questions.q: Why is the 2 in 2,000 ten times the 2 in 200?
questions.a: 2,000 is 20 hundreds and 200 is 2 hundreds; 20 hundreds is 10 times 2 hundreds (each thousand cube is 10 flats).

weeks.assessment_key: Practice set answers (10 × relationship): 1) 7 in 700 vs 70: 10×. 2) 4 in 4,000 vs 400: 10×. 3) 9 in 90,000 vs 9,000: 10×. 4) 6 in 6,300 vs 630: 10×. 5) 8 in 800 vs 8: 100×. 6) 2 in 25,000 vs 2,500: 10×. 7) 1 in 100,000 vs 10,000: 10×. 8) 3 in 3,000 vs 30: 100×. 9) 5 in 50 vs 5: 10×. 10) 4 in 40,000 vs 400: 100×. Written explanation rubric: 4 = drawing shows 2 thousands as 20 hundreds and the sentence says 2,000 is 10 times 200 because each place is ten times the one to its right; 3 = correct drawing and statement but reasoning brief; 2 = correct answer, drawing or reasoning missing; 1 = incorrect relationship.

weeks.prep: Digit cards (two sets 0-9), long paper strips for number lines. Write these mountain heights on cards: Whitney 14,505 ft; White Mountain Peak 14,252; Shasta 14,179; Lassen Peak 10,457; San Gorgonio 11,503; Mount Diablo 3,849; Mount Tamalpais 2,571; Half Dome 8,839.
misconceptions: Comparing by the first digit you see without lining up places (thinking 9,876 > 12,001). First count digits: more digits means larger.
Placing a number like 47,800 at '47.8' on the number line or near the middle: find the two thousands it falls between first, then decide which it is closer to.

days.guide: Write two numbers stacked with places lined up and model comparing from the left until the digits differ. The child compares 12 pairs, writing the symbol and naming the deciding place.

questions.q: Compare 45,302 and 45,230. Which place decides?
questions.a: 45,302 > 45,230; the hundreds place decides (3 hundreds > 2 hundreds).

questions.q: Compare 9,876 and 12,001.
questions.a: 9,876 < 12,001 — a 4-digit number is less than a 5-digit number.

days.guide: Lay out the eight mountain cards; have the child order them least to greatest by lining up places on paper, then read the order aloud.

questions.q: Order Whitney 14,505, Shasta 14,179 and White Mountain 14,252 from least to greatest.
questions.a: 14,179 (Shasta) < 14,252 (White Mountain) < 14,505 (Whitney).

questions.q: Which is the shortest of the eight mountains?
questions.a: Mount Tamalpais, 2,571 ft.

days.guide: Each player draws 6 digit cards and builds the largest number possible, then both write the comparison with >, < or =. Ask the child to explain the strategy (largest digits in the biggest places).

questions.q: Build the largest and smallest 6-digit numbers with 8, 2, 5, 9, 0, 4.
questions.a: Largest 985,420; smallest 204,589 (0 cannot be first).
853,210 — they differ first in the tens place (1 ten > 0 tens).

days.guide: Draw a line from 40,000 to 50,000 and mark 45,000 in the middle. The child places five numbers, marking the nearest thousands first, and explains each position aloud.

questions.q: Where does 47,800 go?
questions.a: Between 47,000 and 48,000, closer to 48,000 — to the right of the 45,000 halfway mark.

questions.q: Is 43,900 to the left or right of 45,000?
questions.a: Left, because 43,900 < 45,000.

days.guide: Give the quiz without help. Correct together and have the child redo any wrong comparison by lining up places.

questions.q: Order 30,450; 30,045; 34,005 from least to greatest.

weeks.prep: Number line strips, place value chart. Approximate stadium attendance cards: Dodger Stadium game 43,651; Levi's Stadium 68,500; Oracle Park 41,915; Petco Park 40,209. Make a review game board or question cards for Day 4 and a written Unit 1 test for Day 5 (key below).
misconceptions: Rounding 4,850 to the nearest hundred as 4,800 — the 5 rule: if the digit to the right is 5 or more, round up.
Changing every digit when rounding (648,372 to nearest ten thousand written as 650,372). After rounding, every place to the right becomes 0.

days.guide: Draw a number line for 367: mark 360 and 370 and the halfway point 365, then ask where 367 sits. The child rounds 10 numbers to the nearest ten and hundred using lines, then without them.

questions.q: Round 367 to the nearest ten and nearest hundred.
questions.a: 370 (it is past 365); 400 (it is past 350).

questions.q: Round 4,850 to the nearest hundred.
questions.a: 4,900 — it is exactly halfway, and halfway rounds up.

days.guide: Model: underline the rounding place, look at the digit to its right, then round and fill zeros. The child completes 15 problems; check the first 3 before continuing.

questions.q: Round 648,372 to the nearest thousand, ten thousand and hundred thousand.
Round 295,600 to the nearest ten thousand.
questions.a: 300,000 (9 ten-thousands round up to 30 ten-thousands).

days.guide: Have the child round each stadium attendance to the nearest thousand and add the rounded numbers. Discuss when an estimate is good enough (planning, news headlines).

questions.q: Estimate 43,651 + 41,915 by rounding to the nearest thousand.
Round 40,209 to the nearest thousand.

days.guide: Play the review game, mixing cards on number forms, comparison, 'ten times' and rounding. For each miss, have the child explain the correct answer before moving on.

questions.q: Write eight hundred four thousand, sixty in standard form.
The 7 in 7,000 is how many times the 7 in 700?
questions.a: 10 times.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test independently. Score it and have the child correct misses; reteach the weakest skill next week during warm-ups.

questions.q: Round 85,499 to the nearest thousand.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test sample key: 1) 306,402 in word form: three hundred six thousand, four hundred two. 2) Expanded form of 58,217: 50,000 + 8,000 + 200 + 10 + 7. 3) Value of 6 in 462,018: 60,000. 4) The 3 in 30,000 is 10 times the 3 in 3,000. 5) 74,312 > 74,231. 6) Order 9,580; 9,058; 9,805 → 9,058 < 9,580 < 9,805. 7) Round 6,749 to nearest hundred: 6,700. 8) Round 351,826 to nearest ten thousand: 350,000. 9) Round 351,826 to nearest hundred thousand: 400,000. 10) Round 2,498 to nearest thousand: 2,000. Proficient = 8/10.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and grid paper (one digit per box). Write the 10 regrouping problems and 5 road-trip problems ahead of time, or use the samples below.
misconceptions: Forgetting to add the regrouped 1 (carried ten) in the next column. Have the child write the small 1 at the top of the next column immediately.
Misaligning places when numbers have different lengths (e.g., 4,567 + 892). Use grid paper and line up the ones column on the right.

days.guide: Model 3,456 + 2,738 with partial sums (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones), then with the standard algorithm side by side. Ask the child where the regrouped 1s in the algorithm appear in the partial sums.

questions.q: Solve 3,456 + 2,738 with partial sums.
Solve 2,519 + 1,364 with the standard algorithm.

days.guide: The child solves 10 problems on grid paper, one digit per square. Watch the first two and have the child say 'regroup' aloud every time a column is 10 or more.
Before each problem, the child rounds both addends and writes the estimate; after solving, compares the answer to the estimate and circles any answer that is far off.

questions.q: Estimate 3,892 + 4,156, then solve.
questions.a: Estimate 4,000 + 4,000 = 8,000; exact 8,048 — reasonable.

questions.q: A student got 6,084 for 2,975 + 4,109. Is that reasonable?
questions.a: No — estimate 3,000 + 4,000 = 7,000; correct answer is 7,084.

days.guide: Read each road-trip problem together and have the child underline the numbers and the question. They solve, then write the answer in a full sentence with 'miles.'

questions.q: A family drove 382 miles, then 245 miles, then 96 miles. How far in all?
Los Angeles to San Francisco is about 383 miles and San Francisco to Sacramento about 88 miles. How far is LA to Sacramento by that route?
questions.a: About 471 miles.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; the child estimates first on each problem. Score together and redo any misses.

questions.q: Estimate, then solve: 6,812 + 2,950.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks and grid paper. Prepare 12 'across zeros' problems and 5 worked problems with planted mistakes (examples below).
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column (602 - 158 = 556). Ask 'Is the top digit big enough?' before each column; if not, regroup.
Regrouping across zeros incorrectly (40,000 - 13,586). Teach: rename 4 ten-thousands as 3 ten-thousands, 9 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones.

days.guide: Build 5,203 with blocks and take away 1,476, trading a ten for ones and a hundred for tens as needed. Then record the same steps in the standard algorithm and match each trade to a crossed-out digit.

questions.q: Why did you have to trade in the tens place?
questions.a: There were 0 tens after trading one for the ones, so a hundred had to be traded for 10 tens.

days.guide: Model 40,000 - 13,586 by renaming 40,000 as 3 ten-thousands, 9 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones. The child solves 12 problems and writes a sentence explaining the regrouping for one.
For each of 8 subtraction problems, the child adds the answer to the number subtracted and checks that it equals the starting number.

questions.a: 5,655 + 2,345 = 8,000, so it is correct.
No: 4,474 + 4,836 = 9,310. The correct difference is 4,374.

days.guide: Show a worked problem with a mistake and ask the child to be the teacher: find the error, fix it and write what went wrong. Repeat for all five.

questions.q: A student wrote 602 - 158 = 556. What went wrong?
questions.a: They subtracted smaller from larger in each column instead of regrouping. Correct answer: 444.

questions.q: A student wrote 3,005 - 1,238 = 2,867. Find the error.
questions.a: Regrouping across zeros was wrong; correct answer 1,767 (1,767 + 1,238 = 3,005).

days.guide: Give the quiz and the error-analysis item independently. Have the child check each answer with addition before turning it in.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 7,302 - 2,857 = 4,445 2) 50,000 - 24,618 = 25,382 3) 63,415 - 28,739 = 34,676 4) 9,006 - 3,478 = 5,528 5) 800,000 - 1 = 799,999 6) 41,250 - 9,875 = 31,375 7) 6,004 - 2,999 = 3,005. Error analysis (8,000 - 3,627 written as 5,627): the student did not regroup across the zeros (subtracted 0 from 7, 0 from 2, etc. instead of renaming 8,000 as 7 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones); correct answer 4,373, check 4,373 + 3,627 = 8,000. Proficient: 6/7 computations plus a correct written explanation.

weeks.prep: Bar model (tape diagram) templates or blank paper. Look up or use sample state park visitor numbers for Day 3 (any realistic values). Prepare a Unit 2 test (key below).
misconceptions: Choosing the operation by keywords ('more' means add) instead of the situation. Always draw the bar model first and ask: are we finding a whole or a part?
Doing only the first step of a two-step problem. Have the child write a plan: 'First I find..., then I find...'

days.guide: Model a part-whole bar (whole on top, parts below) and a comparison bar (two bars, difference marked). The child draws 4 diagrams, labels the unknown with a letter and writes an equation.

questions.q: Mia read 1,250 pages; Sam read 375 fewer. Draw a model and find Sam's pages.
questions.a: Two bars, Sam's shorter by 375: s = 1,250 - 375 = 875 pages.

questions.q: A school has 846 students; 429 are girls. How many boys? Write an equation.

days.guide: Have the child estimate, then solve 5 two-step problems, showing each step. Ask 'Is your answer close to your estimate?'

questions.q: A library had 12,450 books, gave away 1,375 and bought 2,060. How many now?
A farm picked 3,240 apples Monday and 2,875 Tuesday and sold 4,500. How many are left?

days.guide: The child writes two multistep problems using park visitor data, solves them on a separate sheet, and trades with you. Check that each problem needs two steps and has one clear question.

questions.q: If a park had 15,400 visitors in May and 22,980 in June, how many more in June?
questions.a: 7,580 more visitors.

days.guide: The child completes the mixed review, then self-checks with the key and redoes misses. Discuss which problem types felt hardest.
Give the Unit 2 test independently; require estimates on word problems. Score and correct together.

questions.q: A theater has 2,500 seats. 1,368 adult and 947 child tickets were sold. How many seats are empty?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: 1) 34,507 + 18,965 = 53,472 2) 60,000 - 27,384 = 32,616 3) 482,716 + 39,584 = 522,300 4) 8,103 - 4,567 = 3,536 5) A park had 45,320 visitors in June and 38,915 in July; how many more in June? 6,405. 6) Theater: 2,500 - (1,368 + 947) = 185 empty seats. 7) Bar model: Jo has 1,200 stamps, Lee has 350 more than Jo; total? Lee 1,550, total 2,750. Scoring: 1 point per computation, 2 points per word problem (model/equation + correct answer). Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Counters (beans or coins), tape diagram templates. Write 10 word problems for Day 3 mixing 'how many more' and 'how many times as many.'
misconceptions: Confusing 'times as many' with 'more than': 4 times as many as 3 is 12, not 7. Build both with counters to see the difference.
In unknown-smaller problems (300 ft is 6 times as tall as the oak), multiplying 300 × 6 instead of dividing. Draw the tape: the big bar is 6 small bars.

days.guide: Build Ana's 3 shells, then 4 groups of 3 for Ben. Model the sentence '12 is 4 times as many as 3' and the equation 12 = 4 × 3; the child builds and writes 5 more.

questions.q: Ana has 3 shells. Ben has 4 times as many. How many does Ben have?
Write 35 = 5 × 7 as a comparison sentence.
questions.a: 35 is 5 times as many as 7 (or 7 times as many as 5).

days.guide: Draw a tape diagram with one small bar and a large bar made of copies of it. The child solves 6 problems, finding either the larger amount or the multiplier.

questions.q: A rope is 8 feet long. Another rope is 5 times as long. How long is it?
A tree is 42 feet tall and a bush is 7 feet tall. How many times as tall is the tree?

days.guide: The child reads each of 10 problems and sorts it into 'how many more' (subtract) or 'how many times as many' (multiply/divide), then solves.

questions.q: Sam has 18 stickers and Ana has 6. How many more does Sam have? How many times as many?
questions.a: 12 more (18 - 6); 3 times as many (18 ÷ 6).

days.guide: Model the redwood problem both ways on a tape diagram. The child solves comparison problems where the smaller quantity is unknown by dividing.

questions.q: A redwood is 6 times as tall as a 50-ft oak. How tall is the redwood?
A giraffe is 18 feet tall, which is 3 times as tall as a man. How tall is the man?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; the child must draw a tape diagram for each word problem. Correct together.

questions.q: Write a comparison statement for 24 = 6 × 4.
questions.a: 24 is 6 times as many as 4 (or 4 times as many as 6).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Statements — 1) 35 = 5 × 7: 35 is 5 times as many as 7. 2) 24 = 6 × 4: 24 is 6 times as many as 4. 3) 56 = 8 × 7: 56 is 8 times as many as 7. 4) 45 = 9 × 5: 45 is 9 times as many as 5 (either order accepted). Problems — 5) A blue ribbon is 9 in; a red one is 4 times as long: 36 in. 6) Kim has 48 cards, 6 times as many as her brother: brother has 8. 7) 72 is how many times as many as 8? 9 times. 8) A cat weighs 7 lb and a dog 35 lb: the dog is 5 times as heavy and 28 lb heavier. Proficient: 7/8 with tape diagrams.

weeks.prep: Square tiles (or paper squares), a hundreds chart, crayons. Write three riddles for Day 4 (samples below).
misconceptions: Thinking 1 is prime. A prime has exactly two factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51). Test small factors: 51 = 3 × 17.
Confusing factors and multiples. Factors go INTO a number (factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12); multiples come OUT of skip-counting (12, 24, 36...).

days.guide: Build all rectangles for 12 tiles (1×12, 2×6, 3×4) and record factor pairs. The child does 18 and 24, organizing pairs from 1 upward so none are missed.

questions.q: List the factor pairs of 18.
List the factor pairs of 24.

days.guide: For each number 1-30, the child tries to build rectangles; if only one row works, it is prime. Record a two-column chart.

questions.q: Which numbers from 1 to 30 are prime?
Is 27 prime or composite? Why?
questions.a: Composite — 27 = 3 × 9, so it has more than two factors.

days.guide: On the hundreds chart, cross out 1, circle 2 and shade its multiples, then 3, 5 and 7. The child circles the remaining numbers as primes and counts them.

questions.q: How many primes are less than 100?
Is 91 prime?

days.guide: The child lists the first 10 multiples of 6 and of 8, circles common ones, then solves riddles by listing multiples.

questions.q: What are the common multiples of 6 and 8 up to 80?
I am a multiple of 7 between 40 and 50, and I am odd. What am I?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; allow tiles. Correct together.

questions.q: List the factor pairs of 36.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Factor pairs of 36: 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6. 2) Factor pairs of 48: 1×48, 2×24, 3×16, 4×12, 6×8. 3) Prime or composite: 17 prime; 21 composite (3×7); 29 prime; 51 composite (3×17); 1 neither. 4) First 5 multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35. 5) Is 6 a factor of 84? Yes, 6 × 14 = 84. 6) Is 45 a multiple of 4? No. 7) Common multiple of 3 and 4 less than 20: 12. Proficient: 6/7.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, base-ten blocks. Prepare 8 problems for Day 3 (4-digit × 1-digit) and 8 for Day 4 (3-digit × 1-digit).
misconceptions: Partial products added incorrectly because places weren't lined up. Write each partial product on its own line, right-aligned.
In the algorithm, adding the regrouped digit before multiplying (e.g., in 6 × 378, adding the carried 4 to 7 before multiplying). Rule: multiply first, then add what was regrouped.

days.guide: Write 4 × 3, 4 × 30, 4 × 300, 4 × 3,000 and have the child solve each and say '4 times 3 tens is 12 tens = 120.' The child explains the pattern in words.

questions.q: What is 6 × 500?
questions.a: 3,000 (6 × 5 hundreds = 30 hundreds).

days.guide: Draw a rectangle for 6 × 47 split into 6 × 40 and 6 × 7. The child computes each section and adds, then does 3 × 215 split into three sections.

questions.q: 6 × 47 using an area model.
3 × 215 using an area model.

days.guide: The child solves 8 problems like 4 × 2,316 by splitting into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Check that each partial product is labeled.

Solve 3 × 254 with partial products, then with the standard algorithm, and point out where 12 (from 3 × 4) shows up as a regrouped 1. The child does 8 problems both ways at first, then algorithm only.
Give the quiz independently; area model items must show sections. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, colored pencils. Prepare 8 partial-products problems and 5 word problems.
misconceptions: Forgetting the 'cross' products in 2-digit × 2-digit (23 × 14 = 20×10 + 3×4 = 212). An area model shows all four parts.
Multiplying 20 × 30 as 60 instead of 600. Think 2 tens × 3 tens = 6 hundreds.

days.guide: Draw a rectangle for 23 × 14 split into 20 + 3 by 10 + 4 and shade each of the four parts a different color. Find each part and add. The child repeats with 36 × 25.

questions.q: 23 × 14 using an area model.
36 × 25 using an area model.

days.guide: Model listing the four partial products with labels (40 × 30, 40 × 6, 7 × 30, 7 × 6). The child solves 8 problems the same way.

questions.q: 47 × 36 with partial products.

days.guide: The child rounds both factors to the nearest ten, estimates, then computes exactly and compares.

questions.q: Estimate, then solve 48 × 31.
questions.a: Estimate 50 × 30 = 1,500; exact 1,488.

questions.q: Estimate 62 × 19.

days.guide: Read each word problem together and have the child draw a quick model, then solve and write a sentence answer.

questions.q: A theater has 24 rows with 18 seats each. How many seats?
questions.a: 432 seats.

questions.q: A Central Valley farm ships 35 cases of oranges with 64 oranges per case. How many oranges?
questions.a: 2,240 oranges.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; any strategy is allowed but work must show. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Grid paper. Prepare 6 problems for Day 1 and 4 multistep problems for Day 2; review cards for Day 4; Unit 3 test for Day 5 (key below).
misconceptions: Using the wrong order in multistep problems (adding before multiplying when the story says otherwise). Write the equation with parentheses to show the order.
Picking a slow strategy for easy numbers (area model for 25 × 4). Discuss when mental math or the algorithm is most efficient.

days.guide: The child solves 6 problems, choosing a strategy for each, and writes 2-3 sentences justifying one choice. Accept any correct strategy with a clear reason.

questions.q: 25 × 16 = ? Which strategy is quick?

days.guide: Model writing a plan and an equation with a letter. The child solves 4 multistep problems.

questions.q: Leo bought 15 packs of 24 cards and gave away 75 cards. How many are left?
A store had 6 boxes of 125 pens and sold 290. How many remain?

days.guide: Present the field trip budget: tickets for 24 students at $14 and 3 buses at $215. The child computes each cost and the total, then explains the steps.

questions.q: What is the total cost?
How much more do the buses cost than the tickets?

days.guide: Play the review game with cards on comparison, factors and multiplication. Have the child explain each answer.

questions.q: Is 57 prime or composite?
questions.a: Composite: 57 = 3 × 19.

questions.q: 36 is 4 times as many as what number?

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test independently. Score and correct together.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) 28 = 4 × 7 as a comparison: 28 is 4 times as many as 7. 2) A pine is 9 times as tall as a 5-ft bush: 45 ft. 3) Factor pairs of 30: 1×30, 2×15, 3×10, 5×6. 4) 43 is prime. 5) Common multiples of 4 and 6 below 30: 12, 24. 6) 6 × 3,208 = 19,248. 7) 54 × 27 = 1,458. 8) 12 bags of 48 marbles plus 36 loose = 612 marbles. 9) 9 × 400 = 3,600. 10) 73 × 46 = 3,358. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: 30 counters, base-ten blocks. Write the 4 remainder stories for Day 3 and 6 estimation problems for Day 4.
misconceptions: Ignoring the context when there is a remainder (answering '4 R5 vans'). Always reread the question: do we need another van (round up), drop the leftovers, or is the leftover the answer?
A remainder bigger than the divisor (23 ÷ 4 = 4 R7). If the remainder is as big as the divisor, another group can be made.

days.guide: Model 23 ÷ 4 two ways: share 23 counters into 4 piles (how many in each?) and make groups of 4 (how many groups?). Record 23 ÷ 4 = 5 R3 for both and discuss what the 3 means each time.

questions.a: 5 remainder 3.

questions.q: Share 17 counters among 5 plates. How many on each, and how many left?
questions.a: 3 on each plate, 2 left over (17 ÷ 5 = 3 R2).

days.guide: Use the fact 24 ÷ 6 = 4 to reason that 24 tens ÷ 6 = 4 tens. The child solves 12 problems saying the 'basic fact plus place value' aloud.

questions.a: 500 (35 hundreds ÷ 7 = 5 hundreds).

days.guide: Solve four stories with the child deciding what to do with the remainder each time and writing a sentence answer.

questions.q: 29 kids go on a trip; each van holds 6. How many vans?
questions.a: 29 ÷ 6 = 4 R5, so 5 vans (round up so everyone rides).

questions.q: 50 cookies go in boxes of 8. How many full boxes?
questions.a: 6 full boxes (50 ÷ 8 = 6 R2; the 2 extra are dropped).

days.guide: Model choosing a nearby number that divides easily (418 ÷ 7: 420 is 7 × 60). The child estimates 6 quotients and explains the compatible number chosen.

questions.q: Estimate 418 ÷ 7.
questions.a: About 60, because 420 ÷ 7 = 60.

questions.q: Estimate 356 ÷ 6.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. For remainder stories, require a sentence telling what was done with the remainder.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 35 ÷ 8 = 4 R3 2) 3,600 ÷ 9 = 400 3) 480 ÷ 6 = 80 4) 27 kids, 4 per canoe: 7 canoes (round up) 5) 46 in of ribbon, 6 in per bow: 7 bows (drop the 4 in) 6) Estimate 356 ÷ 6 ≈ 360 ÷ 6 = 60 7) 2,800 ÷ 7 = 400 8) 59 ÷ 9 = 6 R5. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, grid paper. Prepare 4 area-model problems, 8 partial-quotient problems and 6 check problems (samples below).
misconceptions: In partial quotients, forgetting to add the partial quotients at the end (writing only the last one). Keep a column on the right and add it.
Checking division by multiplying but forgetting to add the remainder. Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.

days.guide: Build 156 with 1 flat, 5 rods, 6 units and share into 3 groups; trade the flat for 10 rods when it can't be shared. The child records each trade.

questions.q: Why did you trade the hundred flat?
questions.a: One hundred can't be split into 3 equal groups of hundreds, so trade it for 10 tens (15 tens total) and share those.

days.guide: Draw a rectangle labeled area 432 with one side 4 and find the other side in chunks (4 × 100 = 400, 4 × 8 = 32). The child solves 3 more.

questions.q: 432 ÷ 4 using an area model.

days.guide: Model subtracting friendly multiples (×100, ×10, ×5, ×2) and listing them to the side. The child solves 8 problems.

questions.q: 584 ÷ 4 with partial quotients.

days.guide: The child multiplies each quotient by the divisor and adds the remainder to check 6 problems; mark any that don't match and fix them.

questions.q: Is 389 ÷ 4 = 96 R5 correct?
questions.a: No — the remainder 5 is bigger than 4. Correct answer 97 R1.

days.guide: Give the quiz; the child chooses area model or partial quotients but must show work and check two answers.

weeks.prep: Grid paper. Prepare a missing-digit puzzle sheet and 3 worked problems with errors for Day 4 (samples below).
misconceptions: Leaving out a zero in the quotient (1,824 ÷ 6 written as 34). Estimate first: 1,800 ÷ 6 = 300, so the answer must be in the hundreds.
Stopping partial quotients too early. Keep going until what's left is less than the divisor.

days.guide: Model 3,624 ÷ 6 using big chunks first (6 × 600 = 3,600, then 6 × 4 = 24). The child solves 6 problems.
Solve 1,824 ÷ 6 and estimate first (about 300). Discuss why there are 0 tens in the quotient (after taking 1,800 only 24 is left, which is less than 6 tens). The child solves 6 problems.

questions.q: Why is there a zero in the quotient of 2,436 ÷ 4?
questions.a: After 4 × 600 = 2,400, only 36 is left; 36 is not enough for 4 groups of 10, so the tens digit is 0. Answer 609.

days.guide: The child solves the same 3 problems with an area model and with partial quotients, then writes which was faster for each and why.
Work the puzzle sheet together for the first item, then independently. For error analysis, the child finds and fixes each mistake.

questions.q: A student wrote 2,436 ÷ 4 = 69. What's wrong?
questions.a: They dropped the zero; 69 × 4 = 276, not 2,436. Correct answer 609.

questions.q: Fill the blank: ___ ÷ 7 = 908 R1.

days.guide: Give the quiz with 8 problems; require an estimate before each. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Bar model templates. Prepare 4 multistep problems, the packing problems and the Yosemite camping task card: 7 people, 3 days; 1 food pack per person per meal, 3 meals a day; food packs come in boxes of 4 and cost $7 each; tents sleep 2; campsite costs $35 a night for 3 nights. Unit 4 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Using the wrong operation order in multistep problems. Write the plan in steps and an equation like (6 × 48) ÷ 8 = s.
Answering with a remainder when the question asks 'how many full bags' or 'how many boxes needed.' Reread the question before writing the answer.

days.guide: Model writing a plan ('First... then...') and an equation with a letter. The child solves 4 problems the same way.

questions.q: 4 boxes of 36 pencils are shared equally among 9 students. How many each? Write an equation.
Sara saved $15 a week for 8 weeks and spent $47. How much is left?

days.guide: Solve the oranges problem together, discussing what the quotient and remainder each mean. The child does 3 more packing problems.

questions.q: 1,250 oranges are packed 8 per bag. How many full bags and how many left?
questions.a: 156 full bags and 2 oranges left (156 × 8 = 1,248).

questions.q: 100 students ride buses that hold 30 each. How many buses?
questions.a: 4 buses (100 ÷ 30 = 3 R10; round up).

days.guide: Hand over the camping task card and let the child plan the steps. Check each answer and require written explanations.

questions.q: How many food packs are needed and how many boxes of 4?
questions.a: 7 people × 3 meals × 3 days = 63 packs; 63 ÷ 4 = 15 R3, so 16 boxes.

questions.q: How many tents? What does the trip cost per person (63 packs at $7 plus campsite)?

days.guide: Mixed review of division strategies and multistep problems; the child self-checks with multiplication.

questions.q: 6 packs of 48 stickers shared among 8 friends. How many each?

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test independently. Score and correct together.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) 7,236 ÷ 4 = 1,809 2) 1,250 oranges in bags of 8: 156 bags, 2 left 3) 100 students, buses of 30: 4 buses 4) (6 × 48) ÷ 8 = 36 stickers 5) 845 ÷ 5 = 169 6) 912 ÷ 6 = 152 7) 4,200 ÷ 7 = 600 8) 75 ÷ 4 = 18 R3. Camping task rubric: 4 = all answers correct (63 packs, 16 boxes, 4 tents, $546 total, $78 per person) with clear steps and remainders interpreted; 3 = one computation error but correct reasoning; 2 = several errors or remainders not interpreted; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paper strips (5 per child) for folding, fraction strips, crayons. Draw three aligned number lines 0-1 split into fourths, eighths and twelfths for Day 3.
misconceptions: Thinking 4/8 is bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger. Fold the strips: same amount of paper is shaded.
Adding the same number to top and bottom (2/3 = 3/4). Equivalent fractions come from multiplying both by the same number (cutting each piece into equal smaller pieces).

days.guide: Fold one strip in half, shade 1/2; fold again into fourths and eighths and see the shading still covers half. The child records 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 and finds 1/4 = 2/8.

questions.q: What fractions equal 1/2 on your strips?
What is 3/4 in eighths?

days.guide: Draw a rectangle in thirds, shade 2, then draw lines to split each third into 4 pieces. Count: 8 of 12. The child repeats with 3/4 = 9/12.

questions.q: Show 2/3 = 8/12 with an area model. Why does it work?
questions.a: Each third is split into 4 pieces, so there are 4 times as many pieces in the whole (12) and in the shaded part (8).

questions.q: Use an area model: 1/2 = ?/6.

days.guide: The child marks 3/4, 6/8 and 9/12 on the three aligned lines and explains why they line up.

questions.q: Why do 3/4, 6/8 and 9/12 land on the same point?
questions.a: They are the same distance from 0 — each fourth is split into 2 or 3 equal parts, so the length doesn't change.

questions.q: Name another fraction at the same point as 1/3 on a twelfths line.

days.guide: Teach the rule: multiply numerator and denominator by the same number (n/n = 1). The child generates 3 equivalents for 8 fractions and explains one with a drawing.

questions.q: Write 3 fractions equivalent to 2/5.
Why does multiplying by 3/3 not change the value?
questions.a: 3/3 equals 1, and multiplying by 1 doesn't change a number; it just cuts each piece into 3 smaller pieces.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; one item requires a model. Correct together.

questions.q: Is 3/4 = 6/8? Show how.
questions.a: Yes: 3 × 2 = 6 and 4 × 2 = 8; a drawing of fourths split into halves shows 6 of 8.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12 2) 3/5 = 6/10 3) 2/4 = 4/8 4) 5/6 = 10/12 5) 3/4 = 6/8 (yes) 6) 1/2 = 50/100 7) 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. Model explanation rubric: 4 = accurate area model or number line, explains that each part is split into the same number of smaller parts so the amount stays the same; 3 = correct model, explanation brief; 2 = correct answer, model inaccurate; 1 = incorrect.

misconceptions: Dividing the numerator and denominator by different numbers. Find a common factor and divide both by it.
Choosing a common denominator that isn't a multiple of both (rewriting 1/3 and 1/4 as tenths). List multiples of both denominators and find one in both lists.

days.guide: Model 6/8: both 6 and 8 have factor 2, so 6/8 = 3/4; check by laying fraction strips side by side. The child simplifies the rest and checks with strips.

questions.q: Rename 6/8 and 9/12 in simplest form.
Rename 10/100 in simpler form.

days.guide: List multiples of 3 and 4 to find 12; rewrite 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. The child renames several pairs.

questions.q: Rename 1/3 and 1/4 with denominator 12.
Rename 3/4 and 5/8 with a common denominator.

days.guide: Lay cards face down and play memory; a match counts only if the child explains why the two are equal.

questions.q: Is 4/10 equal to 2/5? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes — divide 4 and 10 by 2 to get 2/5.

days.guide: Pose the flour question and have the child draw measuring cups. Then solve 2-3 more recipe equivalence problems.

questions.q: Is 2/4 cup of flour the same as 1/2 cup?
questions.a: Yes — a cup split into 4 parts with 2 filled is the same amount as half the cup.

questions.q: A recipe needs 3/4 cup of milk but you only have a 1/8 cup measure. How many scoops?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; allow strips for checking. Correct together.

questions.q: Simplify 8/12.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, number lines. Write 12 fractions on cards for sorting (e.g., 1/3, 3/8, 2/5, 4/10, 1/2, 3/6, 6/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4, 7/10, 5/6).
misconceptions: Thinking larger denominators mean larger fractions (1/8 > 1/4). Show strips: more pieces means smaller pieces.
Comparing numerators only when denominators differ (3/5 < 4/10?). Rename to a common denominator or use a benchmark first.

days.guide: Model: a fraction is half when the numerator is half the denominator. The child sorts 12 cards into <1/2, =1/2, >1/2 and explains each.

questions.q: Is 3/8 less than, equal to or greater than 1/2?
questions.a: Less — half of 8 is 4, and 3 < 4.

questions.q: Compare 2/5 and 5/8 using 1/2.

days.guide: Compare 3/5 and 3/8 with strips: same number of pieces, but fifths are bigger. The child solves 8 more and explains with piece size.

questions.q: Compare 3/5 and 3/8.
questions.a: 3/5 > 3/8 — both have 3 pieces, but fifths are larger than eighths.

questions.q: Compare 2/3 and 2/5.

days.guide: Model renaming 5/6 and 7/8 to 24ths (20/24 and 21/24). The child solves 10 problems.

questions.q: Compare 5/6 and 7/8.
Compare 3/4 and 7/12.

days.guide: The child places sets of four fractions on a 0-1 number line and writes a justification.

questions.q: Order 1/2, 1/3, 3/4, 5/12 from least to greatest.
Which is closest to 1: 7/8, 4/5, 9/10?
questions.a: 9/10 — it is only 1/10 away; 4/5 is 1/5 away and 7/8 is 1/8 away.

days.guide: Give the quiz; each comparison needs a reason (benchmark, piece size or common denominator).

questions.q: Compare 7/10 and 68/100.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 2/3 > 2/5 2) 3/10 < 1/2 3) 5/6 < 7/8 4) 4/8 = 2/4 5) 3/4 > 7/12 6) 1/5 < 1/4 7) Order 1/4, 3/8, 2/3, 5/6 (already least to greatest) 8) 7/10 > 68/100. Explanation rubric: proficient answers name a valid method (benchmark 1/2, same numerator/piece size, or common denominator) for each.

weeks.prep: Paper circles of two sizes (one about 4 in across, one about 8 in). Write 4 student claims for Day 2, e.g., '1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4'; '2/3 = 3/4 because each is one piece away from a whole'; '4/6 = 2/3'; '1/2 of my pizza is more than 1/2 of yours'. Unit 5 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Comparing fractions of different-sized wholes. Fraction comparisons only work when the wholes are the same size.
'Missing one piece' reasoning (2/3 = 3/4 because both are one piece short). The missing pieces are different sizes: 1/3 > 1/4, so 2/3 < 3/4.

days.guide: Cut 1/2 of the small circle and 1/4 of the large circle and compare. Discuss: which is more? The child writes why the whole matters.

questions.q: Can 1/4 of a large pizza be more than 1/2 of a small pizza?
questions.a: Yes — fractions of different wholes can't be compared by the fraction alone; a quarter of a big pizza can be more food.

days.guide: Read each claim aloud; the child decides agree or disagree and writes an argument with a model.

questions.q: Claim: 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4. Agree or disagree?
questions.a: Disagree — eighths are smaller pieces; 1/8 < 1/4.

questions.q: Claim: 2/3 = 3/4 because each is one piece away from a whole.
questions.a: Disagree — the missing 1/3 is bigger than the missing 1/4, so 2/3 < 3/4.

days.guide: The child solves 6 comparison stories, writing the comparison with a symbol and a sentence.

questions.q: Lily ran 3/4 mile and Ben ran 5/8 mile. Who ran farther?
Jo ate 2/6 of a pan of brownies and Max ate 1/3 of the same pan. Who ate more?
questions.a: They ate the same amount: 2/6 = 1/3.

days.guide: Review game with equivalence and comparison cards. The child explains each answer.

questions.q: Write two fractions equivalent to 3/5.
Compare 4/6 and 5/8.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test independently. Correct together.

questions.q: Compare 2/3 and 7/12.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: 1) 2/3 = 8/12 2) 3/4 = 75/100 3) 10/12 = 5/6 (simplest form) 4) 3/8 < 1/2 5) 4/5 > 4/7 6) 5/6 > 3/4 (10/12 vs 9/12) 7) 2/10 < 25/100 8) Order 1/6, 2/3, 1/2 → 1/6, 1/2, 2/3 9) Explain: 1/3 of a big pizza vs 1/3 of a small pizza — not equal because the wholes are different sizes. 10) Ben: 3/8 mi, Ana 1/2 mi — Ana ran farther. Proficient: 8/10 with explanations.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, number lines drawn in fourths and fifths.
misconceptions: Thinking a fraction can only be broken into unit fractions. 5/8 = 2/8 + 3/8 too — any parts that add to 5 eighths work.
Converting 9/4 to a mixed number as 9 1/4 or 2 4/1. Count groups of 4/4: 9/4 = 4/4 + 4/4 + 1/4 = 2 1/4.

days.guide: Lay out five 1/8 strips to show 5/8 and write it as a sum of unit fractions, then regroup the strips to show other sums.

questions.q: Write 5/8 three different ways as a sum.
Write 3/5 as a sum of unit fractions.

days.guide: The child writes 3 decompositions for each of 6 fractions and builds one with strips to justify it.

questions.q: Give three decompositions of 7/10.
Decompose 1 3/8 using 1 whole.

days.guide: On a number line in fourths, count past 1 and 2 and label both 9/4 and 2 1/4 at the same point. The child converts 10 problems both directions.

questions.q: Write 13/5 as a mixed number.
Write 3 2/3 as a fraction.

days.guide: Draw jumps of 1/4 from 0 to 2 1/4 and count them. The child writes the matching equation.

questions.q: How many jumps of 1/4 reach 2 1/4? Write the equation.
How many jumps of 1/3 reach 2?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

questions.q: Write 7/4 as a mixed number.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, number lines.
misconceptions: Adding denominators (3/8 + 4/8 = 7/16). The pieces stay eighths; count how many eighths you have.
Subtracting from 1 without renaming (1 - 3/8 = 2/8?). Rename 1 as 8/8 first: 8/8 - 3/8 = 5/8.

days.guide: Model 3/8 + 4/8 with strips and say 'three eighths plus four eighths is seven eighths.' The child solves 10 problems writing equations.

questions.a: The pieces are still fifths; you have 3 fifths, 3/5. The size of the pieces doesn't change when you add.

days.guide: On a number line show 1 - 3/8 by starting at 8/8 and jumping back 3 eighths. The child solves several subtraction problems.
The child solves 6 word problems, drawing a strip or number line for each and writing a sentence.

questions.q: Maya painted 3/6 of a fence and Leo painted 2/6. How much is painted? How much is left?
questions.a: 5/6 painted; 1/6 left.

questions.q: A pizza had 8 slices; Sam ate 3/8 and Kim ate 2/8. How much was eaten?
questions.a: 5/8 of the pizza.

days.guide: Add 5/6 + 4/6 with strips and show that 6/6 make a whole, leaving 3/6 more: 1 3/6. The child renames several sums.
Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips (several wholes). Write 8 addition and 8 subtraction mixed-number problems plus trail/rainfall problems.
misconceptions: Leaving an improper part in the answer (3 6/4). Regroup: 6/4 = 1 2/4, so 3 6/4 = 4 2/4.
Subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger when the top fraction is too small (3 1/4 - 1 3/4 = 2 2/4). Rename 1 whole: 3 1/4 = 2 5/4.

days.guide: Model 2 3/8 + 1 2/8: add wholes (3), add parts (5/8). Then show the same by renaming as 19/8 + 10/8 = 29/8 = 3 5/8. The child solves 8 problems.
Model 1 3/4 + 2 3/4 = 3 6/4 and regroup to 4 2/4. The child solves problems and regroups each answer.
Model 3 1/4 - 1 3/4 by trading one whole for 4/4 (2 5/4 - 1 3/4 = 1 2/4). The child solves 8 problems.

questions.a: 2 2/3 (rename 5 as 4 3/3).

days.guide: The child solves trail and rainfall problems, writing units in each answer.

questions.q: A trail has two parts: 3 5/8 miles and 2 7/8 miles. How long is it?
questions.a: 6 4/8 miles (= 6 1/2 miles).

questions.q: It rained 3 7/10 inches in January and 2 4/10 inches in February. How much more in January?
questions.a: 1 3/10 inches.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips, measuring cups (including 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 3/4 cup if available), flour or rice for scooping, a muffin recipe that uses 3/4 cup amounts.
misconceptions: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the whole number (3 × 2/5 = 6/15). Think 3 groups of 2 fifths = 6 fifths = 6/5.
Not knowing where the answer lies between whole numbers. Rename the improper fraction as a mixed number: 10/3 = 3 1/3 is between 3 and 4.

days.guide: Lay out five 1/4 strips and write 5/4 = 5 × 1/4. The child writes 6 similar equations from strips.

questions.q: Write 5/4 as a multiple of a unit fraction.

days.guide: On a number line in fifths, make 3 jumps of 2/5 and see they land at 6/5. The child solves 10 problems.
Measure 3/4 cup three times into a bowl and see how many cups result. Record 3 × 3/4 = 9/4 = 2 1/4 cups, then scale 2 more ingredients.

questions.q: Triple 3/4 cup of milk.
Triple 2/3 cup of sugar.
questions.a: 6/3 = 2 cups.

days.guide: The child solves 6 word problems and names the two whole numbers each answer lies between.

questions.q: 5 students each drink 2/3 cup of juice. How much juice? Between which whole numbers?
questions.a: 10/3 = 3 1/3 cups; between 3 and 4.

questions.q: A recipe uses 3/8 cup of oil per batch. How much for 6 batches?
questions.a: 18/8 = 2 2/8 (= 2 1/4) cups; between 2 and 3.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

weeks.prep: A ruler marked in eighths of an inch, 15 pencils or leaves, grid paper for the line plot. Unit 6 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Starting measurement at the end of the ruler instead of the 0 mark. Line the object up with 0.
Uneven or unlabeled scales on the line plot. Mark every 1/8 between the smallest and largest values at equal spaces, even if no data lands there.

days.guide: Model measuring one pencil: line up at 0, find the last whole inch, then count eighths past it. The child measures and records all 15 to the nearest 1/8 inch.

questions.q: A pencil ends 3 marks past 5 on a ruler with eighths. How long is it?
questions.a: 5 3/8 inches.

questions.q: How many eighths are in 1/2 inch?
questions.a: 4 eighths (4/8).

days.guide: Draw a number line from the shortest to the longest measurement in eighths, label every tick, and place an X for each item. Check that equal spaces represent equal amounts.

questions.q: If the data run from 4 2/8 to 6 1/8 inches, what are the first and last labels on the plot?
questions.a: 4 2/8 (or 4 1/4) and 6 1/8, with every eighth between them labeled.

days.guide: Ask questions from the plot; the child shows each computation with fractions.

questions.q: The longest pencil is 6 7/8 in and the shortest 5 3/8 in. What is the difference?
questions.a: 1 4/8 inches (= 1 1/2 in).

questions.q: Three leaves each measure 4 1/2 inches. What is their total length?

days.guide: Mixed review of fraction addition, subtraction, multiplication and line plots; self-check with a key.
Give the Unit 6 test independently and collect the line plot as the product.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 2) 4 2/5 + 1 4/5 = 6 1/5 3) 1 - 5/12 = 7/12 4) 5 1/3 - 2 2/3 = 2 2/3 5) 4 × 2/5 = 8/5 = 1 3/5 6) 3 × 3/4 cup = 2 1/4 cups 7) 3 6/8 - 2 3/8 = 1 3/8 (line plot range) 8) 5 - 1 3/4 = 3 1/4. Line plot rubric: 4 = title, fraction scale in equal eighths labeled, all 15 data points correct, two questions answered correctly; 3 = one labeling or plotting error; 2 = scale uneven or several data errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: 10 dimes and 30 pennies (real or play), printed hundred grids (10+), a 0-1 number line strip marked in tenths.
misconceptions: Writing 3/100 as 0.3. Tenths are the first place after the decimal point and hundredths the second: 3/100 = 0.03.
Thinking 0.30 is more than 0.3 because it has more digits. 3 dimes = 30 pennies: 0.3 = 0.30.

days.guide: Show 3 dimes as 3/10 of a dollar and trade them for 30 pennies: 30/100. Write both as $0.30 and as decimals 0.3 and 0.30.

questions.q: Write 3 dimes as a fraction of a dollar and as a decimal.
7 pennies is what fraction of a dollar? As a decimal?

days.guide: Shade 45 squares on a hundred grid and write 45/100 = 0.45. The child shades 10 grids for given decimals and writes both forms.

questions.q: Shade 0.6 on a hundred grid. How many squares?
questions.a: 60 squares (6 columns) — 6/10 = 60/100.

questions.q: Write 0.08 as a fraction.

days.guide: Model 3/10 = 30/100, so 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100. The child solves 10 problems.
The child places 0.3, 0.45, 0.7 and 0.09 on a 0-1 line marked in tenths, estimating hundredths between tenths.

questions.q: Where does 0.45 go?
questions.a: Halfway between 0.4 and 0.5.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

questions.q: Write 52/100 as a decimal and 0.9 as a fraction.

weeks.prep: Hundred grids, a meter stick marked in centimeters, a list of race times for Day 4 (e.g., Ana 12.45 s, Ben 12.5 s, Cal 12.09 s, Dee 12.4 s).
misconceptions: Thinking 0.38 > 0.4 because 38 > 4. Write 0.4 as 0.40 or shade both on grids.
In race times, thinking the larger number wins. In races, the smallest time is fastest.

days.guide: Shade 0.4 on one grid and 0.38 on another and compare. Teach writing 0.4 as 0.40 to compare hundredths.

questions.q: Which is greater, 0.4 or 0.38? Why?
questions.a: 0.4 — it is 40 hundredths, and 40 > 38.
