questions.q: Compare 0.7 and 0.71.

days.guide: Measure a table: 1 meter and 23 centimeters = 1.23 m. The child measures 6 objects, writes meters with hundredths, and orders them.

questions.q: An object is 85 cm long. Write it in meters.

days.guide: The child compares 12 pairs and orders 3 sets, lining up decimal points.

questions.q: Compare 2.06 and 2.6.
questions.a: 2.06 < 2.6 (6 hundredths < 60 hundredths).

days.guide: Rank the runners by time and discuss why the smallest time wins.

questions.q: Who ran faster: 12.45 seconds or 12.5 seconds?
questions.a: 12.45 seconds — it is less time than 12.50.

questions.q: Rank 12.45, 12.5, 12.09, 12.4 from fastest to slowest.

days.guide: Give the quiz; one comparison must be explained with a shaded grid.

questions.q: Compare 0.6 and 0.59 with a grid model.
questions.a: 0.6 > 0.59: 60 squares shaded vs 59 squares.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 0.4 > 0.38 2) 0.7 < 0.71 3) 0.25 < 0.3 4) 0.09 < 0.1 5) 0.5 = 0.50 6) 1.2 > 1.02 7) 0.83 > 0.8 8) 0.6 > 0.59 9) 3.45 < 3.5 10) 0.99 < 1.0. Grid explanation: proficient shows both grids correctly shaded and says which has more hundredths. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: Play money (bills, dimes, pennies), grocery ads or printed prices. Unit 7 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Writing $1.05 as $1.5. Cents are hundredths: 5 cents = 0.05.
Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points when adding money. Line up decimal points (or think in cents).

days.guide: Show $2.45 with bills and coins and write it as 2 45/100 dollars. The child writes 10 amounts as decimals and fractions.

questions.q: Write 3 dollars and 45 cents as a decimal and a mixed number.
Write 6 dimes and 2 pennies as a decimal of a dollar.
questions.a: $0.62 = 62/100 of a dollar.

days.guide: Give two prices from the ads (e.g., cereal $3.89 vs $3.98) and have the child decide which costs less by comparing places.

questions.q: Which costs less: $3.89 or $3.98?
questions.a: $3.89 — 8 dimes is less than 9 dimes.

questions.q: Which is greater: $5.09 or $5.10?

days.guide: Model thinking in cents: $4.75 + $2.80 = 475 + 280 = 755 cents = $7.55. The child solves 5 problems.

questions.q: You buy items for $4.75 and $2.80 and pay with $10. How much change?
Milk costs $3.29. How much for 2 cartons?

days.guide: Mixed review of tenths, hundredths and comparison; the child self-checks.

questions.q: Write 0.4 as hundredths.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test independently. Correct together.

weeks.prep: Meter stick and tape measure, kitchen scale (grams and ounces), measuring cups, a 1-liter bottle and a 250 mL cup, a clock. Key facts: 1 m = 100 cm; 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 lb = 16 oz; 1 L = 1,000 mL; 1 hr = 60 min; 1 min = 60 s; 1 ft = 12 in; 1 yd = 3 ft.
misconceptions: Converting in the wrong direction (3 m = 3/100 cm). A bigger unit becomes MORE of the smaller unit, so multiply.
Confusing mass and size (a big balloon weighs more than a small rock). Weigh to check.

days.guide: Measure the hallway in meters and leftover centimeters and convert to centimeters. The child completes a table for 1-10 meters.

questions.q: How many centimeters are in 3 meters? In 10 meters?
The hallway is 4 m 35 cm. How many centimeters?

days.guide: Weigh 5 items and record grams and ounces. The child builds kg-g and lb-oz tables for 1-5.

questions.q: How many grams are in 4 kilograms?
How many ounces are in 3 pounds?
questions.a: 48 oz.

days.guide: Fill the liter bottle with the 250 mL cup and count (4 cups). The child makes a liter-milliliter table for 1-5 liters.

questions.q: How many 250 mL cups fill 1 liter?
How many milliliters are in 3 liters?

days.guide: The child converts hours to minutes and minutes to seconds and makes a soccer schedule table (e.g., two 25-minute halves and a 10-minute break).

questions.q: How many minutes is 2 hours?
questions.a: 120 minutes.

questions.q: A game has two 25-minute halves and a 10-minute halftime. How long is it?
questions.a: 60 minutes = 1 hour.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

questions.q: Which is longer, 1 km or 900 m?
questions.a: 1 km, because 1 km = 1,000 m.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 7 m = 700 cm 2) 4 kg = 4,000 g 3) 3 lb = 48 oz 4) 2 L = 2,000 mL 5) 5 hr = 300 min 6) 4 min = 240 s 7) 6 ft = 72 in 8) 1 km > 900 m 9) Complete the table yd → ft: 1→3, 2→6, 3→9, 4→12 10) Which unit to measure a pencil's mass: grams. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: Number line templates and an analog clock. Prepare 6 elapsed-time problems and mixed-unit problems (samples below).
misconceptions: Subtracting times like regular numbers (12:20 - 9:45 = 2:75). Use a number line jumping to the next hour.
Regrouping 1 foot as 10 inches. 1 ft = 12 in, 1 hr = 60 min; regroup using the right number.

days.guide: Draw a number line from 9:45: jump 15 min to 10:00, 2 hours to 12:00, 20 min to 12:20, and add the jumps. The child solves 6 problems.

questions.q: A train leaves Sacramento at 9:45 and arrives at 12:20. How long is the trip?
questions.a: 2 hours 35 minutes.

questions.q: A movie starts at 1:50 and lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. When does it end?

days.guide: Model 3 ft 4 in - 1 ft 10 in by regrouping 1 ft as 12 in (2 ft 16 in - 1 ft 10 in). The child solves 5 problems.

questions.q: 3 ft 4 in - 1 ft 10 in = ?
questions.a: 1 ft 6 in.

questions.q: 2 hr 40 min + 1 hr 35 min = ?
questions.a: 4 hr 15 min.

days.guide: Use the clock to show 3/4 of an hour and a scale or table to show 1/2 kg. The child solves several fractions-of-units problems.

questions.q: How many minutes are in 3/4 of an hour?
questions.a: 45 minutes.

questions.q: How many grams are in 1/2 kg?

days.guide: The child plans a weekend schedule with start/end times and drive times, checking each elapsed time.

questions.q: You leave at 8:30 a.m. and drive 2 hours 50 minutes. When do you arrive?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

questions.q: 5 yd 1 ft - 2 yd 2 ft = ?
questions.a: 2 yd 2 ft.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 9:45 to 12:20 = 2 hr 35 min 2) Start 1:50, 1 hr 45 min later = 3:35 3) 3 ft 4 in - 1 ft 10 in = 1 ft 6 in 4) 2 hr 40 min + 1 hr 35 min = 4 hr 15 min 5) 3/4 hr = 45 min 6) 1/2 kg = 500 g 7) 2 L - 750 mL = 1,250 mL 8) 5 yd 1 ft - 2 yd 2 ft = 2 yd 2 ft. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: Tape measure, grid paper. Formulas: area = length × width; perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width. Unit 8 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Mixing up area and perimeter. Perimeter is the distance around (a fence, in feet); area is the space inside (carpet, in square feet).
Forgetting to label units, or using 'feet' for area. Area is in square units.

days.guide: Measure one room together to the nearest foot and compute area and perimeter; the child measures a second room alone.

questions.q: A room is 12 ft by 10 ft. Find the area and perimeter.
questions.a: Area 120 sq ft; perimeter 44 ft.

questions.q: Which would you need to know to buy carpet?
questions.a: Area.

days.guide: Model: area 48 sq ft and length 8 ft → 8 × w = 48, w = 6. The child solves 10 problems.

questions.q: A rectangle has area 48 sq ft and length 8 ft. What is the width?
questions.a: 6 ft.

questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 30 ft and length 9 ft. What is the width?

days.guide: The child draws every whole-foot rectangle with perimeter 24 ft on grid paper, finds each area, and picks the largest.

questions.q: Which rectangles have perimeter 24 ft and what are their areas?
Which gives the largest garden?
questions.a: The 6 ft by 6 ft square, 36 sq ft.

days.guide: Mixed review of conversions, measurement problems, area and perimeter.

questions.q: How many inches are in 4 feet?
questions.a: 48 in.

questions.q: A square has sides of 7 cm. Area and perimeter?
questions.a: Area 49 sq cm; perimeter 28 cm.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test and collect the garden design as the task.

questions.q: A patio is 15 ft by 6 ft. What is its area?
questions.a: 90 sq ft.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test key: 1) 6 m = 600 cm 2) 5 lb = 80 oz 3) 3 hr = 180 min 4) 10:40 to 1:15 = 2 hr 35 min 5) 4 ft 2 in - 1 ft 8 in = 2 ft 6 in 6) 12 ft by 10 ft room: area 120 sq ft, perimeter 44 ft 7) Area 56 sq m, length 8 m: width 7 m 8) Perimeter 40 in, width 5 in: length 15 in 9) 1/4 hr = 15 min. Garden task rubric: 4 = lists all 6 whole-number rectangles with perimeter 24 ft, areas correct, identifies 6×6 (36 sq ft) as largest and explains; 3 = most rectangles with correct conclusion; 2 = some areas wrong or conclusion unsupported; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Ruler, an index card (its corner is a right angle), colored pencils, a printed map of a San Francisco grid neighborhood (e.g., the Sunset District, where numbered avenues run north-south and named streets run east-west), a paper circle cut into fourths.
misconceptions: Confusing a line (arrows both ends, goes on forever), a ray (one endpoint, one arrow) and a segment (two endpoints).
Thinking an angle's size depends on the length of its sides. The size is the amount of turn between the rays.

days.guide: Model drawing and labeling a point A, line AB, segment CD and ray EF. The child makes a geometry dictionary page for each with a picture and definition.

questions.q: What is the difference between a ray and a line segment?
questions.a: A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction; a segment has two endpoints.

questions.q: How many endpoints does a line have?
questions.a: None — it goes on forever in both directions.

days.guide: Hold the index card corner in an angle: if it matches, it is right; smaller is acute; bigger (but less than a straight line) is obtuse. The child finds and classifies 10 angles at home.

questions.q: An angle is smaller than the corner of the card. What type is it?
questions.a: Acute (less than 90°).

questions.q: What is the angle formed by the hands of a clock at 3:00?
questions.a: A right angle (90°).

days.guide: Explain parallel (never meet, always same distance) and perpendicular (meet at right angles). The child traces examples of each on the map.

questions.q: On a street grid, are two numbered avenues parallel or perpendicular?
questions.a: Parallel — they run side by side and never meet.

questions.q: An avenue crossing a street at a square corner is ___.
questions.a: Perpendicular.

days.guide: Turn a paper circle-fourth around the center: 1/4 turn = 90°, 1/2 turn = 180°, 3/4 turn = 270°, full = 360°.

questions.q: How many degrees is a 1/4 turn? A 3/4 turn?
How many degrees in a full turn?

days.guide: Give the quiz independently. Correct together.

questions.q: Classify an angle of 135°.
questions.a: Obtuse.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Draw a ray: one endpoint with an arrow 2) Draw a segment: two endpoints 3) Draw parallel lines: never meet 4) Draw perpendicular lines: meet at a right angle 5) 40° = acute 6) 90° = right 7) 150° = obtuse 8) 180° = straight angle 9) 1/2 turn = 180° 10) Point = an exact location. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: Protractor, ruler, a printed sheet of 10 angles, pattern blocks (hexagon, square, triangle, trapezoid, blue rhombus, tan rhombus).
misconceptions: Reading the wrong scale on the protractor (calling a 40° angle 140°). First decide if the angle is acute or obtuse, then choose the scale that matches.
Not lining up the center point and the zero line. Put the center hole on the vertex and one ray on 0.

days.guide: Model placing the protractor's center on the vertex, one ray on 0, and reading where the other ray crosses, starting from the 0 used. The child measures 10 angles and estimates first.

questions.q: An acute angle's ray crosses at 50 on one scale and 130 on the other. Which is right?
questions.a: 50° — an acute angle is less than 90°.

questions.q: Measure a right angle. What should it read?

days.guide: Model drawing a 35° angle: draw a ray, place the protractor, mark 35, connect. The child draws 35°, 90°, 125° and 160° and you check.

questions.q: Is a 125° angle acute, right or obtuse?
questions.a: Obtuse.

questions.q: When drawing 160°, about how open should it look?
questions.a: Nearly a straight line — only 20° short of 180°.

days.guide: Draw a ray inside a right angle to split it and measure both parts; the parts add to 90°. The child solves 6 unknown-angle problems.

questions.q: A right angle is split into 35° and x. Find x.
A straight angle is split into 110° and y. Find y.

days.guide: Fit copies of each block around a point; since a full turn is 360°, divide by the number of copies.

questions.q: How many hexagons fit around a point? What is each angle?
Six triangles fit around a point. Each angle?

days.guide: Give the quiz; you check drawn angles with the protractor (±2°).

questions.q: Angles of 25° and 40° together make what angle?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Measuring items should be checked against the printed sheet (±2°). Sample answers: 1) Measure angle shown at 70°: 70° 2) Draw 45°, 3) draw 120° (checked ±2°) 4) x + 30° = 90°: x = 60° 5) 180° - 75° = 105° 6) 25° + 40° = 65° 7) A square block corner = 90° 8) Four 90° angles around a point = 360°. Proficient: 7/8.

weeks.prep: Paper shapes (12 triangles: right, acute, obtuse; and squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms, trapezoids), a small mirror, scissors, printed capital letters. Unit 9 test for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking a square isn't a rectangle. A rectangle has 4 right angles; a square has 4 right angles plus 4 equal sides, so every square is a rectangle.
Calling a diagonal of a rectangle a line of symmetry. Fold to test: the halves must match exactly.

days.guide: Use the index card corner to check each triangle's angles; sort into right (one 90°), obtuse (one more than 90°) and acute (all less than 90°).

questions.q: A triangle has angles 30°, 60°, 90°. What type is it?
questions.a: Right triangle.

questions.q: Can a triangle have two right angles?
questions.a: No — two 90° angles would already be 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.

days.guide: Sort quadrilaterals by parallel sides and right angles into a hierarchy chart: quadrilateral → trapezoid/parallelogram → rectangle, rhombus → square.

questions.q: Which quadrilaterals have two pairs of parallel sides?
questions.a: Parallelograms, including rectangles, rhombuses and squares.

questions.q: Is every square a rhombus?
questions.a: Yes — it has 4 equal sides.

days.guide: Fold shapes and letters to find lines where halves match; check with the mirror.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? A rectangle (non-square)?
How many lines of symmetry in the letters A and H?
questions.a: A has 1 (vertical); H has 2 (vertical and horizontal).

days.guide: Play shape riddles: you give clues, the child names the shape.

questions.q: I have 4 equal sides and no right angles. What am I?
questions.a: A rhombus.

questions.q: I have exactly one pair of parallel sides.
questions.a: A trapezoid.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test independently. Correct together.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key: 1) Ray: one endpoint 2) Perpendicular lines form right angles 3) 65° = acute, 90° = right, 115° = obtuse 4) Measure/draw 140° (±2°) 5) x + 55° = 90°: x = 35° 6) Triangle with angles 100°, 40°, 40°: obtuse 7) A square is a rectangle and a rhombus 8) A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides (by the definition used in this course) 9) Lines of symmetry: square 4, rectangle 2, equilateral triangle 3 10) Letter with no line of symmetry: e.g., F, G, J, L, N, P, R, S, Z. Proficient: 8/10.

weeks.prep: Pattern blocks, graph paper. Prepare 6 input/output tables (rules like +5, ×4, ×2 + 1).
misconceptions: Assuming a pattern rule from only two terms. Check the rule against every term in the table.
Describing only the step ('add 3') without noticing features. Ask: what else do you notice (odd/even, ones digits)?

days.guide: Generate 'start at 1, add 3' together for 10 terms. Ask why the terms alternate odd and even (adding an odd number switches odd to even and back).

questions.q: List the first 6 terms of 'start at 1, add 3'.
Why do the terms alternate odd and even?
questions.a: Odd + odd (3) = even, and even + odd = odd, so each step switches.

days.guide: Build figure 1 (4 tiles), figure 2 (7 tiles), figure 3 (10 tiles), adding 3 each time. The child predicts figure 10 without building it.

questions.q: If figure 1 has 4 tiles and each figure adds 3, how many in figure 10?
How many in figure 5?
questions.a: 16 tiles.

days.guide: The child completes 6 input/output tables and writes the rule for each, testing it on every pair.

questions.q: In: 2, 5, 7 → Out: 8, 20, 28. What is the rule?
questions.a: Multiply by 4.

questions.q: In: 1, 3, 6 → Out: 3, 7, 13. What is the rule?
questions.a: Multiply by 2, then add 1.

days.guide: The child designs an original pattern with a rule and writes 3 observations about it.

questions.q: Rule: start at 5, add 5. Name 2 features.
questions.a: Terms: 5, 10, 15, 20...; ones digits alternate 5 and 0; every term is a multiple of 5; terms alternate odd and even.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the project.

questions.q: Rule 'start at 2, multiply by 2'. List 5 terms.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Start at 3, add 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 2) Feature: all terms are odd 3) Start at 50, subtract 6: 50, 44, 38, 32, 26 4) Table In 2, 4, 6 → Out 7, 9, 11: rule add 5 5) In 3, 5, 8 → Out 9, 15, 24: rule ×3 6) Figure n has 3n + 1 tiles pattern: figure 10 = 31 tiles. Project rubric: 4 = clear rule, at least 6 correct terms, 3 accurate observations; 3 = rule and terms correct, observations weak; 2 = errors in terms; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print the week 1 diagnostic for comparison, a self-check review key, an end-of-year test (key below), poster paper and markers.
misconceptions: Rushing on cumulative tests. Teach: estimate first, then check each answer with the inverse operation.
Forgetting units and labels on project work. Every answer gets a unit (miles, dollars, hours).

days.guide: The child completes the mixed whole-number review, then self-checks and redoes misses.

questions.q: Round 476,512 to the nearest ten thousand.

days.guide: The child completes the fraction, decimal and measurement review and self-checks.

questions.q: Compare 3/4 and 0.7.

days.guide: Give the cumulative assessment without help, then compare scores with the week 1 diagnostic together and celebrate growth.
The child plans a California road trip poster: distances, gas cost and drive time, showing all work.

questions.q: A 360-mile trip at 60 miles per hour takes how long?
questions.a: 6 hours.

questions.q: Gas costs $5 per gallon and the car uses 12 gallons. What is the cost?

days.guide: The child presents the poster to family and writes a reflection on the most improved skill.

questions.q: What skill improved most this year, and what evidence shows it?
questions.a: Answers vary; a strong answer names a skill (e.g., fraction comparison) and cites a test score or example from work.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year assessment key (sample items): 1) 504,309 in word form: five hundred four thousand, three hundred nine 2) Round 476,512 to nearest ten thousand: 480,000 3) 63,207 - 28,519 = 34,688 4) 4 × 2,345 = 9,380 5) 38 × 26 = 988 6) 6,432 ÷ 8 = 804 7) 3/4 = 9/12 8) 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 4 2/5 9) 5 × 2/3 = 3 1/3 10) 0.75 > 0.7 11) 3 hr 20 min = 200 min 12) Perimeter of 9 ft by 4 ft: 26 ft; area 36 sq ft 13) Angle of 120° is obtuse 14) Factor pairs of 20: 1×20, 2×10, 4×5. Proficient: 80%. Project presentation rubric: 4 = all computations correct and labeled, clear explanation, answers questions; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several errors or unclear; 1 = incomplete.

PE.overview: Fourth-grade PE runs 30 minutes a day: the child leads the dynamic warm-up, practices a skill with 3–5 cues, applies it in a game or challenge, and cools down. Demonstrate each skill, give one specific correction at a time, and use the weekly skill check or log so the child compares to their own earlier results. FITNESSGRAM-style tests in weeks 2 and 34 frame the year; stress safety (spotting, soft landings, bat and rope safety), honest calls and encouraging teammates in every game.

weeks.prep: Clear a safe area with cones for boundaries; sneakers and a water bottle. Stopwatch or phone timer. Make a heart-rate log (activity, beats in 15 seconds, × 4 = bpm) and a water tally.
misconceptions: Thinking static stretching is the best warm-up. Warm up with moving (dynamic) exercises; save held stretches for the cool-down.
Counting the pulse for a full minute while it drops. Count for 15 seconds right after exercise and multiply by 4.

days.guide: Demonstrate the 5 moves (high knees, butt kicks, arm circles, walking lunges, inchworms), about 1 minute each. Then the child leads it once, calling out each move and checking form (knee over ankle in lunges, flat back in inchworms).

questions.q: Name the 5 moves in our warm-up.
questions.a: High knees, butt kicks, arm circles, lunges, inchworms.

questions.q: Why do we warm up?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and muscle temperature and loosen joints so the body performs better and is less likely to get hurt.

days.guide: Find the pulse at the neck or wrist with two fingers. Count 15 seconds at rest, × 4, log it. Do 2 minutes of jumping jacks and count again right away.

questions.q: You counted 21 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
questions.a: 21 × 4 = 84 beats per minute.

questions.q: Why don't you use your thumb to take a pulse?
questions.a: The thumb has its own pulse, which can confuse the count.

days.guide: Walk 2 minutes, then take a pulse; jog 2 minutes, pulse; sprint 20–30 seconds, pulse. Record and compare.

questions.q: Which activity gave the highest heart rate? Why?
questions.a: Sprinting, because it is the most intense, so muscles need the most oxygen and the heart pumps fastest.

questions.q: Walk: 100 bpm; jog: 140 bpm; sprint: 176 bpm. How much higher is sprint than walk?
questions.a: 76 bpm higher.

days.guide: After a short walk, teach 4 static stretches held 20–30 seconds (quad, hamstring, calf, cross-body shoulder). Track water cups through the day.

questions.q: How long should you hold a static stretch?
questions.a: About 20–30 seconds without bouncing.

questions.q: When should you drink water during activity?
questions.a: Before, during and after.

days.guide: The child explains why heart rate rises with intensity and leads the full warm-up and cool-down for the family.

questions.q: Why does heart rate rise as exercise gets harder?
questions.a: Harder work means muscles need more oxygen and fuel, so the heart beats faster to pump more blood to them.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart rate log and led warm-up: log should show resting heart rate (15-second count × 4), heart rate after jumping jacks, and after walk, jog and sprint, with values increasing as intensity increases. Rubric: 4 = log complete and correctly calculated, explains the link between intensity and heart rate, leads all 5 warm-up moves and 4 cool-down stretches with good form; 3 = one calculation error or one move missed; 2 = log incomplete or needs prompts; 1 = cannot lead.

weeks.prep: Set up a 20-meter PACER lane with cones (free PACER audio cadence tracks are online) or a measured 1-mile route. Mat, a 12-inch ruler or yardstick for trunk lift, a box for back-saver sit-and-reach (or yardstick taped to a step), a cadence app or recording (one curl-up/push-up every 3 seconds). Print a fitness record sheet and look up the FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zone charts for the child's age and sex.
misconceptions: Thinking these tests are a contest. They measure your own health-related fitness so you can set goals and track growth.
Trading good form for more reps. Only reps with correct form at the cadence count.

days.guide: Teach the 5 components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition. Match 10 activities (e.g., swimming laps, push-ups, plank, yoga, biking, carrying groceries, toe-touch stretch, jump rope, long hike, eating balanced meals plus activity).

questions.q: Which component does a long bike ride build?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance.

questions.q: What's the difference between muscular strength and muscular endurance?
questions.a: Strength is the most force a muscle can make at once; endurance is how many times or how long a muscle can keep working.

days.guide: Warm up. Run the PACER: run 20 m before each beep, which gets faster each minute; the test ends the second time the child doesn't reach the line before the beep. Record laps (or time the 1-mile walk/run). Cool down.

questions.q: When does the PACER end?
questions.a: The second time you don't reach the line before the beep.

questions.q: Which fitness component does the PACER measure?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance.

days.guide: Curl-ups: knees bent, feet flat, arms straight, fingertips slide 3 inches (a measuring strip) at one every 3 seconds until two form errors. Push-ups: straight body, lower to a 90-degree elbow, one every 3 seconds until two form errors. Record.

questions.q: What is the cadence for curl-ups and push-ups?
questions.a: One every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

questions.q: What does 90 degrees mean in the push-up?
questions.a: Lowering until the elbows are bent at a right angle (upper arms parallel to the floor).

days.guide: Trunk lift: lie face down, toes pointed, hands under thighs; slowly lift the upper body as high as comfortable (up to 12 inches) and hold while you measure from floor to chin; best of 2. Back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight, the other bent; reach forward 4 times, hold the 4th; measure each side.

questions.q: Why lift slowly in the trunk lift and stop at 12 inches?
questions.a: To protect the lower back; lifting higher or jerking can cause injury and isn't needed.

questions.q: What does the sit-and-reach test measure?
questions.a: Flexibility of the hamstrings (back of the legs) and lower back.

days.guide: Compare each result to the Healthy Fitness Zone chart for the child's age and sex. Circle areas in the zone and areas to improve.

questions.q: What does it mean if a score is in the Healthy Fitness Zone?
questions.a: Your fitness level in that area is enough for good health for your age.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline fitness data check: the record sheet should include PACER laps (or mile time), curl-ups, push-ups, trunk lift (inches, max 12), sit-and-reach left and right (inches), and each compared to the Healthy Fitness Zone chart (in zone / needs improvement). Proficient = all tests completed with correct form and cadence, all scores recorded, comparison done with a parent.

weeks.prep: Baseline results from week 2, 6 station cards, cones, jump rope, mat, a sturdy step, a timer that beeps every 40/20 seconds (interval app). Circuit log sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking the circuit is a race. Quality reps with good form matter more than speed.
Setting goals in areas you already do well in only. Choose at least one area below the Healthy Fitness Zone or where you want to grow.

days.guide: The child writes two SMART goals from the baseline data (e.g., 'I will increase my PACER from 18 to 25 laps by the spring test by jogging 20 minutes 3 times a week').

questions.q: Why must a goal be measurable?
questions.a: So you can tell exactly whether you reached it by comparing numbers.

questions.q: Which area should you pick for a goal?
questions.a: An area that was below the Healthy Fitness Zone or that you most want to improve.

days.guide: Set up 6 stations: jumping jacks, plank, wall sit, jump rope, step-ups, crab walk. Label each card with the fitness component it builds. Do a walk-through.

questions.q: Which component does a wall sit build?
questions.a: Muscular endurance (legs).

questions.q: Which component does jump rope build most?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance.

days.guide: Complete the circuit twice: 40 seconds work, 20 seconds rest/rotate. Log reps or seconds held at each station.

questions.q: How long is one full round of 6 stations with 40 s work and 20 s rest?
questions.a: 6 × 60 seconds = 6 minutes.

days.guide: The child teaches a family member each station's form and safety cues, then they do the circuit together.

questions.q: What form cue would you give for a plank?
questions.a: Straight line from head to heels, tight stomach, elbows under shoulders, don't let hips sag or pike up.

days.guide: Repeat the circuit and compare reps to Day 3.

questions.q: Day 3: 24 step-ups. Today: 29. How many more?
questions.a: 5 more.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal sheet and circuit log rubric: 4 = two SMART goals tied to baseline data (specific test, number, plan, date) and a circuit log with reps for every station on Day 3 and Day 5 with improvements noted; 3 = goals missing one SMART part or log missing a station; 2 = vague goals or incomplete log; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Tennis balls (10–30), a taped wall target (about 2 feet square), a 15-foot throwing line, open field for distance, measuring tape, phone for slow-motion video. Print a 5-cue checklist.
misconceptions: Stepping with the throwing-side foot. Step with the opposite foot to allow hip rotation and more force.
Throwing 'all arm' while facing the target. Start sideways and rotate the hips and shoulders toward the target.

days.guide: Teach 5 cues: side to target, arm back (making an 'L'), step with opposite foot, rotate hips (and shoulders), follow through across the body. Shadow-throw 20 times.

questions.q: List the 5 overhand throw cues.
questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step with opposite foot, rotate hips, follow through.

questions.q: A left-handed thrower steps with which foot?
questions.a: The right foot.

days.guide: Throw 30 balls at the wall target from 15 feet, focusing on a big step with the opposite foot. Tally hits.

questions.q: You hit 18 of 30. How many missed?

days.guide: Record a throw in slow motion. Pause the video at each stage and check off each cue.

questions.q: What should the video show at release?
questions.a: Opposite foot stepped forward, hips and shoulders turned toward the target, arm coming through high.

days.guide: Throw for distance 10 times; measure the best three.

questions.q: Best three throws: 62, 58, 65 feet. What's the average?

days.guide: Parent scores 5 throws on the 5 cues.

questions.q: Why does hip rotation add force?
questions.a: Turning the hips and shoulders uses the big muscles of the body to whip the arm forward faster.

weeks.assessment_key: Throwing cue checklist: score 5 throws × 5 cues (side to target, arm back, opposite-foot step, hip rotation, follow through) = 25 points. 4 = 22–25; 3 = 17–21; 2 = 11–16; 1 = 0–10.

weeks.prep: Tennis balls, a playground ball, open space, a partner. Score sheet for the 20-catch test (high, middle, low).
misconceptions: Catching with stiff arms. Reach, then 'give' by bending elbows to absorb the ball.
Using the same hand position at every level. Above the waist: thumbs together; below: pinkies together.

days.guide: Toss 30 balls at high and low levels; the child uses thumbs-together for high and pinkies-together for low, calling out the position.

questions.q: A ball is coming at your shins. Hand position?
questions.a: Pinkies together, palms up.

days.guide: Partner catch; step back after every 3 successful catches in a row. Record the farthest distance.

questions.q: Why step back only after 3 in a row?
questions.a: To build success before making the task harder.

days.guide: Run a pattern (straight then cut); partner tosses ahead. Catch on the move with hands, eyes on the ball.

questions.q: Where should the passer aim for a moving catcher?
questions.a: Ahead of them, into the space they are running to.

days.guide: Play a reaction-bounce game: partner bounces the ball at different angles and speeds; catch it after one bounce.

questions.q: What helps you react faster?
questions.a: A ready position (knees bent, weight on balls of feet, hands ready) and watching the ball.

days.guide: 20-catch test: 7 high, 7 middle, 6 low tosses from about 15 feet. Score clean catches with correct hand position.

questions.q: You caught 17 of 20. What fraction is that?

weeks.assessment_key: Catching test score: 1 point per clean catch with correct hand position (20 max). 4 = 18–20; 3 = 14–17; 2 = 10–13; 1 = below 10.

weeks.prep: Flying disc, junior football, cones, a partner who can jog. Place cones at 10, 15 and 20 feet for the target game.
misconceptions: Throwing at the receiver instead of ahead of them. Lead the receiver by aiming at where they will be.
Throwing a disc with the arm only. Step toward the target and snap the wrist, releasing the disc flat.

days.guide: Partner jogs across the yard; the child throws lead passes ahead of them. Adjust lead for speed.

questions.q: If your partner runs faster, how should your aim change?
questions.a: Aim farther ahead of them.

days.guide: Teach the backhand disc throw: thumb on top, fingers under the rim, side stance, curl across the body, step and snap the wrist, release flat. 20 partner throws.

questions.q: Why must the disc be flat when released?
questions.a: A flat disc flies straight; a tilted disc curves or dives.

days.guide: Teach the football grip (fingers on laces, toward the back), throw over the top and let the ball roll off the fingertips for a spiral.

questions.q: Which fingers touch the laces?
questions.a: Usually the ring and pinky fingers rest across the laces, with the thumb underneath and the index finger near the back tip of the ball.

days.guide: Hit-the-cone accuracy: 5 throws from each distance (10, 15, 20 ft). Count hits.

questions.q: Hits: 4 at 10 ft, 3 at 15 ft, 1 at 20 ft. Total hits out of 15?

days.guide: Score 10 throws to a jogging partner (catchable passes).

questions.q: What makes a pass 'catchable'?
questions.a: It arrives ahead of the receiver at chest height, at a speed they can handle.

weeks.assessment_key: Moving-target accuracy score: number of catchable lead passes out of 10 (any throw type). 4 = 8–10; 3 = 6–7; 2 = 4–5; 1 = 0–3. Note whether the child adjusted lead for speed.

weeks.prep: Soft balls, cones for a small ultimate field with end zones, flying disc, a timer. Sportsmanship list and self-rating sheet.
misconceptions: Running with the disc in ultimate. Once you catch it, you must stop and pivot on one foot; pass within 10 seconds.
Thinking sportsmanship only means shaking hands at the end. It includes honest calls, encouraging teammates, respecting opponents and controlling emotions throughout the game.

days.guide: Teach ultimate: move the disc by passing only; no running with the disc (pivot foot); defender counts a 10-second stall; drops, out-of-bounds or interceptions are turnovers; catch it in the end zone to score; no contact. Play 2-on-2.

questions.q: What happens if a pass is dropped in ultimate?
questions.a: It is a turnover; the other team gets the disc.

questions.q: How do you score in ultimate?
questions.a: Catch the disc in the end zone you're attacking.

days.guide: List 5 sportsmanship behaviors (honest calls, encouraging teammates, shaking hands/saying good game, accepting calls calmly, including everyone). Practice them in a game.

questions.q: Give 3 sportsmanship behaviors.
questions.a: Any 3: playing fair and honestly, encouraging teammates, respecting opponents and officials, accepting results calmly, saying 'good game.'

days.guide: Play a timed hot potato relay: throw and catch down a line and back; record times and try to beat them.

questions.q: What should you do if a teammate drops the ball?
questions.a: Encourage them ('You've got this!') and keep going.

days.guide: The child teaches the throwing and catching cues to a sibling or parent.

questions.q: What is the most important catching cue to teach?
questions.a: Watch the ball into your hands and reach and give (with correct hand position).

days.guide: Skills test (see key) and sportsmanship self-rating (1–4 on each behavior).

questions.q: Rate yourself: what is one sportsmanship behavior you'll work on?
questions.a: Answers vary; should be a specific behavior with a plan.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: 5 overhand throws to a target scored on the 5 cues (25 points) + 10 catches at mixed levels (10 points). Proficient = 20+ throw points and 8+ catches. Sportsmanship self-rating: 1–4 on honest calls, encouragement, respect, self-control; proficient = honest ratings with one specific goal.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball (size 4), 6 cones spaced about 4 feet apart, a whistle, stopwatch.
misconceptions: Kicking the ball too far ahead. Use small touches so the ball stays within a stride.
Looking only at the ball. Glance up between touches to see space and defenders.

days.guide: Practice toe taps (alternate soles on top of the ball), inside-inside touches (ball between insides of feet), sole rolls (roll the ball sideways with the sole) for 5 minutes.

questions.q: Which surfaces of the foot are used for dribbling?
questions.a: Inside, outside and sole (and laces for speed).

days.guide: Dribble through 6 cones using inside and outside of the foot, keeping close control.

questions.q: When weaving left around a cone, which part of the right foot might you use?
questions.a: The inside of the right foot (or outside of the left foot) to cut the ball left.

days.guide: On the whistle, change dribble speed: walk, jog, run. Bigger touches at speed, smaller when slow.

questions.q: How do touches change when dribbling fast in open space?
questions.a: Touches can be slightly bigger and pushed ahead with the laces so you can run.

days.guide: Play red light, green light: on 'red,' stop the ball with the sole; late stops go back to the start.

questions.q: How do you stop the ball quickly?
questions.a: Put the sole of your foot on top of it.

days.guide: Time 3 cone-weave runs and record the best.

questions.q: Times 21.4, 19.8 and 20.6 seconds. Best?
questions.a: 19.8 seconds.

weeks.assessment_key: Cone-weave time: record best of 3. Form rubric: 4 = weaves all 6 cones with close control using inside and outside of both feet, eyes up at times; 3 = misses one cone or ball gets away once; 2 = several misses; 1 = cannot complete with the ball.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, a wall, cones to make 4–6 'gates' (two cones about 3 feet apart), stopwatch.
misconceptions: Pointing the plant foot away from the target. Plant foot beside the ball, toes pointing at the target.
Stopping the ball with a stiff foot so it bounces away. Cushion the trap by giving with the foot as the ball arrives.

days.guide: 30 inside-foot passes to a wall with each foot: plant foot beside the ball, ankle locked, strike the middle of the ball, follow through.

questions.q: Where should your plant foot be?
questions.a: Beside the ball, toes pointing at the target.

questions.q: Why lock the ankle?
questions.a: A firm foot makes the pass accurate and strong.

days.guide: Roll balls at slow, medium and fast speeds; the child traps with the sole and with the inside of the foot, giving on contact.

questions.q: How do you trap a fast ball?
questions.a: Meet it with the inside of the foot and pull back slightly (cushion) as it arrives.

days.guide: Pass back and forth with a partner, starting 10 feet apart and moving back after 5 good passes.

questions.q: What should the receiver do before the ball arrives?
questions.a: Get in line with the ball, on the balls of the feet, ready to trap.

days.guide: Set gates around the yard. Pass through as many gates as possible to a partner (or rebound off a wall).

questions.q: Why move to a new gate after each pass?
questions.a: It practices passing from different angles and moving after passing.

days.guide: Count successful passes through a gate in 2 minutes.

questions.q: You made 14 passes in 2 minutes. How many per minute?
questions.a: 7 per minute.

weeks.assessment_key: Gate pass count: record the number of successful passes through gates in 2 minutes. Benchmarks: 4 = 15+ with good plant-foot form and soft traps; 3 = 10–14; 2 = 5–9; 1 = fewer than 5.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, cones for a small field and two small goals (2 cones each, about 4 feet apart), pinnies or colored shirts, paper for the strategy diagram. Gather 2–3 players.
misconceptions: Bunching around the ball. Spread out; width and depth make passing lanes.
Defenders chasing the ball everywhere. Stay goal-side (between attacker and goal) and wait for a chance to win the ball.

days.guide: 2-on-1 keep-away in a square: the receiver moves to open space (a passing lane not blocked by the defender) and calls for the ball.

questions.q: What is a passing lane?
questions.a: A clear path between the passer and a teammate that a defender isn't blocking.

questions.q: What should you do after you pass?
questions.a: Move to a new open space to get the ball back.

days.guide: Defensive stance: low, knees bent, side-on, on balls of feet. Shadow an attacker, staying goal-side and between them and the goal.

questions.q: What does 'goal-side' mean?
questions.a: Positioned between the attacker and the goal you are defending.

days.guide: Play 2-on-2 with small goals. Freeze play to point out open space; reward calling for the ball when open.

questions.q: Why call for the ball?
questions.a: To let your teammate know you're open and where you are.

days.guide: Draw a diagram (dots for players, arrows for movement and passes) showing how to create space: spread wide, move away from the defender, then cut into space.

questions.q: On offense, why spread out wide?
questions.a: It stretches the defense, creating gaps and passing lanes.

days.guide: Self-assess on a 3-point checklist: I moved to open space; I called for the ball; I passed and moved.

questions.q: Which checklist item will you improve?
questions.a: Answers vary; should name one item and how.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy diagram and self-assessment: diagram shows at least 2 attackers spreading out and moving into space with arrows for movement and passes and a labeled defender. Self-assessment rated honestly against observed play. 4 = clear diagram plus all 3 checklist behaviors seen in play; 3 = 2 behaviors; 2 = 1 behavior; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, cones for stations (dribble course, gates, goal), whistle. Plan a 15-minute family game. Score sheet for the foot skills test.
misconceptions: Thinking the referee is the enemy. The referee keeps the game fair and safe; respect calls.
Arguing to win a disputed call. Use a quick fair method like rock-paper-scissors or a do-over.

days.guide: Rotate 5 minutes each through dribbling (cone weave), passing (gates) and shooting (laces shots on goal).

questions.q: Which surface of the foot is best for a powerful shot?
questions.a: The laces (top of the foot), toe pointed down.

days.guide: Practice resolving a disputed call: both players state what they saw calmly, then use rock-paper-scissors or a do-over.

questions.q: Why use rock-paper-scissors for a disputed call?
questions.a: It is quick and fair, so the game can continue without arguing.

days.guide: Play a 15-minute family game: kick-ins when the ball goes out of bounds, no hands except the goalie, fair-play rules.

questions.q: What happens if the ball goes out over the sideline?
questions.a: The other team restarts with a kick-in (or throw-in) from where it went out.

days.guide: The child referees a short game, making and explaining calls for out-of-bounds and handballs.

questions.q: What is a handball?
questions.a: When a field player deliberately touches the ball with their hand or arm; the other team gets a free kick.

days.guide: Foot skills test (see key).

questions.q: When trapping, what does 'give' mean?
questions.a: Pulling the foot back as the ball arrives to cushion it and keep it close.

weeks.assessment_key: Foot skills test (scored by parent): Cone-weave dribble — 4 = all cones with close control using both feet; 3 = one miss; 2 = several misses; 1 = cannot. 10 gate passes — count successes (proficient = 7+). 5 traps — count controlled traps that stop within one step (proficient = 4+). Overall proficient = 3+ on dribble, 7+ passes, 4+ traps.

weeks.prep: Jump rope sized to the child's height (stand on the center; handles reach the armpits), stopwatch, interval log (interval #, jumps, heart rate). Flat, non-slip surface.
misconceptions: Using big arm circles to turn. Keep elbows close to the body and turn with the wrists.
Crossing arms at the elbows for the criss-cross. Cross at the waist so the hands go past the hips, making a big enough loop to jump through.

days.guide: Size the rope. Basic bounce: feet together, small jumps on the balls of the feet. 4 sets of 30 seconds with rests.

questions.q: How do you check rope size?
questions.a: Stand on the center with one foot; the handles should reach the armpits.

questions.q: How high should you jump?
questions.a: Only about 1–2 inches, just enough to clear the rope.

days.guide: Teach skier (side-to-side) and bell (front-to-back). Practice over a line, then with the rope; 20 of each without missing.

questions.q: Which jump moves side to side?
questions.a: The skier.

days.guide: Criss-cross: on every third jump, cross arms at the waist, jump through the loop, then uncross. Count successful crosses.

questions.q: Where should arms cross for a criss-cross?
questions.a: At the waist/hips, crossing far enough that the hands reach past the opposite hips.

days.guide: Five 30-second jumping intervals with 30-second rests; record jumps per interval and heart rate after the last.

questions.q: Intervals: 52, 50, 48, 47, 45 jumps. What is the total?
questions.a: 242 jumps.

questions.q: Why did the count drop each interval?
questions.a: Muscles tired (muscular fatigue) and heart and lungs worked harder.

days.guide: The child performs a 4-trick routine (bounce, skier, bell, criss-cross) for a parent who scores it.

questions.q: Name your 4 tricks in order.
questions.a: Bounce, skier, bell, criss-cross (or the order the child planned).

weeks.assessment_key: 4-trick routine scoring: each trick 0–2 (0 = not attempted, 1 = attempted with misses, 2 = 5+ in a row with good form) = 8 points. 4 = 7–8; 3 = 5–6; 2 = 3–4; 1 = 0–2. Interval log: all 5 intervals recorded with heart rate.

weeks.prep: Long rope about 16 feet, two turners (or tie one end to a post at about waist height). Practice in a clear area. Look up the traditional chant 'Teddy Bear, Teddy Bear' (public domain).
misconceptions: Running in at the wrong moment. Front door: the rope comes over the top toward you and hits the ground — run in right after it hits. Back door: the rope comes up toward you and goes over away — wait until it passes over and hits the ground, then follow it in.
Jumping near the turner. Jump in the middle where the rope is highest.

days.guide: Teach turning: hold the handle at waist level, turn big circles from the shoulder so the rope just taps the ground at the bottom on each beat, staying in rhythm with the other turner.

questions.q: What makes a good turn?
questions.a: Big, steady circles that tap the ground every time, in rhythm with the other turner.

days.guide: Front door entry: stand next to a turner; as the rope comes over toward you and hits the ground, run in to the middle, jump 5 times, and exit out the far side right after a jump.

questions.q: Where do you exit the rope?
questions.a: Out the far side, diagonally, right after the rope passes under your feet.

days.guide: Back door entry: the rope comes up toward you and over away. Wait for it to pass over and hit the ground, then follow it in. Practice 10 times.

questions.q: Why is back door harder?
questions.a: The rope is coming up toward your face, so you must wait for it to go over and down before running in.

days.guide: Jump to 'Teddy Bear, Teddy Bear' doing the actions (turn around, touch the ground).

questions.q: How do you turn around while jumping?
questions.a: Turn a quarter turn on each jump so you don't break rhythm.

days.guide: Perform: front door entry, 10 jumps including a turn-around, clean exit.

questions.q: Name 2 safety rules for long rope.
questions.a: Jump in the middle; turners hold handles firmly and don't let go; wait your turn outside the rope's path.

weeks.assessment_key: Long-rope entry/exit check: front door entry without stopping the rope (1), 10 consecutive jumps (1), turn-around while jumping (1), clean exit (1). 4 = all 4; 3 = 3; 2 = 2; 1 = 0–1. Bonus: back door entry.

weeks.prep: Two long ropes, a post or second turner, one long single rope for partner jumping. Paper for the routine plan.
misconceptions: Thinking double Dutch ropes turn together. They turn in opposite directions, alternating like an eggbeater: when one rope is at the top, the other is at the bottom.
Rushing the entry. Rock in rhythm with the back rope first, then enter.

days.guide: Partners stand side by side, each holding one handle with the outside hand, and turn together while jumping in unison.

questions.q: What is the key to partner jumping?
questions.a: Turning and jumping at the same time — count aloud together.

days.guide: Eggbeater turning: two ropes turned inward toward the center, alternating so one hits the ground as the other is at the top. Practice saying 'right, left' with each hit.

questions.q: In double Dutch, how do the two ropes move?
questions.a: In opposite, alternating circles — one up while the other is down.

days.guide: Entry: stand by a turner, rock in rhythm with the back rope, enter as it hits the ground, and jump each rope (quick small jumps). Count best streak.

questions.q: Why are double Dutch jumps quicker?
questions.a: Two ropes pass under per full cycle, so you jump twice as often.

days.guide: Design a 4-part partner routine mixing partner jumps and single-rope tricks; write it down.

questions.q: Write your 4-part routine.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., partner bounce ×10, skier ×8, solo criss-cross ×4, partner turn-around ×4.

days.guide: Perform; give one compliment and one tip to each other.

questions.q: Give an example of a helpful tip.
questions.a: E.g., 'Count out loud so we start together.'

weeks.assessment_key: Partner routine performance rubric: 4 = 4 planned parts performed in order, partners stay in rhythm, at most 2 misses, specific compliment and tip given; 3 = 4 parts with 3–4 misses; 2 = 2–3 parts; 1 = cannot complete. Double Dutch best streak recorded (any number).

weeks.prep: Jump rope, a music track with a steady beat (about 1 minute, previewed), a Tabata timer (20 s on / 10 s off × 8 rounds), stopwatch for the 1-minute speed test, long rope and turners.
misconceptions: Thinking Tabata means jumping as fast as possible for 4 minutes straight. It is 8 rounds of 20 seconds hard work with 10 seconds of rest.
Choosing tricks you can't do yet for the show. Choose tricks you can do reliably and practice the transitions.

days.guide: Do a Tabata: 8 rounds of 20 seconds jumping and 10 seconds rest (4 minutes). Take heart rate right after.

questions.q: How many rounds are in a Tabata, and how long is it?
questions.a: 8 rounds of 20 s work + 10 s rest = 4 minutes.

days.guide: Choose a song and plan a 1-minute routine with at least 5 tricks matched to the beat (write counts for each).

questions.q: If each trick lasts 8 counts and your song is at 120 beats per minute, how many counts fit in 1 minute?
questions.a: 120 counts, so about 15 tricks of 8 counts.

days.guide: Rehearse 5 times; mark where misses happen and practice that spot slowly.

questions.q: What's a good way to fix a trouble spot?
questions.a: Practice just that transition slowly several times, then add it back into the full routine.

days.guide: Perform the 'Jump Rope Show' for family.

questions.q: How do you recover from a miss during a show?
questions.a: Reset the rope quickly and rejoin on the next beat without stopping the music.

days.guide: Skills test: 1-minute speed count (count right-foot landings ×2, or all jumps), 3 tricks, long-rope entry.

questions.q: In a 1-minute speed test, what form keeps speed high?
questions.a: Small, quick jumps on the balls of the feet and fast wrist turns.

weeks.assessment_key: Jump rope skills test: 1-minute speed count recorded (compare to week 12 practice); 3 tricks performed 5 in a row each (1 point each); long-rope entry and 5 jumps (1 point). 4 = speed recorded + 4 points; 3 = 3 points; 2 = 2 points; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Mat or carpet, pillows for safe falls, a timer.
misconceptions: Thinking balance is just 'standing still.' Balance is controlling your center of gravity over your base of support, whether still or moving.
Thinking a narrow stance is more stable. A wider base of support and a lower center of gravity are more stable.

days.guide: Call out 8 balances on different bases of support (two hands and one foot; one knee and one hand; seat only; one foot; etc.), holding each 5 seconds.

questions.q: What is a base of support?
questions.a: The parts of the body touching the ground and the area between them.

days.guide: Test standing on one foot, feet together, and feet wide while a parent gently nudges. Explain center of gravity (the balance point of the body, near the belly button).

questions.q: Which is more stable: feet together or feet wide? Why?
questions.a: Feet wide — the base of support is bigger, so the center of gravity stays over it more easily.

questions.q: How does bending your knees help balance?
questions.a: It lowers your center of gravity, making you more stable.

days.guide: Practice tree, warrior III and boat pose, holding each 15 seconds; focus eyes on one spot.

questions.q: In boat pose, what is your base of support?
questions.a: Your seat (sitting bones).

days.guide: Teach safe falling: tuck chin, bend knees, roll sideways onto the side of the body, don't reach out with a straight arm. Spotting rules: spot only when asked and taught, hands ready at the waist or hips.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you catch a fall with a straight arm?
questions.a: It can break your wrist or arm; rolling spreads out the force.

days.guide: Perform 3 balances of choice and explain the base of support for each.

questions.q: Explain your hardest balance's base of support.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., 'Warrior III — one foot, small base, so I keep my core tight.'

weeks.assessment_key: Balance demonstration rubric: 4 = 3 different balances held still for 5+ seconds each, and the child correctly names the base of support and explains stability using center of gravity and base size; 3 = holds balances with a wobble and explains basics; 2 = holds 1–2 or cannot explain; 1 = unable.

weeks.prep: A tumbling mat or soft lawn; a cushion under one end to make a gentle incline. Clear space. Parent spots forward rolls. Skip forward rolls if the child has neck/back problems.
misconceptions: Rolling on the top of the head. Tuck the chin to the chest so the back of the head and shoulders touch first.
Doing a cartwheel with bent arms and hands together. Hands go down one at a time, shoulder-width apart, arms straight; hand-hand-foot-foot along a line.

days.guide: Practice log and egg rolls, then the forward roll down an incline: squat, hands shoulder-width, chin to chest, push with legs, roll on rounded back, stand. Spot at the back of the neck and hips.

questions.q: Where should your chin be during a forward roll?
questions.a: Tucked to your chest.

days.guide: Cartwheel progression: lunge facing the line, place hand-hand on the line, kick legs over landing foot-foot. Start with low 'bunny' kicks, then higher.

questions.q: What is the order of hands and feet in a cartwheel?
questions.a: Hand, hand, foot, foot.

days.guide: Hold bridge (from lying on back), straddle stretch and butterfly stretch for 20–30 seconds each.

questions.q: Why does flexibility help tumbling?
questions.a: It allows a greater range of motion, so skills are smoother and safer.

days.guide: Link forward roll → stand → balance (e.g., arabesque) in a smooth sequence.

questions.q: What makes a sequence smooth?
questions.a: No extra steps or pauses between skills; each finishes in a controlled position.

days.guide: Perform the forward roll and cartwheel; parent checks safety cues.

questions.q: Name one safety cue for each skill.
questions.a: Forward roll: chin to chest. Cartwheel: straight arms, hands shoulder-width apart.

weeks.assessment_key: Tumbling cue checklist: Forward roll — chin tucked (1), hands shoulder-width (1), rounded back (1), stands up without hands (1). Cartwheel — lunge start (1), hand-hand-foot-foot along line (1), straight arms (1), controlled finish (1). Proficient = 6+ of 8 with all safety cues (chin tucked, straight arms).

weeks.prep: Mat, family members to partner and spot. Discuss rules: stand only on hips and thighs (never the lower back), communicate before moving, come down slowly together.
misconceptions: Thinking partner stunts are about one strong person. Both partners must communicate, lean together and keep their bodies tight.
Climbing on the back or knees. Base supports on strong points (hips, thighs over the knees, shoulders over hands).

days.guide: Practice back-to-back sit-to-stand (push backs together, walk feet in, rise together) and lean-away holds with hands joined.

questions.q: Why must both partners push equally?
questions.a: If one pushes harder or lets go, both lose balance and fall.

days.guide: With a spotter, try a thigh stand: base in a deep squat, flyer steps onto the base's thighs near the hips, both lean back holding wrists. Hold 3 seconds and dismount forward.

questions.q: Where does the flyer stand in a thigh stand?
questions.a: On the base's thighs close to the hips (never on the knees).

days.guide: Do planks (30 s), superman holds (20 s) and wall sits (30 s) ×2.

questions.q: Which muscles does a superman hold strengthen?
questions.a: The back muscles (and glutes).

days.guide: With 2–3 family members, design a group balance with at least 4 points of contact with the floor.

questions.q: What does '4 points of contact' mean?
questions.a: Four body parts total (hands, feet, knees, etc.) touching the floor.

days.guide: Perform 2 partner stunts and the group balance; discuss what communication helped.

questions.q: Give an example of good communication in a stunt.
questions.a: E.g., counting '1, 2, 3, up' together and saying 'down' before releasing.

weeks.assessment_key: Group balance performance rubric: 4 = 2 partner stunts held 3+ seconds with safe base points and controlled dismounts, group balance with 4+ points of contact held still, clear communication; 3 = all performed with a wobble; 2 = one stunt unsafe or not held; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Mat, routine planning sheet (start shape, balance 1, balance 2, roll, jump, finish; level for each), phone for video.
misconceptions: Rushing through elements. Hold each balance for 3 seconds and show a clear start and finish.
Using only one level. Plan high (jumps, relevé), medium (standing balances) and low (rolls, seated balances) levels.

days.guide: Plan a routine: start shape, 2 balances, 1 roll, 1 jump (soft landing), finish shape. Label each with high, medium or low level.

questions.q: Give an element for each level.
questions.a: High: straight jump or tiptoe balance; medium: standing scale/arabesque; low: forward roll or V-sit.

days.guide: Practice transitions between elements so there are no extra steps or stops.

questions.q: What is a transition?
questions.a: The movement that links one skill to the next.

days.guide: Rehearse 5 times, then record a final run-through.

questions.q: Why rehearse several times?
questions.a: To build memory and smoothness so the routine is controlled.

days.guide: Watch the video with a parent and revise one transition.

questions.q: Which transition did you change and how?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., 'I rolled straight into my V-sit instead of standing first.'

days.guide: Perform the final routine; score with the rubric.

questions.q: How do you land a jump safely?
questions.a: On the balls of both feet, bending knees and hips, arms out for balance.

weeks.assessment_key: Gymnastics routine rubric (score 1–4 each): Control (balances held 3 seconds, steady landings), Levels (high, medium and low all used), Transitions (smooth, no extra steps), Safety (chin tucked in roll, soft landing). Proficient = 3 or higher in each category.

weeks.prep: Basketball (size 5 or 6) or playground ball, flat surface, 6 cones, stopwatch.
misconceptions: Slapping with the palm. Push the ball with finger pads, wrist flexing.
Dribbling high and away from the body. Keep it at or below the waist and close to the body for control.

days.guide: Stationary: pound dribbles (hard, waist high), low dribbles (below knee), and figure-8s around the legs, each hand.

questions.q: Which part of your hand controls the dribble?
questions.a: The finger pads.

days.guide: Dribble while calling out the number of fingers held up by a parent.

questions.q: Why dribble with eyes up in a game?
questions.a: To see teammates, defenders and the basket.

days.guide: Dribble down and back on a line with right hand, then left, then alternating.

questions.q: Why practice with your weaker hand?
questions.a: So you can dribble away from defenders on either side.

days.guide: Crossover: low, quick bounce in front of the body from one hand to the other, weaving around 6 cones.

questions.q: Where should the crossover bounce happen?
questions.a: Low and in front of your body, below the knees.

days.guide: Time the cone course using both hands; record best of 3.

questions.q: Best time 18.2 s; earlier best 21.0 s. Improvement?
questions.a: 2.8 seconds faster.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course time: record best of 3 times. Form rubric: 4 = uses both hands, ball stays low and controlled, crossovers at cones, eyes up much of the time, no lost balls; 3 = one lost ball or weak hand avoided; 2 = several losses; 1 = cannot complete.

weeks.prep: Basketball, a wall with a tape target at chest height, a partner.
misconceptions: Passing with only the arms. Step toward the target and push through with both thumbs down (follow through).
Bouncing the bounce pass at the receiver's feet. The ball should hit the floor about two-thirds of the way to the receiver so it bounces up to their waist.

days.guide: Chest pass: ball at chest, step toward target, push and snap wrists so thumbs point down. 30 passes to the wall target.

questions.q: How do your thumbs finish after a chest pass?
questions.a: Pointing down, palms facing out.

days.guide: Bounce pass: aim at a spot two-thirds of the way to the partner so it bounces up to their waist.

questions.q: Where should a bounce pass hit the floor?
questions.a: About two-thirds of the way to the receiver.

days.guide: Overhead pass: ball above the forehead, step and snap forward. Use it to pass over a defender or for long passes.

questions.q: When would you use an overhead pass?
questions.a: To pass over a defender or make a longer pass.

days.guide: Pass to a partner jogging across the yard; receiver shows 'target hands' (hands up, fingers spread) where they want the ball.

questions.q: What are 'target hands'?
questions.a: The receiver holds hands up showing where to throw the ball.

days.guide: Score 10 chest, 10 bounce and 10 overhead passes to target hands.

questions.q: You completed 8 chest, 7 bounce and 6 overhead. Total out of 30?

weeks.assessment_key: Pass accuracy score: count passes that reach the partner's target hands (30 max). 4 = 25–30 with correct form for each pass type; 3 = 19–24; 2 = 12–18; 1 = below 12.

weeks.prep: Basketball and a lowered hoop or a laundry basket on a chair; phone for video; BEEF checklist (Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through).
misconceptions: Shooting with two hands pushing from the chest. Use one shooting hand with the guide hand on the side; elbow under the ball.
Watching the ball instead of the target. Eyes stay on the rim (front or back) throughout the shot.

days.guide: Teach BEEF: Balance (feet shoulder-width, knees bent), Eyes (on the target), Elbow (under the ball, in an L), Follow-through (snap wrist, 'hand in the cookie jar'). 30 shots close to the hoop.

questions.q: What does BEEF stand for?
questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through.

days.guide: Give-and-go: pass to a partner, cut toward the basket, receive the return pass and shoot.

questions.q: What is a give-and-go?
questions.a: Passing to a teammate, then cutting toward the basket to get a return pass.

days.guide: Defensive slide: low stance, slide feet without crossing, stay between your player and the basket.

questions.q: Why not cross your feet when sliding on defense?
questions.a: Crossing makes you slower to change direction and easier to trip.

days.guide: 2-on-1: one passer, one cutter, one defender. Attackers use passes and cuts to get an open shot.

questions.q: In 2-on-1, when should the ball handler pass?
questions.a: When the defender commits to them, leaving the teammate open.

days.guide: Record 5 shots and self-assess each BEEF cue.

questions.q: Your video shows your elbow sticking out. Which cue do you fix?
questions.a: Elbow — keep it under the ball.

weeks.assessment_key: BEEF self-assessment: for 5 recorded shots, check Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through (20 checks). 4 = 17–20 and accurate self-assessment matching the video; 3 = 13–16; 2 = 8–12; 1 = below 8.

weeks.prep: Basketball, hoop or basket, cones for stations, scoring sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking any hand switch is a double dribble. Double dribble is dribbling with both hands at once or starting to dribble again after stopping (holding) the ball.
Thinking a foul means any touch. A foul is illegal contact that affects play, like pushing, holding or hitting arms.

days.guide: Demonstrate traveling (taking steps while holding the ball without dribbling), double dribble (two hands at once, or dribble-stop-dribble) and common fouls (pushing, holding, reaching in and hitting arms).

questions.q: What is traveling?
questions.a: Moving your feet (taking extra steps) while holding the ball without dribbling.

questions.q: What is a double dribble?
questions.a: Dribbling with both hands at the same time, or dribbling, stopping (holding the ball) and then dribbling again.

days.guide: Play 2-on-2 half-court to 7 points using the rules. After a defensive rebound or steal, 'clear' the ball past the 3-point line (or a cone) before scoring.

questions.q: Why 'clear' the ball in half-court?
questions.a: It gives both teams a fair reset after the ball changes possession.

days.guide: Act out 3 disputed calls; resolve each fairly (honest call, do-over, rock-paper-scissors).

questions.q: You're not sure if you traveled. What's a fair way to settle it?
questions.a: Be honest; if unsure, agree on a do-over or use rock-paper-scissors.

days.guide: Rotate through dribble, pass and shoot stations.

questions.q: Which pass is best to get the ball under a defender's raised arms?
questions.a: A bounce pass.

days.guide: Skills test (see key).

questions.q: What does a defender try to stay between?
questions.a: The offensive player and the basket.

weeks.assessment_key: Basketball skills test: Hand dribble — complete the cone course with both hands and a crossover (score 1–4: 4 = no losses, eyes up). Passing — 5 chest, 5 bounce, 5 overhead passes to target hands (proficient = 12+ of 15). Rules quiz: traveling, double dribble, foul defined correctly (3 points).

weeks.prep: A video of a ballet folklórico performance (many are online) and a recording of 'La Raspa' (a traditional Mexican folk dance tune) — preview both. Hard floor, shoes.
misconceptions: Thinking all Mexican folk dances are the same. Each region of Mexico has its own dances, music and costumes.
Hopping heavily in the bleking step. It is a light hop, extending one heel forward at a time in rhythm.

days.guide: Watch ballet folklórico. Describe the footwork (zapateado — rhythmic stamping), the wide, colorful skirts dancers swirl, and the charro suits and sombreros.

questions.q: What is zapateado?
questions.a: Rhythmic stamping footwork in Mexican folk dance, making the feet sound like percussion.

questions.q: Why do dancers swirl their skirts?
questions.a: The wide, colorful skirts add to the visual beauty and help show the movement and story of the dance.

days.guide: Teach the bleking step: hop and extend the right heel forward, hop and switch to the left heel, hop switch to right, then pause (clap twice). Repeat starting with left.

questions.q: Describe the bleking step.
questions.a: Light hops switching feet so one heel at a time touches forward — right, left, right, then hold/clap.

days.guide: Teach the elbow swing: partners hook right elbows and skip around 8 counts, then left elbows 8 counts. Connect to the bleking section.

questions.q: How many counts do you swing each way?
questions.a: 8 counts with the right elbow, then 8 with the left.

days.guide: Perform La Raspa start to finish with a family member 3 times.

questions.q: What helps you know when to switch from bleking to the elbow swing?
questions.a: Listening for the change in the music (the second section of the tune).

days.guide: Perform for family and explain the dance is a Mexican folk dance (commonly associated with Veracruz), danced at celebrations and fiestas.

questions.q: Where does La Raspa come from?
questions.a: Mexico (it is a Mexican folk dance commonly associated with Veracruz).

weeks.assessment_key: La Raspa performance rubric: 4 = bleking step on the beat, smooth elbow-swing section, transitions with the music, performs 3 times with a partner, explains origin (Mexico, danced at celebrations); 3 = minor timing errors; 2 = frequent errors or needs cues; 1 = cannot perform.

weeks.prep: Square dance music with a caller (or you call), Virginia Reel music (fiddle tune), an open floor, and as many family members as possible (4 couples is a full square; adapt with fewer). Cha-Cha Slide recording (preview).
misconceptions: Turning around to face backward in a do-si-do. Partners pass right shoulders, go back to back and return walking backward, always facing the same direction.
Confusing allemande left with swing. Allemande left: face your corner, take left hands (or forearms), walk around each other and return to your partner.

days.guide: Teach calls: do-si-do (pass right shoulders, back to back, return), swing your partner (hook elbows or hold hands and turn), promenade (walk with partner counterclockwise around the square, hands crossed), allemande left (left hand to corner, walk around, return home).

questions.q: Which direction do you promenade?
questions.a: Counterclockwise around the square (with your partner).

questions.q: What is your 'corner'?
questions.a: The person beside you who is not your partner.

days.guide: Dance the Virginia Reel: lines facing, forward and back, right-hand turn, left-hand turn, two-hand turn, do-si-do, head couple sashays down and back, reel (alternate turning partner and the others), then head couple forms an arch and others pass under.

questions.q: What does the head couple do during the arch?
questions.a: They join hands and raise them to make an arch, and the other couples pass under it.

days.guide: Teach the grapevine (step side, cross behind, step side, touch) and a 4-wall line dance like the Cha-Cha Slide.

questions.q: What is a 4-wall line dance?
questions.a: A dance that repeats a pattern, turning a quarter each time so you face all four walls.

days.guide: Dance 3 songs, then take heart rate (15 s × 4). Compare to a jogging heart rate.

questions.q: Dance HR 132 bpm vs. jogging HR 148 bpm. Which is more intense?
questions.a: Jogging (16 bpm higher), though dancing is still moderate-to-vigorous activity.

days.guide: Perform a sequence of called square dance moves without stopping.

questions.q: In what order would you dance: allemande left, promenade, do-si-do, swing?
questions.a: Any order called; the child must respond correctly to each call without stopping.

weeks.assessment_key: Called sequence check: call 5 moves in random order (e.g., do-si-do, swing, allemande left, promenade, do-si-do). 1 point each for correct, on-time response. 4 = 5; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Music of the child's choice (preview content), planning sheet with four 8-count sections, a family audience.
misconceptions: Thinking dance needs special training. Planned movement with clear changes in level, pathway, tempo and force makes a strong dance.
Repeating the same level and direction throughout. Include intentional contrasts.

days.guide: Choose music and plan four 8-count sections, each with at least one change in level, pathway, tempo or force. Write it down.

questions.q: How many counts are in four 8-count sections?
questions.a: 32 counts.

questions.q: Give an example of a force change.
questions.a: Moving from strong, sharp punches to light, floating arms.

days.guide: Teach the dance to a family member one 8-count at a time, demonstrating and counting.

questions.q: Why teach one 8-count at a time?
questions.a: Small chunks are easier to learn and remember.

days.guide: Rehearse with music and smooth the transitions.

questions.q: How do you make a transition smooth?
questions.a: End one section in a position that leads naturally into the first move of the next.

days.guide: Perform; ask the audience to identify one level change and one pathway change.

questions.q: What did your audience notice?
questions.a: Answers vary; should be specific changes, e.g., 'You went low in section 3 and traveled in a zigzag.'

days.guide: Self-assess with the rubric; dance steps check: perform grapevine, do-si-do and a La Raspa bleking step on cue.

questions.q: Perform a grapevine right. Describe it.
questions.a: Step right, left foot crosses behind, step right, touch left beside.

weeks.assessment_key: Original dance rubric: 4 = four 8-count sections (32 counts) with clear changes in level, pathway, tempo and force, on the beat, smooth transitions, taught one section to someone; 3 = most elements; 2 = few changes or off beat; 1 = incomplete. Dance steps check: grapevine, do-si-do and bleking each correct (3/3 proficient).

weeks.prep: Paddle (ping-pong or paddleball), foam or tennis ball, a smooth wall, string between two chairs for a low net.
misconceptions: Swinging with the wrist only. Swing from the shoulder with a firm wrist and turn the body.
Facing the wall for a backhand. Turn the paddle-side shoulder toward the wall before swinging.

days.guide: Shake-hands grip. Bump the ball upward 20 times with a flat paddle face.

questions.q: Describe the shake-hands grip.
questions.a: Hold the handle like shaking hands, with the paddle face perpendicular to the ground.

days.guide: Forehand against a wall from a side stance (non-paddle shoulder toward the wall), swing low to high, follow through.

questions.q: What are the forehand cues?
questions.a: Side to the target, swing low to high, follow through toward the target.

days.guide: Backhand: turn so the paddle-side shoulder faces the wall, swing across the body from low to high with the back of the hand leading. 30 strikes.

questions.q: For a right-hander's backhand, which shoulder points to the wall?
questions.a: The right shoulder.

days.guide: Rally with a partner over the string net, counting consecutive hits.

questions.q: Why should you return to a ready position between hits?
questions.a: So you can move quickly to the next ball.

days.guide: Count the longest wall rally using forehand and backhand.

questions.q: Tries: 12, 17, 15. Best?

weeks.assessment_key: Wall rally count: record the longest rally (any mix of forehands and backhands). Benchmarks: 4 = 15+ with both strokes and correct side stance; 3 = 10–14; 2 = 5–9; 1 = fewer than 5.

weeks.prep: Plastic bat, tee or tall cone, whiffle balls, a glove optional, bases (paper plates), safety zone marked around the batter.
misconceptions: Swinging down at the ball (chopping) or up (uppercut). Swing level through the ball.
Fielding grounders standing straight up. Get low, glove/hands on the ground, and bring the ball to the belly.

days.guide: Grip: hands together, knuckles aligned (door-knocking knuckles in a line), right-handers left hand bottom. Stance: side-on, feet shoulder-width, knees bent, bat up behind the back shoulder. 20 dry swings.

questions.q: What does 'knuckles aligned' mean in the grip?
questions.a: The middle (door-knocking) knuckles of both hands line up along the bat.

days.guide: Hit 30 balls off a tee at waist height with a level swing, stepping toward the target.

questions.q: Why place the tee in front of the front foot area?
questions.a: You make contact out in front of your body, where the swing is strongest.

days.guide: Soft toss: parent tosses underhand from the side or front from a safe distance; the child steps toward the pitcher and swings level. 20 swings.

questions.q: Which way do you step when hitting?
questions.a: Toward the pitcher (target) with the front foot.

days.guide: Fielding: ready position, move in front of the ball, glove/hands down, bring it in, then step and throw to a base.

questions.q: How do you field a ground ball?
questions.a: Get in front of it, low with hands down (glove open), watch it in, then bring it to your belly before throwing.

days.guide: Play family whiffle ball and track hits.

questions.q: Why place the bat down after hitting?
questions.a: A thrown bat can hurt someone.

weeks.assessment_key: Batting self-assessment checklist: grip with knuckles aligned, side stance, step toward pitcher, level swing, eyes on ball, bat placed down. Child checks each after the game and records hits/at-bats (e.g., 5 hits in 8 at-bats). Proficient = 5 of 6 cues checked by both child and parent.

weeks.prep: Beach ball or volleyball trainer (soft), a rope tied between two chairs or posts at about head height.
misconceptions: Hitting a volley with the palms. A set (overhead volley) uses the finger pads in a triangle shape above the forehead.
Swinging the arms for a bump. Keep a flat platform with arms straight and lift with the legs.

days.guide: Overhead volley: hands above forehead, thumbs and index fingers forming a triangle, push up with finger pads and extend legs. 20 in a row.

questions.q: Where are your hands for an overhead volley?
questions.a: Above the forehead, forming a triangle 'window' with thumbs and index fingers.

days.guide: Forearm pass (bump): clasp hands, arms straight forming a flat platform, contact on the forearms, lift with legs.

questions.q: Where should the ball hit in a bump?
questions.a: On the flat part of the forearms, just above the wrists.

days.guide: Rally with a partner using sets and bumps; count hits.

questions.q: When do you use a bump instead of a set?
questions.a: For low balls (below the chest).

days.guide: Cooperative over-the-net game: count consecutive hits across the net.

questions.q: What is cooperative play?
questions.a: Working together toward a shared goal (like a long rally) rather than against each other.

days.guide: Record best rally of 3 tries; compare to the start of the week.

questions.q: Monday best: 6. Friday best: 14. Improvement?
questions.a: 8 more hits.

weeks.assessment_key: Rally count: record the best cooperative rally of 3 tries and compare to the week's start. 4 = 15+ hits with correct set and bump form; 3 = 10–14; 2 = 5–9; 1 = fewer than 5.
