days.guide: Read the challenge and have the child restate it in their own words.

questions.q: Restate the challenge.
questions.a: Build a device that uses wind from a fan to turn something and wind up a string to lift 10 pennies 30 cm.

days.guide: List measurable criteria in a table.

questions.q: Give three measurable criteria.
questions.a: Lifts at least 10 pennies; lifts them 30 cm; does so within a set time (e.g., 60 seconds).

days.guide: List constraints.

questions.q: What are the constraints?
questions.a: Only household materials listed, 3 days of building, no batteries (wind only).

days.guide: Study windmill and turbine photos; note how blades and axles convert wind to rotation.

questions.q: Why are turbine blades angled?
questions.a: Angled blades catch the wind so it pushes them sideways, making them rotate.

days.guide: The child writes a one-page design brief with a first sketch.

questions.q: What goes in a design brief?
questions.a: The problem, criteria, constraints and an initial idea/sketch.

weeks.assessment_key: Design brief rubric: 4 = problem clearly stated, 3+ measurable criteria, all constraints, labeled first sketch showing blades, axle, string and cup; 3 = criteria partly measurable; 2 = missing criteria or constraints; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paper, ruler, colored pencils; straws, skewers, cardstock for blade tests; box fan; timer.
misconceptions: Judging ideas during brainstorming. First generate many ideas, then evaluate.
Choosing the 'coolest' design instead of the one that best meets criteria. Use the decision matrix.

days.guide: Brainstorm at least 5 blade and axle ideas, sketching quickly without judging.

questions.q: Why brainstorm without judging?
questions.a: So more ideas come out; a strange idea might lead to a good one.

days.guide: Test flat, angled and cupped blades on a straw axle; count rotations in 10 seconds.

questions.q: Which blade shape spun fastest?
questions.a: Answer from data; angled or cupped blades usually turn faster than flat blades facing straight into the wind.

days.guide: Draw three full designs with labels and energy flow.

questions.q: Describe the energy changes in your design.
questions.a: Wind (moving air) → blades rotate → axle turns and winds string → pennies are lifted (stored energy from height).

days.guide: Score each design 1-3 on each criterion and constraint in a matrix.

questions.q: How does a decision matrix help?
questions.a: It compares designs fairly on the same criteria using scores.

days.guide: The child chooses one design and justifies it in a paragraph.

questions.q: What should the justification include?
questions.a: Matrix scores, test data (e.g., rotation counts), and how the design meets the criteria and constraints.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = matrix with 3 designs scored on all criteria/constraints, chosen design has the highest or well-justified score, paragraph cites blade-test data; 3 = matrix complete, weak justification; 2 = incomplete matrix; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Cups, straws, skewers, cardstock, string, tape, 10 pennies, box fan, meter stick, stopwatch, phone camera.
misconceptions: Changing the fan distance or speed between trials. Keep conditions identical for a fair test.
Hiding failures. Failures show what to improve; record them.

days.guide: Build the base and axle from the chosen sketch.

questions.q: Why must the axle turn freely?
questions.a: Friction wastes energy; a smooth axle lets more wind energy go into lifting.

days.guide: Attach blades, string and penny cup; first trial run.

questions.q: What happened on the first run?
questions.a: Record actual results; common issues: string slips off axle, blades hit the base.

days.guide: Write the test plan: fan distance, fan speed and load constant.

questions.q: Name the variables kept the same.
questions.a: Fan distance, fan speed setting, number of pennies, string length.

days.guide: Run 5 trials; record lift height and time.

questions.q: How do you find the average time?
questions.a: Add the 5 times and divide by 5.

days.guide: Identify and sketch/photograph failure points.

questions.q: Give an example of a failure point and fix.
questions.a: Axle wobbles → add a second support or tape a straw bearing; blades slip → glue blades to a cork hub.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = test plan lists controlled variables; data table with 5 trials (height, time, average); at least two failure points identified with evidence and possible fixes; 3 = data complete, analysis weak; 2 = fewer than 5 trials; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prototype and spare materials, graph paper, poster board or slides.
misconceptions: Changing several things at once in the redesign. Change one variable to know what caused the improvement.
Comparing single trials instead of averages.

days.guide: Change one variable to fix the biggest failure point.

questions.q: Why change only one variable?
questions.a: So you know that change caused any difference in results.

days.guide: Run 5 new trials under the same conditions.

questions.q: Why must conditions match the first tests?
questions.a: To compare fairly; otherwise you can't tell if the design change made the difference.

days.guide: Graph before-and-after averages; decide whether the change helped.

questions.q: If average lift time went from 40 s to 28 s, did it improve?
questions.a: Yes — it lifted 12 seconds faster on average.

days.guide: Present the device and data, explaining each energy conversion.

questions.q: Explain the energy conversions.
questions.a: Electrical energy runs the fan → moving air (wind) → rotating blades and axle → string winds → pennies gain height (stored energy).

days.guide: The child writes a reflection on what they'd change with more time.

questions.q: What makes a strong reflection?
questions.a: Specific next steps tied to data or failures observed.

weeks.assessment_key: Engineering rubric: 4 = one variable changed with reason; before/after data and graph of averages; correct conclusion; clear presentation of energy conversions; thoughtful reflection; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = no comparison data; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Science notebook, index cards, a ruler, a photo of California coastal cliffs; end-of-year assessment (key below).
misconceptions: Mixing units (e.g., calling erosion 'weathering'). Review vocabulary cards.
Memorizing without explaining. Practice explaining each idea in your own words with an example.

days.guide: The child makes concept-map flashcards for energy, collisions, circuits, waves and light and self-quizzes.

questions.q: What is the relationship between speed and energy?
questions.a: The faster an object moves, the more energy it has.

days.guide: Redo the ruler drop and explain the senses-brain-response model.

questions.q: Explain the model from memory.
questions.a: Sense organ detects a stimulus → nerves send a signal to the brain → brain processes and sends a signal to muscles → response.

days.guide: Explain the cliff photo using weathering, erosion and rock layer vocabulary.

questions.q: Which agent most likely shaped the cliffs?
questions.a: Waves eroding the base, with weathering (water, wind, plant roots) breaking the rock.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment.

questions.q: How do we see objects?
questions.a: Light reflects off them into our eyes.

days.guide: The child presents three favorite investigations to family.

questions.q: What should each explanation include?
questions.a: The question, what was done, the results, and what it showed.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year key (sample): 1) faster = more energy 2) energy transfers in collisions and becomes sound/heat 3) complete circuit needed; metals conduct 4) heat moves warm → cool 5) label wave crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength 6) codes transfer information 7) light reflects into eyes 8) plant/animal structures support survival (example) 9) senses → brain → response 10) weathering vs. erosion 11) bottom rock layer oldest 12) Ring of Fire pattern 13) one hazard solution with trade-off 14) renewable vs. nonrenewable examples. Proficient: 80%.

VAPA.overview: Plan about 30 minutes a day. The year alternates art studios (drawing, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, folk art) with music units (rhythm, recorder, melody, composition, world music), with many links to fourth-grade California history and culture. You don't need art or music training: show the image or recording, try the technique alongside your child, and coach using the cues in each lesson. Keep a sketchbook and portfolio folder all year, use 'I notice / I wonder / I suggest' for feedback, and record recorder playing often so your child can hear their own progress.

weeks.prep: Gather a sketchbook, 2B and 4B pencils (softer, darker than a school HB), a kneaded eraser, and three kitchen objects (mug, spoon, piece of fruit). Find a Van Gogh reed-pen drawing online (e.g., 'Wheat Field with Cypresses' drawing or 'The Harvest' at the Van Gogh Museum / Google Arts & Culture).
misconceptions: Thinking a good drawing needs one even outline. Varying line weight (thick and thin) makes drawings livelier and shows depth.
Peeking during blind contour. The point is to train your eye to look closely; wobbly results are expected.

days.guide: Let your child decorate the cover. Demonstrate a few lines, then they fill a page with 15 labeled line types (zigzag, broken, thick-thin, spiral, wavy, dotted, hatched).

questions.q: Name three kinds of lines and a feeling each could show.
questions.a: Examples: zigzag — excited or angry; wavy — calm or flowing; broken/dotted — uncertain or delicate; thick — strong.

days.guide: Your child draws their hand three times without looking at the paper, moving slowly along edges, then once while looking. Compare.

questions.q: What did blind contour help you notice?
questions.a: Details of the edges — wrinkles, knuckles, fingernail shapes — because you had to look carefully the whole time.

days.guide: Arrange a mug, spoon and fruit; your child draws only the edges and important inner lines (contour), mostly looking at the objects.

questions.q: What is a contour line?
questions.a: A line that follows the edges and important shapes of an object.

days.guide: Look at the Van Gogh drawing; your child lists marks used for grass (short strokes), sky (swirls/dots) and trees (curving lines).

questions.q: How did Van Gogh make different textures with only lines?
questions.a: He changed the kind of mark — dots, dashes, short strokes, swirls — for each area.

days.guide: Your child titles the best contour drawing and explains line choices to a family member. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why might you make some lines darker than others?
questions.a: To show edges closer to you, shadows or important parts (line weight adds emphasis and depth).

weeks.assessment_key: Contour drawing: 4 = three objects drawn with careful continuous contour lines and intentional line variety; 3 = contour accurate, little variety; 2 = sketchy or incomplete; 1 = not attempted. Explanation proficient if the child names at least two line types/weights and why they were used.

weeks.prep: Gather pencils (2B, 4B), paper, a flashlight, a ball and a cylinder object (can or roll). Darken a room for Tuesday. Vocabulary: value = lightness or darkness.
misconceptions: Shading with an outline around the shape. Use value changes to show the edge.
Putting the cast shadow on the same side as the light. The cast shadow falls on the side away from the light.

days.guide: Your child draws 7 boxes and shades from white to darkest black with a 4B, pressing harder step by step.

questions.q: What is value?
questions.a: How light or dark a color or tone is.

days.guide: Shine a flashlight on a ball in a dark room; your child points to highlight, midtone, core shadow and cast shadow.

questions.q: Where is the highlight on the ball?
questions.a: On the spot facing the light most directly.

days.guide: Draw and shade a sphere, cube and cylinder with one light source. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: On a cube lit from the upper left, which face is lightest?
questions.a: The top (facing the light); the face away from the light is darkest.

days.guide: Make a 3-box chart for hatching, cross-hatching and stippling (dots). Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How do you make stippling darker?
questions.a: Put the dots closer together.

days.guide: Shade a fruit from observation; compare with week 1's contour drawing. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How does shading change a drawing?
questions.a: It makes flat shapes look three-dimensional (form).

weeks.assessment_key: Shaded fruit: 4 = light source consistent, highlight, midtone, core shadow and cast shadow all present, smooth value range; 3 = one element missing; 2 = flat with little value; 1 = outline only.

weeks.prep: Plan a nature walk. Cut a cardstock viewfinder (a 1 × 1.5 inch window). Find John James Audubon's bird watercolors (Birds of America) online.
misconceptions: Drawing what you think an object looks like instead of what you see. Keep looking back at the real object.
Drawing too small. Fill the page so details can show.

days.guide: Take a 20-minute walk and collect 5 natural objects with interesting shapes and textures (leaf, pinecone, feather, shell, seed pod). Only collect things already on the ground and leave protected areas alone.

questions.q: Why do artists collect objects to study?
questions.a: To observe real shapes, textures and details closely.

days.guide: Your child cuts a viewfinder, arranges the objects, and looks through it to find 4 interesting views, sketching each as a small thumbnail box.

questions.q: What does a viewfinder help you do?
questions.a: Choose and frame a composition by blocking out everything else.

days.guide: Your child picks the best thumbnail and draws one object large enough to touch at least three edges of the page, first in contour and then adding value and texture.

questions.q: Why fill the page?
questions.a: It shows more detail and makes a stronger composition.

days.guide: Look at two Audubon birds; your child writes a first reaction, then after the drawing week looks again and notes what they now appreciate (feather detail, pose, life-size scale).

questions.q: What did Audubon do to make his birds so accurate?
questions.a: He observed real birds closely and drew them life-size with detailed feathers and natural poses.

days.guide: Your child writes 3 sentences about details they noticed only by drawing, then shares the drawing with family.

questions.q: What's one detail you noticed only by drawing?
questions.a: Answer varies; e.g., veins on the leaf, layered scales on a pinecone.

weeks.assessment_key: Nature study: 4 = object fills page, accurate contour, value, and fine details; 3 = most; 2 = small or few details; 1 = incomplete. Reflection: three specific observations.

weeks.prep: Gather drawings from weeks 1–3 and the sketchbook. Choose a household object for the final drawing (a sneaker, teapot or stuffed animal).
misconceptions: Thinking feedback means you did something wrong. Feedback helps you improve.
Revising by erasing everything. Revise by adding to what's there (more value, more detail).

days.guide: Make a 4-point checklist: fills page, line variety, value range, detail. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why make criteria before judging?
questions.a: So the judgment is fair and specific.

days.guide: Discuss two drawings using 'I notice / I wonder / I suggest.' Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Give an 'I suggest' comment.
questions.a: 'I suggest darkening the shadow under the mug so it looks heavier.'

days.guide: Revise one drawing based on feedback. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What did you change and why?
questions.a: Answer varies; should name a criterion (e.g., more value).

days.guide: Create a finished observational drawing using all skills. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Which skills should the final drawing show?
questions.a: Contour, line variety, value shading, detail, filling the page.

days.guide: Self-assess with the checklist and display. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Which criterion is your strongest?
questions.a: Answer varies; should cite evidence from the drawing.

weeks.assessment_key: Final drawing scored 1–4 on each criterion: fills page, line variety, value range (at least 5 values), detail. Proficient = 12/16 or higher.

weeks.prep: Open Chrome Music Lab Rhythm. Get a bucket or pot to drum on and make 8 rhythm cards (quarter = 'ta', two eighths = 'ti-ti', half = 'ta-a', quarter rest = silent beat). Pick a march (e.g., Sousa) and a waltz (e.g., Strauss 'Blue Danube').
misconceptions: Confusing beat and rhythm. The beat is steady like a heartbeat; the rhythm follows the words.
Skipping rests. A rest is a silent beat — keep counting.

days.guide: Pat the beat while singing 'Old MacDonald,' then clap the words' rhythm. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is the difference between beat and rhythm?
questions.a: Beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds (like the words).

days.guide: Read and clap 8 cards, saying 'ta' and 'ti-ti.' Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How many beats is a half note?
questions.a: Two beats.

days.guide: Conduct 2/4 (down-up), 3/4 (down-out-up) and 4/4 (down-in-out-up) to a march and a waltz. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Which meter fits a waltz?

days.guide: Call-and-response: you play 4 beats, your child answers with improvised 4 beats. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is improvising?
questions.a: Making up music on the spot.

days.guide: Clap 4 patterns; identify the meter of 3 songs. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does a bar line do?
questions.a: Divides music into measures with equal numbers of beats.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythm reading: 4 patterns clapped accurately with steady beat (4 = all correct; 3 = 3; 2 = 2; 1 = 0–1). Meter check: march = 2 or 4; waltz = 3; third song as chosen.

weeks.prep: Get a soprano recorder and fingering chart. B = left thumb + finger 1; A = thumb + 1, 2; G = thumb + 1, 2, 3. 'Hot Cross Buns' = B A G, B A G, G G G G A A A A, B A G.
misconceptions: Blowing hard. Use a gentle, warm breath ('doo').
Using fingertips. Cover holes with the soft pads so no air leaks.

days.guide: Show how to hold the recorder: sit tall, left hand on top, right thumb supporting behind, lips lightly around the mouthpiece (not teeth). Start each note with a soft 'doo' and play B (thumb + finger 1) in long, steady tones.

questions.q: Which hand goes on top?
questions.a: The left hand.

days.guide: Add A (thumb + fingers 1, 2). Your child reads a short line of quarter and half notes on B and A, counting aloud before playing.

questions.q: How long do you hold a half note?
questions.a: Two beats.

days.guide: Add G (thumb + 1, 2, 3). Clap and say the rhythm of 'Hot Cross Buns,' say the note names, then play it from the staff.

questions.q: Where is G on the treble staff?
questions.a: On the second line from the bottom.

days.guide: Your child writes letter names under notes on a staff worksheet (B = middle line, A = second space, G = second line), then plays each line of the worksheet.

questions.q: Where is A?
questions.a: In the second space from the bottom.

days.guide: Your child performs 'Hot Cross Buns' and 'Gently Sleep' for you; give one compliment and one tip (tone, steady beat or tonguing).

questions.q: What causes squeaks?
questions.a: Blowing too hard or leaky fingers.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorder check: 4 = correct notes, steady beat, clear tone, tonguing each note in both songs; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors; 1 = cannot play.

weeks.prep: Recorder, fingering chart and song sheets. High C = thumb + finger 2; high D = finger 2 only (thumb off). 'Merrily We Roll Along' (in G) = B A G A B B B, A A A, B B B, B A G A B B B, A A B A G. 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' is the same tune except the third phrase goes B D D, so it uses high D too.
misconceptions: Leaving the thumb on for high D. High D needs only finger 2; the thumb hole must be open.
Rushing half notes. Count 'one-two' for every half note so the beat stays steady.

days.guide: Teach high C (thumb + 2) and high D (2 only). Play the 'scale' B–C–D–C–B slowly, checking for squeaks.

questions.q: What is the fingering for high D?
questions.a: Left-hand finger 2 only, with the thumb hole uncovered.

days.guide: Your child plays 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' from notation while you tap a steady beat. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Which phrase of 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' uses high D?
questions.a: The third phrase, 'little lamb' — B D D.

days.guide: Rehearse 'Merrily We Roll Along' and the opening of 'Ode to Joy' (B B C D D C B A G G A B B A A), slow first.

questions.q: 'Mary' and 'Merrily' share a melody. What's different?
questions.a: Only the third phrase: Mary goes B D D, Merrily goes B B B.

days.guide: Record both songs; your child rates tone (1–4) and rhythm accuracy (1–4) and names one fix.

questions.q: What is a phrase in music?
questions.a: A musical 'sentence' — a group of notes that makes a complete idea, usually followed by a breath.

days.guide: Your child performs 'Mary' and 'Merrily' while you check tone and steady beat. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.q: How can you make your tone smoother?
questions.a: Use gentle steady breath, cover holes fully with finger pads, and tongue each note softly with 'doo.'

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded songs: 4 = correct notes, steady beat, clear tone with no squeaks; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors or uneven beat; 1 = cannot complete. Self-evaluation proficient when ratings match the recording and one specific fix is named.

weeks.prep: Recorder, a bucket drum (or pot) with a wooden spoon, and a metronome app set to 80 beats per minute. Choose a recorder song your child plays well ('Hot Cross Buns' or 'Merrily').
misconceptions: Thinking the ostinato player can change the pattern. An ostinato repeats the same pattern the whole time.
Speeding up when playing together. Listen to the metronome and each other.

days.guide: Your child creates a 4-beat ostinato (e.g., ta ta ti-ti ta) and repeats it 8 times. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is an ostinato?
questions.a: A short rhythm or melody pattern repeated over and over.

days.guide: Your child plays the recorder melody while you play the ostinato on the bucket (then switch).

questions.q: What is an ensemble?
questions.a: A group performing music together.

days.guide: Rehearse with a metronome at 80 bpm. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why practice with a metronome?
questions.a: It keeps the tempo steady so performers stay together.

days.guide: Practice etiquette: bow, quiet listening, applause at the end. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: When should the audience clap?
questions.a: At the end of the piece, when the performer finishes and bows.

days.guide: Perform the mini-concert; evaluate with a 3-point rubric (steady beat, correct notes, etiquette).

questions.q: What does a performer do after finishing?
questions.a: Bows to thank the audience.

weeks.assessment_key: Mini-concert rubric (each 1–3): steady beat with the ostinato; correct notes on recorder; performer etiquette (introduction, bow). Proficient = 7/9 or higher.

weeks.prep: Gather watercolor or tempera paints (red, yellow, blue, white, black), brushes, water cups, palette and paper. Draw a 12-section circle.
misconceptions: Thinking you need to buy green or orange. Secondary colors are mixed from primaries.
Adding too much black to make a shade. Add black a tiny bit at a time; it's very strong.

days.guide: Your child paints primaries (red, yellow, blue), mixes secondaries (orange, green, violet), then tertiaries in between.

questions.q: What two primaries make green?
questions.a: Blue and yellow.

days.guide: Make a tint strip (adding white) and a shade strip (adding black). Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is a tint?
questions.a: A color mixed with white, making it lighter.

days.guide: Paint two small abstract designs, one in warm colors and one in cool. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Name the warm and cool colors.
questions.a: Warm: red, orange, yellow. Cool: blue, green, violet.

days.guide: Paint complementary pairs side by side. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What happens when complements sit next to each other?
questions.a: They create strong contrast and make each other look brighter.

days.guide: Quiz on color vocabulary. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What is a tertiary color?
questions.a: A mix of a primary and a neighboring secondary color (like red-orange).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: primary = red, yellow, blue; secondary = orange, green, violet; tertiary = primary + secondary neighbor; complementary = opposite pairs (red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet); warm = red/orange/yellow; cool = blue/green/violet; tint = + white; shade = + black. Color wheel: all 12 colors in correct order.

weeks.prep: Find a painting by California Impressionist Guy Rose (e.g., 'Laguna Eucalyptus' or 'Incoming Tide') and photos of Yosemite, the coast and a desert. Gather paper and colored pencils.
misconceptions: Thinking the background should be as detailed as the foreground. Distant things show less detail.
Placing far objects lower on the page. Objects farther away are placed higher, nearer the horizon.

days.guide: Look at a Guy Rose painting; find foreground, middle ground and background. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Which ground is closest to the viewer?
questions.a: The foreground (bottom of the picture).

days.guide: Draw three mountain ranges getting lighter as they recede. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why do distant mountains look lighter and bluer?
questions.a: Air and haze between you and the mountains soften color and detail (atmospheric perspective).

days.guide: Sketch a California landscape with overlapping layers. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How does overlapping show depth?
questions.a: An object in front blocks part of the one behind it, so we know it's closer.

days.guide: Add warm colors in front, cool behind. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why use cool colors in the background?
questions.a: Cool colors seem to recede, making things look farther away.

days.guide: Explain how overlap, size, placement and color show depth. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How does size show depth?
questions.a: Farther objects are drawn smaller.

weeks.assessment_key: Landscape sketch: 4 = clear foreground/middle/background, overlap, size change, placement and warm/cool color; 3 = three of these; 2 = two; 1 = flat.

weeks.prep: Gather watercolors, watercolor paper, masking tape and brushes. Find Ansel Adams' 'Monolith, the Face of Half Dome' (1927) online. A phone camera with a black-and-white setting works for photos.
misconceptions: Painting foreground first in watercolor. Work light to dark, sky and background first.
Thinking black-and-white photos are boring. Adams used strong contrast and value to create drama.

days.guide: Practice flat wash, gradated wash (light to dark) and wet-on-wet skies. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is wet-on-wet?
questions.a: Painting on wet paper so colors spread and blend softly.

days.guide: Paint the week 10 landscape: sky first, foreground last. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why paint the sky first?
questions.a: Watercolor goes light to dark; background layers go under foreground details.

days.guide: Study Adams' 'Monolith' and discuss value and contrast. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How did Ansel Adams create drama in 'Monolith'?
questions.a: Strong contrast: a very dark sky (he used a red filter) against the bright granite face of Half Dome.

days.guide: Take 5 black-and-white photos with strong contrast. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is contrast?
questions.a: A big difference between light and dark areas.

days.guide: Compare painting and photos in writing. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How are painting and photography alike?
questions.a: Both use composition, value and contrast to show a scene and mood.

weeks.assessment_key: Watercolor: sky first, at least two techniques, depth shown. Photos: 5 black-and-white images with clear contrast. Comparison: 4 = two similarities and two differences with art terms; 3 = some; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Find images of a Bierstadt landscape (e.g., 'Among the Sierra Nevada, California'), Hokusai's 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa,' and a California Impressionist landscape. Have your child's finished landscapes.
misconceptions: Judging art only by 'like' or 'don't like.' Use criteria and evidence.
Thinking all landscapes should look realistic. Different artists and cultures have different styles and goals.

days.guide: Develop criteria (depth, color, mood, technique). Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why use criteria to evaluate art?
questions.a: So judgments are fair, specific and based on evidence.

days.guide: Apply criteria to three master landscapes. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How does Hokusai show depth in 'The Great Wave'?
questions.a: The huge wave in the foreground makes tiny Mount Fuji in the background look far away (size and overlapping).

days.guide: Apply criteria to your own landscape. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Which criterion did your landscape meet best? Give evidence.
questions.a: Answer varies; should cite a specific feature.

days.guide: Add finishing details to improve one criterion. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Give an example of improving depth.
questions.a: Darken and add detail in the foreground, lighten distant mountains.

days.guide: Present the landscape and evaluation. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What mood does your landscape show, and how?
questions.a: Answer varies; should connect colors/light to mood.

weeks.assessment_key: Written evaluation: 4 = applies all four criteria to three master works and own work with specific evidence; 3 = most; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Recorder and fingering chart; staff paper; recordings of 'Twinkle, Twinkle,' 'Ode to Joy' and 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow.' Low E = thumb + left 1, 2, 3 + right 1, 2; low D = thumb + left 1, 2, 3 + right 1, 2, 3 (only the bottom hole open). For the D-to-D scale you'll also need F-sharp — find it on your fingering chart (it differs slightly between baroque and German recorders).
misconceptions: Squeaks on low notes from blowing too hard. Low notes need slow, gentle 'warm' air.
Thinking a skip is any jump. A step moves to the very next note; a skip jumps over one note; a leap is bigger than a skip.

days.guide: Play the three melodies; your child draws each melody's up-and-down shape as a line. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Which song begins with a big leap up?
questions.a: 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' — 'Some-where' leaps up an octave.

days.guide: Teach low E and low D; play long tones (4 beats each), checking every hole is sealed. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why do low notes squeak more easily?
questions.a: Any tiny leak or too much breath causes squeaks; low notes need all holes sealed and gentle air.

days.guide: Circle steps, skips and leaps in 'Ode to Joy' notation; then play it. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: 'Ode to Joy' starts B B C D D C B A. Are these steps, skips or leaps?
questions.a: Mostly steps (plus repeated notes).

days.guide: Name 20 notes from low D to high D on a worksheet. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Name the treble staff lines from bottom to top.
questions.a: E, G, B, D, F.

days.guide: Play the D-to-D scale up and down; sight-read a 4-measure stepwise melody. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is melodic contour?
questions.a: The shape of a melody as it goes up, down or stays the same.

weeks.assessment_key: Scale check: D–E–F#–G–A–B–C–D up and down with correct fingerings and steady tone (4 = no errors; 3 = 1–2; 2 = several; 1 = cannot). Sight-reading: correct notes and rhythm in a 4-measure stepwise melody (proficient = 3 of 4 measures correct).

weeks.prep: Print lyrics of 'Oh My Darling, Clementine' and 'Sweet Betsy from Pike,' and a California/US map. Find recordings. Clementine on recorder in G uses low D, G, A, B, C and high D — teach two phrases at a time.
misconceptions: Thinking ballads are just silly songs. Ballads tell stories and often show real conditions (hard travel, mining life), sometimes with humor.
Thinking Gold Rush songs were written for school. They were sung by miners and travelers for entertainment and comfort.

days.guide: Sing 'Clementine'; discuss: a miner (forty-niner) lives with his daughter in a canyon while 'excavating for a mine.'

questions.q: What does 'forty-niner' mean in the song?
questions.a: A person who came to California in the 1849 Gold Rush to look for gold.

days.guide: Sing 'Sweet Betsy from Pike'; trace her journey from Pike County, Missouri, across the plains, deserts and mountains to California.

questions.q: What hardships did Betsy and Ike face?
questions.a: Long overland travel, crossing deserts and mountains, losing animals, hunger and tiredness (told with humor).

days.guide: Learn the 'Clementine' melody on recorder two phrases at a time. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why learn a song two phrases at a time?
questions.a: Short chunks are easier to master before putting them together.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences on what the ballads reveal about Gold Rush life. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why did people sing during the Gold Rush?
questions.a: For entertainment, comfort, to share stories and pass long hours of travel and work.

days.guide: Perform one Gold Rush song and explain why you chose it. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What is a refrain?
questions.a: A part of a song that repeats, like 'Oh my darling, oh my darling.'

weeks.assessment_key: Performance: 4 = accurate melody and lyrics, steady beat, expressive; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete. Explanation proficient if it links the song to Gold Rush history (miners, overland travel).

weeks.prep: Recorder, a metronome app, and a recording of Grieg's 'In the Hall of the Mountain King.' Vocabulary: piano (p) = soft, forte (f) = loud, crescendo = gradually louder; largo = very slow, moderato = medium, allegro = fast.
misconceptions: Thinking faster means louder. Tempo (speed) and dynamics (volume) are separate.
Playing piano by blowing weakly so the note goes flat. On recorder, soft dynamics are limited; play gently but keep steady air.

days.guide: Play 'Clementine' piano, then forte; add a crescendo to one phrase. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does forte mean?
questions.a: Loud.

days.guide: Play 'Ode to Joy' at largo (~50 bpm), moderato (~100) and allegro (~130). Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Which tempo is fastest: largo, moderato or allegro?
questions.a: Allegro.

days.guide: Listen to 'Mountain King'; draw a listening map that grows bigger and closer together. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How do tempo and dynamics change in 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'?
questions.a: It starts slow and soft, then gets faster and louder (accelerando and crescendo) to a wild ending.

days.guide: Mark dynamics and tempo on a folk song's music to match its mood. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What tempo and dynamics fit a sad verse of 'Clementine'?
questions.a: Slower tempo and softer dynamics (piano).

days.guide: Perform with planned expression and explain choices. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.q: What is a crescendo?
questions.a: Gradually getting louder.

weeks.assessment_key: Expressive performance: 4 = clearly different dynamics and tempo that match the mood, each choice explained; 3 = choices performed but not all explained; 2 = little change; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Recorder, song sheets from this unit, recording device, and a 4-point rubric (tone, rhythm, notes, expression).
misconceptions: Practicing only from the beginning. Isolate the hardest measures.
Stopping after mistakes in a run-through. Keep going to build performance stamina.

days.guide: Choose two pieces and explain why they fit skill level and interests. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why choose pieces that fit your skill level?
questions.a: So you can perform confidently and accurately while still being challenged.

days.guide: Rehearse the hardest 4 measures of each piece slowly, then at tempo. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why practice the hard part slowly first?
questions.a: Slow practice builds correct finger patterns before adding speed.

days.guide: Record a full run-through of both pieces without stopping. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why not stop when you make a mistake in a run-through?
questions.a: In a performance you keep going; it builds recovery skill.

days.guide: Listen and score tone, rhythm, notes, expression; fix two problems. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Name a way to fix a rhythm problem.
questions.a: Count aloud or use a metronome slowly.

days.guide: Perform for family with spoken introductions. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What should an introduction include?
questions.a: The title, composer or origin, and something interesting about the piece.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (1–4 each): tone, rhythm, notes, expression; plus introduction. Proficient = 3+ in each.

weeks.prep: Open Calisphere's 'Native Americans: Arts and Traditions' set (Pomo and Chumash baskets). Gather a paper plate, scissors, yarn in 2–3 colors, and paper strips. Cut an odd number of slits around the plate rim for the loom.
misconceptions: Thinking California basketry is only in the past. Pomo, Chumash and other California Native weavers continue the tradition today.
Copying exact designs. Create your own motifs inspired by, not copied from, cultural designs.

days.guide: Study Pomo and Chumash baskets; describe shapes, patterns and materials. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What materials did California Native weavers use?
questions.a: Local plants such as willow, sedge root, bulrush, juncus and sumac, and sometimes feathers and shell beads.

days.guide: Write what baskets suggest about makers' environment, skills and life. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What can you infer from a very tightly woven basket?
questions.a: The weaver was highly skilled; it might hold water or seeds; the plants came from local wetlands or hillsides.

days.guide: Make the paper-plate loom; begin weaving. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is the over-under pattern?
questions.a: Yarn alternates over one spoke and under the next.

days.guide: Design a repeating geometric motif and finish the weaving. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.a: A repeated design element or shape in a pattern.

days.guide: Explain pattern choices and basketry as a living tradition. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why is basketry called a living tradition?
questions.a: Native weavers today still gather materials and make baskets, passing skills to new generations.

weeks.assessment_key: Weaving: complete with an intentional repeating pattern and tight over-under weaving. Written inference rubric: 4 = three inferences supported by details from the baskets; 3 = two; 2 = one; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Gather tissue paper, scissors, string, glue stick; find images of papel picado, alebrijes and Talavera pottery.
misconceptions: Cutting without folding. Folding first makes symmetrical designs.
Thinking negative space is 'empty.' The cut-out holes are part of the design.

days.guide: Show images of papel picado (cut tissue banners), alebrijes (brightly painted fantasy creatures) and Talavera (tin-glazed pottery from Puebla). Your child describes colors and patterns and you discuss when each is made and used.

questions.q: When is papel picado used?
questions.a: At celebrations such as Día de los Muertos, Christmas, weddings, birthdays and festivals.

days.guide: Fold a square of scrap paper in half (then in quarters), cut small shapes along the folds, and open it. Your child points to positive space (paper left) and negative space (holes).

questions.q: What is negative space in papel picado?
questions.a: The cut-out holes where the paper was removed.

days.guide: Your child picks a theme (celebration, nature, family) and sketches a design on folded paper, shading the parts to cut out and keeping a solid border at the top for the string.

questions.q: What is symmetry?
questions.a: When both halves of a design are mirror images.

days.guide: Stack two sheets of tissue, fold and cut carefully, then unfold. Make 3 banners and glue each over a string along the top edge.

questions.q: Why fold paper before cutting?
questions.a: To make symmetrical repeating shapes with one cut.

days.guide: Hang the banner and have your child explain its symbols and the tradition to a family member.

questions.q: Where does papel picado come from?
questions.a: Mexico.

weeks.assessment_key: Banner: 3 cut panels with symmetry, clear theme, balance of positive/negative space, neat cuts. Explanation: identifies Mexican origin and meaning of symbols.

weeks.prep: Gather a soft round watercolor brush, black watercolor or ink, water, and rice paper or newsprint. Find a classical Chinese bamboo painting (e.g., by Wen Tong or a Qing-dynasty ink bamboo) and information about Tyrus Wong (Chinese American artist whose paintings inspired the look of Disney's 'Bambi').
misconceptions: Filling every part of the paper. In Chinese brush painting, empty space is an important part of the composition.
Holding the brush like a pencil at a slant. Hold it upright and move from the arm for confident strokes.

days.guide: Study the bamboo painting; discuss balance and empty space. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why do Chinese painters leave empty space?
questions.a: It creates balance and calm, suggests air or mist, and lets the viewer's imagination fill in.

days.guide: Demonstrate the four strokes: stalk (press-lift segments), leaf (press then lift to a point), dot and line. Your child practices each on newsprint, holding the brush upright.

questions.q: How do you make a bamboo leaf stroke?
questions.a: Touch the tip down, press to widen, then lift as you pull to make a pointed end.

days.guide: Mix three values of ink wash (dark, medium, light). Paint a bamboo stalk with leaves, darker leaves in front and lighter behind.

questions.q: How do you make lighter ink?
questions.a: Add more water.

days.guide: Read about Tyrus Wong: born in China, came to California as a boy through Angel Island, his misty paintings inspired 'Bambi's' backgrounds.

questions.q: How did Tyrus Wong influence American art?
questions.a: His Chinese-style landscape paintings gave Disney's 'Bambi' its soft, misty look; he also painted and designed kites and greeting cards.

days.guide: Finish a painting with a red seal-style signature (draw a small square with initials) and compare with earlier work.

questions.q: What is a seal in Chinese painting?
questions.a: A carved stamp with the artist's name printed in red ink as a signature.

weeks.assessment_key: Brush painting: 4 = confident stalk and leaf strokes, at least three ink values, balanced composition with intentional empty space, seal signature; 3 = most; 2 = hesitant strokes or one value; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find photos of murals in Chicano Park (San Diego) and Balmy Alley (San Francisco). Get a large sheet of butcher paper, markers or paint, and invite family members to collaborate.
misconceptions: Thinking a mural is just a big painting. Murals usually share a public message about a community.
Letting one person decide everything. Collaboration means combining ideas fairly.

days.guide: Look at mural photos; discuss messages. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What messages do Chicano Park murals share?
questions.a: Pride in Mexican American/Chicano culture and history, community struggle and identity.

days.guide: With family, choose a community theme and set goals. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why set goals before drawing?
questions.a: So everyone agrees on the message and plan.

days.guide: Each person sketches; combine the best into one plan. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How can you combine different ideas fairly?
questions.a: Choose the strongest parts of each sketch and agree as a group.

days.guide: Create the mural together. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What makes collaboration successful?
questions.a: Sharing tasks, listening, respecting ideas and working toward the goal.

days.guide: Write an artist statement explaining the message. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What should the mural statement explain?
questions.a: The theme, symbols used and the message to the community.

weeks.assessment_key: Mural and statement: 4 = clear community theme, symbols support message, all contributed, statement explains message and symbols; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = unclear message; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find recordings of a two-part (AB) song, 'Twinkle, Twinkle,' and Mozart's 'Rondo alla Turca' (Piano Sonata K. 331, third movement). Cut colored paper shapes (A = red circle, B = blue square, C = green triangle).
misconceptions: Thinking a section is a single line. A section is a larger part of the piece, often several phrases.
Thinking every piece has three sections. Forms vary: AB has two, ABA has three with a return, rondo returns to A many times.

days.guide: Listen to an AB song; hold up shapes when sections change. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is AB (binary) form?
questions.a: Two different sections, A then B.

days.guide: Label 'Twinkle, Twinkle' as ABA in the lyrics. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Which lines of 'Twinkle' are the B section?
questions.a: 'Up above the world so high, like a diamond in the sky.'

days.guide: Listen to 'Rondo alla Turca' and track the main theme each time it returns. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What happens in rondo form?
questions.a: The A section keeps returning between different sections (A B A C A).

days.guide: Create a different movement for each section of a rondo and perform it. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How does movement show form?
questions.a: Each section has its own movement, so repeats are easy to see.

days.guide: Identify the form of 3 new pieces with a labeled diagram. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is ABA (ternary) form?
questions.a: A section, a contrasting B section, then A returns.

weeks.assessment_key: Form check: correct form for 3 pieces (AB, ABA, rondo) with labeled diagrams. Proficient = 3/3 or 2/3 with correct definitions.

weeks.prep: Recorder, staff paper, and Chrome Music Lab Song Maker (set to 8 bars).
misconceptions: Thinking a composition must be long and complicated. Good melodies repeat and vary a short idea.
Ending on a random note. Ending on G (home note) makes a melody sound finished.

days.guide: Improvise 4-beat answers with B, A, G to your 4-beat questions. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What makes a good musical answer?
questions.a: It fits the beat, relates to the question and ends on G (home).

days.guide: Create a 2-measure motive; repeat it with changes. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a motive?
questions.a: A short musical idea that can be repeated and changed.

days.guide: Compose an 8-measure melody in Song Maker. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why repeat your motive?
questions.a: Repetition makes a melody memorable and unified.

days.guide: Notate the melody on staff paper. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why write the melody down?
questions.a: So it can be played again exactly.

days.guide: Play on recorder; record for revision. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How should your melody end?
questions.a: On the home note, G.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition draft: 8 measures, uses a repeated/varied motive, notated rhythm and pitch, ends on G. Proficient = all four.

weeks.prep: Staff paper, Song Maker, recorder, and the week 22 melody (A section). Prepare a 3-question feedback form: What did you like? Is B different enough? What could be clearer?
misconceptions: Making B too similar to A. Change tempo, dynamics, rhythm or pitch range.
Forgetting to return to A exactly. ABA means A returns.

days.guide: Plan contrast for B (tempo, dynamics, pitch range). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Name two ways to make B contrast with A.
questions.a: Change tempo, dynamics, rhythm or move to higher/lower notes.

days.guide: Compose an 8-measure contrasting B section. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is contrast in music?
questions.a: A noticeable difference between sections.

days.guide: Play the draft for a parent; gather feedback. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why ask for feedback?
questions.a: Listeners notice things the composer may miss.

days.guide: Revise two measures; record changes. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What did you revise and why?
questions.a: Answer varies; should cite feedback.

days.guide: Write a description of form and mood. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Describe ABA form in your own words.
questions.a: A section, different B section, A section returns.

weeks.assessment_key: Revised ABA composition: 4 = clear A, contrasting B, A returns, two revised measures documented; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = little contrast; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Recorder, recording device; find two youth recorder or band performances online. Prepare criteria (accuracy, tone, expression, stage presence).
misconceptions: Thinking the composer can't perform. Many composers premiere their own music.
Judging others harshly. Use criteria and specific, kind language.

days.guide: Write a program note with title and intent. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a program note?
questions.a: A short explanation of a piece for the audience.

days.guide: Rehearse with dynamics and tempo markings. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why add dynamics and tempo to your composition?
questions.a: They tell the performer how to express the mood.

days.guide: Perform the premiere for family. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What is a premiere?
questions.a: The first public performance of a piece.

days.guide: Evaluate two youth performances with criteria. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Give a specific, kind evaluation comment.
questions.a: 'The tone was clear, but the tempo sped up in the middle.'

days.guide: Self-evaluate the premiere. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Which criterion was strongest in your premiere?
questions.a: Answer varies; cite evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Premiere rubric (1–4 each): accuracy, tone, expression, stage presence, program note. Evaluation: uses all criteria with specific examples.

weeks.prep: Gather air-dry clay, a plastic knife, toothpicks, a water cup, a placemat, and found objects for texture (buttons, leaves, a fork, lace). Make slip by mixing a little clay with water to a yogurt-like paste. Wash hands after clay work.
misconceptions: Joining pieces by pressing only. Without score and slip, parts fall off as the clay dries.
Adding too much water. Soggy clay slumps and cracks; use just enough to keep it workable.

days.guide: Show safe handling (work on a mat, keep clay away from face, wash hands). Your child makes a pinch pot: thumb in the center, pinch while turning.

questions.q: How do you make a pinch pot?
questions.a: Roll a ball, press your thumb into the center, then pinch the walls evenly while turning the ball.

days.guide: Roll even coils and stack them onto the pinch pot, scoring and slipping each layer, to build a taller vessel or animal body.

questions.q: What does 'score and slip' mean?
questions.a: Scratch both surfaces and add slip (clay paste) before pressing them together.

days.guide: Press found objects into a clay slab to make a texture sampler. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is texture?
questions.a: How a surface feels or looks like it would feel.

days.guide: Sculpt a California animal (sea otter, quail, bear), joining legs, ears or tails with score and slip.

questions.q: Why should parts be joined with score and slip?
questions.a: So they stick firmly and don't crack off when dry.

days.guide: Let dry slowly (cover loosely); your child describes process and safety steps. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two clay safety steps.
questions.a: Work on a mat, keep clay away from your mouth/face, wash hands, clean tools.

weeks.assessment_key: Clay sculpture: 4 = recognizable California animal, secure score-and-slip joins, intentional texture, even walls; 3 = minor weak joins; 2 = parts fall off or little texture; 1 = incomplete. Process description includes at least two methods and two safety steps.

weeks.prep: Gather foam meat trays (washed) or styrofoam sheets, a dull pencil, tempera paint, a brayer or small roller, paper, and newspaper. Find Japanese woodblock prints (Hokusai, Hiroshige) online.
misconceptions: Forgetting the print reverses. Letters must be written backward on the plate.
Pressing too lightly. Lines must be deep enough that paint won't fill them.

days.guide: Look at Japanese woodblock prints; discuss how printmaking allows many copies and repeated designs.

questions.q: Why was printmaking useful in Japan?
questions.a: Artists could make many copies of the same image to sell, so more people could own art.

days.guide: Brainstorm 3 designs; choose one, remembering reversal. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: If you carve the word 'CAT' normally, how will it print?
questions.a: Backward (mirror image).

days.guide: Press the design into foam with a dull pencil. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why use a dull pencil?
questions.a: To press grooves without tearing through the foam.

days.guide: Roll paint thinly; pull 4 prints in different colors. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why roll paint in a thin, even layer?
questions.a: Thick paint fills the grooves and blurs the image.

days.guide: Sign and number the edition (1/4, 2/4...); choose the best. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What does '3/4' on a print mean?
questions.a: The third print in an edition of four.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition: 4 prints, clear lines, even ink, correctly numbered and signed. Proficient = 3 clean prints with correct numbering.

weeks.prep: Find images of a California mission adobe (e.g., Mission Santa Barbara), a San Francisco Victorian ('Painted Ladies'), a Craftsman bungalow (e.g., Gamble House, Pasadena) and a mid-century modern house (e.g., Palm Springs). Plan a neighborhood walk with a camera and sketchbook.
misconceptions: Thinking buildings are just boxes. Architecture uses form, materials and details to fit climate and culture.
Thinking style is only decoration. Materials and shapes often respond to climate (thick adobe walls keep interiors cool).

days.guide: Compare the four styles. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why do adobe buildings have thick walls?
questions.a: Thick earth walls keep interiors cool in hot weather and warm at night.

days.guide: Photograph and sketch 4 neighborhood buildings. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is a facade?
questions.a: The front face of a building.

days.guide: Draw close-up details of one building. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Name two architectural details you drew.
questions.a: Answer varies; e.g., arched windows, shingles, porch columns.

days.guide: Design a building for your community and draw its facade. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How can a design fit California's climate?
questions.a: Shade for sun, large windows for light, materials that stay cool, drought-tolerant landscaping.

days.guide: Explain how the design fits climate and community. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What makes mid-century modern homes distinctive?
questions.a: Flat or low roofs, large glass walls and open plans connecting indoors and outdoors.

weeks.assessment_key: Building design: 4 = detailed facade with clear features explained for climate and community; 3 = most; 2 = little explanation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather the dried clay sculpture, acrylic or tempera paint, brushes, index cards for labels, and a stable display spot.
misconceptions: Displaying art in direct sunlight. Light fades paper and paint.
Placing sculpture near edges. Choose a stable surface away from traffic.

days.guide: Get feedback using 'I notice / I wonder / I suggest.' Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Give an 'I suggest' comment for a sculpture.
questions.a: 'I suggest painting the otter's fur darker to show texture.'

days.guide: Paint the sculpture and add suggested details. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why wait until clay is fully dry to paint?
questions.a: Wet clay can crack and paint won't stick well.

days.guide: Plan the display: stable surface, away from edges and sun; sketch it. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why keep art out of direct sunlight?
questions.a: Sunlight fades colors and can damage materials.

days.guide: Write gallery labels (title, medium, date, description). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is the medium of your sculpture?
questions.a: Air-dry clay with acrylic (or tempera) paint.

days.guide: Install the work; give a 2-minute talk. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What should your talk include?
questions.a: Your process, techniques and what you learned.

weeks.assessment_key: Installation: sculpture painted and stable, prints displayed, labels complete with title, medium, date and description. Talk proficient if it explains process and one revision.

weeks.prep: Find a recording/video of 'El Son de la Negra' (e.g., Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán). Learn the instruments: violin, trumpet, vihuela (small, round-backed, 5-string strummed guitar), guitarrón (large bass guitar).
misconceptions: Thinking the guitarrón is just a big guitar playing chords. It plays the bass line.
Thinking mariachi is only background music. It's central to celebrations and California's Mexican American heritage.

days.guide: Listen and identify violin, trumpet, vihuela and guitarrón. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Which mariachi instrument plays the bass line?
questions.a: The guitarrón.

days.guide: Describe each instrument's timbre with adjectives. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Describe the timbre of mariachi trumpets.
questions.a: Bright, brassy, bold.

days.guide: Read about mariachi at California celebrations (weddings, quinceañeras, Día de los Muertos, Cinco de Mayo).

questions.q: Name two celebrations with mariachi.
questions.a: Weddings, quinceañeras, birthdays, festivals, Día de los Muertos.

days.guide: Clap the alternating 3/4 + 6/8 rhythm: 1-2-3-4-5-6 / 1-2-3-4-5-6 with accents ONE two three FOUR five six, then ONE two THREE four FIVE six.

questions.q: What is sesquialtera?
questions.a: Alternating between 6/8 (two groups of three) and 3/4 (three groups of two).

days.guide: Write how mariachi connects to family celebrations. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Where did mariachi music originate?
questions.a: Jalisco, Mexico.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening response: 4 = identifies 4 instruments with timbre words, explains the rhythm and connects mariachi to celebrations; 3 = three of these; 2 = two; 1 = one.

weeks.prep: Find videos of San Jose Taiko and Balinese gamelan. Gather buckets, drumsticks or wooden spoons, a pot and a shaker.
misconceptions: Thinking taiko is just drumming. Taiko includes choreographed movement, posture and kiai (shouts).
Thinking gamelan parts all play the same rhythm. Players interlock different patterns that fit together.

days.guide: Watch San Jose Taiko; describe movement and sound. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What makes taiko performance visual as well as musical?
questions.a: Big, coordinated arm movements, strong stances and shouts.

days.guide: Learn a 4-beat taiko pattern on a bucket with kiai shouts. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is a kiai?
questions.a: A shout used to show energy and keep the group together.

days.guide: Listen to gamelan; identify layered patterns. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What instruments are in a gamelan?
questions.a: Mostly metal gongs and metallophones (bronze keys), plus drums.

days.guide: Create a 3-part layered rhythm on bucket, pot and shaker; notate it. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a polyrhythm?
questions.a: Two or more different rhythms played at the same time.

days.guide: Perform and compare taiko and gamelan. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: Where does gamelan come from?
questions.a: Indonesia (Bali and Java).

weeks.assessment_key: Taiko performance: steady beat, strong movement, kiai at planned points. Comparison: 4 = two similarities and two differences (instruments, origin, layering); 3 = three; 2 = two; 1 = one.

weeks.prep: Find recordings of Duke Ellington's 'C-Jam Blues,' Dave Brubeck Quartet's 'Take Five' (1959, composed by Paul Desmond; Brubeck grew up in Concord, California), and Ella Fitzgerald scat singing (e.g., 'How High the Moon'). Find a free blues backing track in G.
misconceptions: Thinking improvisation is random. Jazz musicians improvise using scales, rhythms and the song's form.
Playing swung eighths evenly. Swing makes the first of each pair longer: 'doo-ba.'

days.guide: Listen to a 12-bar blues; clap on beat 1 of each bar, counting bars 1–12. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How many bars are in one chorus of a 12-bar blues?
questions.a: Twelve.

days.guide: Practice swung eighths ('doo-ba doo-ba') on B, A and G. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How are swung eighths different from straight eighths?
questions.a: Swung eighths are uneven — long-short; straight eighths are even.

days.guide: Improvise with B, A, G over a blues backing track. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is improvisation in jazz?
questions.a: Making up melodies on the spot that fit the song's chords and rhythm.

days.guide: Listen to 'Take Five'; count the 5 beats per measure (1-2-3, 4-5). Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What meter is 'Take Five' in?
questions.a: 5/4 — five beats per measure.

days.guide: Evaluate a jazz recording with criteria; write a short review. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is scat singing?
questions.a: Improvised singing with nonsense syllables instead of words, like an instrument.

weeks.assessment_key: Improvisation: 4 = stays with the beat and blues form, uses swing rhythm and B-A-G creatively; 3 = mostly; 2 = loses beat; 1 = none. Review: addresses groove, improvisation and expression with specific examples.

weeks.prep: Choose a short film clip (1–2 minutes, family-friendly) and open Chrome Music Lab Kandinsky. Gather recorder and percussion instruments. Pick a short story for the soundtrack.
misconceptions: Thinking film music is just background. It shapes how viewers feel.
Choosing random sounds for a soundtrack. Match tempo, dynamics and timbre to the mood.

days.guide: Watch the clip with and without sound; describe the mood change. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How does music change a film scene?
questions.a: It creates mood—tension, joy, sadness—and tells viewers how to feel.

days.guide: Draw in Kandinsky to turn art into sound. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Who was Wassily Kandinsky?
questions.a: A painter who connected colors and shapes with sounds and music.

days.guide: Create a soundtrack for a short story with recorder and percussion. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What sounds could show suspense?
questions.a: Slow, soft, repeated low notes that build in volume.

days.guide: Make a playlist of 5 songs that represent you; explain choices. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why might a song represent you?
questions.a: Its lyrics, mood or culture connects to your personality or experiences.

days.guide: Unit test on musical traditions and connections. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Name three musical traditions from this unit.
questions.a: Mariachi, taiko, gamelan, jazz/blues.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit check: 1) mariachi instruments (violin, trumpet, vihuela, guitarrón) 2) sesquialtera alternates 6/8 and 3/4 3) taiko from Japan, San Jose Taiko 4) gamelan from Indonesia 5) 12-bar blues 6) 'Take Five' in 5/4 7) film music creates mood. Soundtrack proficient if sounds match story events with clear tempo and dynamics choices.
