weeks.prep: Collect all of the year's artwork; have a camera or phone, folder, and good natural light for photos. Read about the Getty Conservation Institute or a museum's preservation methods.
misconceptions: Thinking a portfolio is a pile of all your work. A curated portfolio selects pieces with a purpose.
Photographing art in dim light or at an angle. Shoot straight on in even daylight.

days.guide: Lay out every artwork, sort by unit, and note skills each shows. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Which skills did your landscape show?
questions.a: Answer varies; e.g., atmospheric perspective, watercolor wash, overlap.

days.guide: Select 6 pieces using one criteria set; score each. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why use criteria to select?
questions.a: So choices are fair and show growth, skill and ideas.

days.guide: Photograph each piece; build a digital slideshow with titles. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why make a digital portfolio?
questions.a: It preserves and shares the art even if the originals are damaged.

days.guide: Read about museum preservation; list 3 ways technology helps. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name three ways museums protect art.
questions.a: Control light and humidity, digital scanning/archives, climate-controlled storage, protective glass.

days.guide: Write a curator's statement on theme and choices. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What does a curator's statement explain?
questions.a: The exhibition's theme and why the works were chosen.

weeks.assessment_key: Curated selection: 6 pieces with criteria scores. Digital portfolio: clear, straight-on photos with titles. Statement: 4 = clear theme and reasons for each choice; 3 = theme and some reasons; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather cardstock for mats, painter's tape, index cards; choose a wall with even light away from direct sun.
misconceptions: Hanging art too high. Center work at about eye level (around 57–60 inches).
Writing long labels. Keep labels short and informative.

days.guide: Compare an art museum, commercial gallery and community art walk in a chart. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How is a commercial gallery different from a museum?
questions.a: A gallery sells art; a museum collects, preserves and displays art for education.

days.guide: Mat 6 artworks; write museum-style labels. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What goes on a museum label?
questions.a: Title, artist, medium, year and a short description.

days.guide: Decide how to protect each piece. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why keep a sculpture on a stable shelf?
questions.a: So it won't fall and break.

days.guide: Sketch a floor plan; hang work at eye level with even spacing. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why use even spacing?
questions.a: It looks organized and gives each piece attention.

days.guide: Lead a family tour; revise unclear labels. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What did you revise after the tour?
questions.a: Answer varies; should name a specific label change.

weeks.assessment_key: Installed exhibition: matted, labeled, evenly spaced at eye level, protected. Venue chart: purpose, visitors and experience for all three venues correctly compared.

weeks.prep: Recorder, all music from the year, metronome, and paper for programs.
misconceptions: Raising tempo too quickly. Increase by small steps only after it's correct.
Forgetting dynamics. Mark them on the music.

days.guide: Choose 4 pieces (folk, classical excerpt, ABA composition, free choice); explain why each belongs.

questions.q: Why include different types of pieces?
questions.a: Variety shows different skills and keeps the audience interested.

days.guide: Practice the two hardest passages slowly, raising tempo 10 bpm at a time. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why raise tempo in small steps?
questions.a: So fingers stay accurate as speed increases.

days.guide: Record a run-through, get feedback, mark dynamics. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What does 'mf' mean?
questions.a: Mezzo forte — medium loud.

days.guide: Design a printed concert program. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What belongs in a concert program?
questions.a: Piece titles, composers and short notes.

days.guide: Hold a dress rehearsal with bows and introductions; fix one problem. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a dress rehearsal?
questions.a: A full practice exactly like the real performance.

weeks.assessment_key: Dress rehearsal checklist: all 4 pieces played; correct notes and rhythm; dynamics shown; spoken introductions; bows; one problem fixed. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Set up the exhibition wall, gather recorder, concert programs, and a recording device. Invite guests.
misconceptions: Thinking reflection means only listing what went well. Honest reflection includes growth and next steps.
Skipping warm-ups. Long tones and scales prepare tone and fingers.

days.guide: Your child leads a 10-minute warm-up: long tones, D-to-D scale, toughest phrase from each piece.

questions.q: Why play long tones in a warm-up?
questions.a: They develop steady breath and clear tone.

days.guide: Host the exhibition opening with a 3-minute tour. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.q: What should you tell guests on the tour?
questions.a: The theme, techniques and stories behind a few pieces.

days.guide: Perform the 4-piece concert with introductions and etiquette. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What should you do if you make a mistake?
questions.a: Keep going without stopping.

days.guide: Write a one-page reflection comparing week 1 to now. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How has your drawing changed since week 1?
questions.a: Answer varies; should cite specific skills (value, detail, perspective).

days.guide: Watch the recording, evaluate with the rubric, set two goals. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Write one art goal and one music goal for grade 5.
questions.a: Example: 'Learn to draw in perspective' and 'Learn F and high E on recorder.'

weeks.assessment_key: Concert and exhibition rubric (1–4 each): tone, notes/rhythm, expression, stage etiquette, exhibition tour. Reflection: 4 = specific comparisons in art and music using vocabulary and two goals; 3 = mostly; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.
